#5582. Today's Market Could Be a Win for Veterans Looking To Buy a Home

If you’re a veteran or active-duty service member who’s been hoping to buy a home, you may have more going for you in today’s housing market than you realize.

VA home loans already come with some pretty powerful benefits. But now, with more homes for sale and buyers having more room to negotiate in many markets, those benefits could go even further.

And if you’ve ever heard that buying with a VA loan is harder, takes longer, or puts you at a disadvantage, there’s something else you should know… a lot of what people believe about VA loans simply isn’t true.

Today, nearly 4 million service members and veterans have an active VA home loan. And according to the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), more than 343,000 homes were purchased using VA loan benefits in its most recent reported fiscal year. And it’s easy to see why.

For eligible veterans and service members, VA loans offer advantages that can make buying a home more affordable, including:

No down payment required for many eligible borrowers.

No monthly mortgage insurance, even with no down payment.

Competitive mortgage rates that can help lower monthly payments.

Benefits like this are powerful in any market – and even more so today. That may be why VA loan usage has grown for the last two years in a row.

A few years ago, when homes were getting multiple offers and buyers were competing for nearly every listing, VA buyers sometimes had a harder time getting their offers accepted.

A 2021 survey from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), found 89% of sellers were likely to accept an offer from a buyer using a conventional loan. But only 30% were likely to accept one using an FHA or VA loan.

The reason? Some sellers were concerned that VA financing would take longer, be more difficult to close, and require them to pay more in costs and repairs. But those concerns don’t necessarily reflect how VA loans actually perform.

A white paper from Vetted VA based on 2025 mortgage data busted a lot of VA loan myths:

Myth #1: VA loans get denied more often than other loans.

The Reality: VA loans actually have the lowest denial rate. Just 8.2% of VA purchase applications were denied, compared to 15.0% for conventional loans, 12.8% for FHA loans, and 12.5% for USDA loans.

The Reality: 90% of VA home loan applications that reached underwriting made it to closing, compared to 81% for conventional loans.

The Reality: VA loan appraisals typically take 7–10 business days, similar to conventional and FHA loans.

Myth #4: Sellers have to pay all the closing costs for VA buyers.

The Reality: VA buyers can pay many standard closing costs themselves. Buyers and sellers can also negotiate which eligible costs the seller will cover.

Since there are more homes for sale and fewer buyers competing in many areas, sellers may be more open to different financing options than they were a few years ago. And the opportunity doesn’t stop at getting your offer accepted.

Depending on the house and your local market, you may also be able to negotiate a lower price, ask for repairs, or request help with closing costs.

VA guidelines allow sellers to cover the buyer’s normal closing costs, plus concessions of up to 4% of the home’s value.

Think about what that combination could mean. You may be able to buy with no down payment, avoid mortgage insurance, and negotiate help with some of the other expenses that come with buying a home.

That could mean keeping thousands of dollars in your savings instead of spending them upfront, giving you more breathing room after you get the keys.

#5581. Google’s latest midtier model Gemini 4 Neon is three times faster than Carbon and wins on some metrics

After laying low during the summer while competitors Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC unleashed powerful new frontier models, Google LLC is hitting back.

Having released its latest flagship model Gemini 4 Carbon one month ago, followed by the cost-effective Gemini 4 Hydrogen, it’s now striking a balance between the two with Gemini 4 Neon. Google announced its latest artificial intelligence offering in a blog post today, saying that Neon is a general-purpose model designed to handle complex coding tasks, multistep agentic workflows and analytical reasoning.

Surprisingly, though Carbon is positioned as the company’s strongest model, Neon’s performance surpassed it on some tasks, according to benchmarks the company published today. Google also said Neon completes most tasks about three times as quickly as Carbon at costs of about 60% lower, making it “competitive with the leading models in its class.”

Digging deeper into Google’s benchmarks, the company said Neon outranked the midtier Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol models on tests such as knowledge work, reasoning, automation, multimodal understanding, cybersecurity, science and math.

Those numbers were from Google’s own tests, but independent research by Artificial Analysis shows that Neon achieved an impressive score of 61 on the Intelligence Index, putting it third overall, just behind Anthropic’s most powerful model, Claude Fable 5.2, which scored 65, and OpenAI’s leading model GPT-6.2 Astra, which achieved a score of 62.

Google continues to accelerate its release cadence with Gemini 4 Neon, delivering a small Intelligence gain over Gemini 4 Carbon at a ~17% lower Cost per Task@GoogleDeepMind has released Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth model in just seven weeks. Neon (xhigh) scores 61 on the… pic.twitter.com/L76oKwyxXa

— Artificial Analysis (@ArtificialAnlys) November 18, 2026

With regard to cost, Neon isn’t quite so impressive. Google said it’s priced at a cost of $3 per million input tokens, 15 cents per million cached input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. That means it falls right in between GPT-6.2 Sol, which costs $2 per million input tokens, 10 cents per million cached tokens and $10 per million output tokens, and Claude Opus 5.5, which is priced at $4 per million input tokens, 20 cents per million cached tokens and $20 per million output tokens.

Google’s choice of pricing is interesting because there’s a lot of debate around which model provider can achieve a genuine competitive advantage over its competitors. Given that these midtier models are so comparable in terms of performance, cost efficiency is becoming a more significant factor for enterprise customers. Although Neon appears to edge out GPT-6.2 Sol and Claude Fable 5.2 in terms of its ability to process several important workloads, many organizations might decide that’s not really enough to justify paying more to use it.

#5580. The Housing Market Is on Solid Ground, Even with More Foreclosures

It’s been nearly two decades since the 2008 housing crash, but the word “foreclosure” can still make people uneasy. And if you’re planning a move, you may be wondering if more foreclosures will flood the market with homes for sale – especially if you’ve seen the headlines lately.

Buyers may be hoping for a rush of bargains. Sellers may be bracing for more competition. The latest data points to neither, and knowing why can help you plan your next move with confidence.

Completed foreclosures are up 33% from last year, according to ATTOM. That sounds like a big leap, but context helps.

Even with that increase, foreclosures are still about 26% below where they were in the first half of 2020.

Zoom out further, and today’s activity is a small fraction of what the market saw during the 2008 crash. Lenders completed about 28,000 foreclosures in the first half of 2026, according to ATTOM. Compare that to the crash years in red, when lenders often completed more than 200,000 in the span of a few months (see graph below):

Experts say today’s numbers reflect a housing market that’s still in good shape. As Rob Barber, CEO at ATTOM, explains:

“While some homeowners are still facing financial challenges, overall foreclosure volumes remain well below historical norms and the broader housing market continues to demonstrate resilience.”

And here’s why we can absorb the slight uptick in foreclosures we are seeing.

During the crash, a lot of homeowners either lost their homes to foreclosure or were forced to sell, which left the market overwhelmed with houses for sale. That isn’t happening now.

One way to see this is through months’ supply, which measures how long it would take to sell every home on the market at the current pace. Four to six months is considered balanced.

Right now, it’s about 4.8 months, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). That’s pretty well-balanced, and less than half of where it peaked around the last crash (see graph below):

If foreclosures were really surging, you’d see it in the number of homes for sale. As Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . a surge of actual foreclosures in 2026 would have easily put the inventory data much higher in 2026.”

Equity is a big reason there’s no surge of distressed sales. Data from the Census Bureau and ATTOM shows nearly two in three homeowners have paid off their mortgage or have more than 50% equity. And Cotality says the average homeowner has about $310,000 in equity.

If a homeowner with equity hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house, pay off the loan, and walk away with money in their pocket instead of facing foreclosure. That’s an option many people didn’t have during the crash. According to HousingWire, nearly one in four homes were underwater back in 2010.

Being underwater means owing more on your mortgage than your home is worth, which makes selling a lot harder. Today, just 2% of homeowners are considered seriously underwater (see graph below):

Not every homeowner has that kind of equity, but most do, and that’s what puts a ceiling on how high foreclosures can go.

If rising foreclosures have you questioning where the housing market is headed, the data says it’s in good shape. The supply of homes for sale is balanced, and most homeowners have plenty of equity.Have questions about what you’re seeing online, your local market, or about how much equity you have? Talk to a local real estate agent.

#5579. Planning To Sell in 2027? Start Prepping Now.

If selling your house is on your calendar for 2027, you may be thinking you’ve got plenty of time. Maybe you’re aiming for January. Maybe you’re waiting for spring. Either way, next year probably feels far enough away that getting ready can wait, too.

But waiting until 2027 to sell doesn’t mean waiting until 2027 to get started.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from than they’ve had in years. So, if you want your house to stand out when it’s time to list, a little preparation now can make a big difference later.

As a general rule of thumb, Zillow recommends giving yourself about 2-3 months to get your house ready to list. And that makes sense when you consider that the vast majority of sellers (78%) did at least one home improvement project before their house hit the market.

That gives you plenty of time to decide what to fix, find contractors, get on their schedules, actually make the updates, and get everything ready for photos and showings.

But don’t worry – that doesn’t mean every seller had some big to-do. The most common? Interior painting (see graph below):

That certainly doesn’t mean you need to tackle everything on this list. You may not need to do any of it. But odds are there’s at least one project you’ll want to do. And starting that conversation now gives you a leg up before next year.

While you might have a long list of things you think need updating, that doesn’t mean they’re all worth the time, effort, or money.

An agent will help you figure out which projects deserve a spot on your to-do list based on what buyers want most and what other sellers are doing. That way, you’re not investing in updates that won’t make much of a difference when you sell.

One thing your agent may recommend today is that you go ahead and get a pre-listing inspection. It’s basically your cheatsheet to what a buyer’s inspection may turn up later on.

And now that buyers have more options, they’re pickier – and you don’t want anything popping up in an inspection that could put them off.

For example, you know that HVAC system you’ve been hoping will make it through one more season? Now’s a good time to give it some attention – along with anything else you know needs a little TLC. That way a repair you could’ve handled months ago won’t become a surprise in the middle of your sale.

According to Angi, a pre-listing inspection typically costs $300-600 and that can be money well spent. As the National Association of Realtors (NAR) explains:

“An inspector will be able to give you a good indication of the trouble areas that will stand out to potential buyers, and you’ll be able to make repairs before open houses begin.”

The advantage isn’t just knowing what may come up, but being able to get ahead of it and space out the projects on your own schedule. So you don’t feel stressed during go-time.

But remember, not everything needs to happen right away. Some things are better saved for when you’re closer to listing.

Think deep cleaning, staging, touching up paint, and tidying up the landscaping. Those are the finishing touches that’ll help your house look its best when buyers walk through the door.

But there’s one thing you can start anytime: decluttering. Go ahead and tackle the closets, garage, or storage room you’ve been avoiding. Future you will appreciate having a few less boxes to pack.

The idea isn’t to get everything done today. It’s to spread the work out so you’re not scrambling when listing day arrives. As Redfin puts it:

“Smart preparation leads to a smoother sale, stronger offers, and fewer surprises during closing. . . Homes that are clean, well-staged, priced right, and professionally photographed tend to sell quickly.”

You don't need to spend the rest of the year renovating your house or packing up your life. But you can start making a plan.The earlier you figure out what needs to be done, the more time you'll have to do it right. #5578. A Fixer-Upper Could Be Your Path To Homeownership

When the homes you love keep landing outside your budget, it may be time to look at the ones other buyers skip.

A fixer-upper won’t be the right call for everyone. Plenty of buyers want a home that’s ready on move-in day. But homes that need some updating could get you in the door for a lot less.

More buyers are starting to realize it too. And Danielle Hale, Chief Economist at Realtor.com, explains why:

“Fixer-uppers give buyers a way to break into the housing market at a time when affordability is still stretched thin. For those with the vision. . . fixer-uppers provide both a starting point in the market and the chance to create a home that’s truly their own.”

If that sounds like you, here’s why a fixer-upper could be worth a closer look.

Because these homes need work, they tend to have a lower asking price up front. According to AmeriSave, fixer-uppers usually sell for 20% to 30% less than what they’re worth on the market.

Here’s what that could look like. KCM applied a 25% discount – the middle of that range – to the median home price from the National Association of Realtors (NAR). This is an example, not the average price of a fixer-upper. But it shows the savings could top $100,000 (see graph below):

That’s a big difference up front and it could be what gets you into a home today. And odds are you don’t have to tackle all the repairs at once – you can space them out over time as it works for you.

Just remember repair costs can add up quickly and eat into those savings if you don’t plan ahead. So, before you make an offer, get estimates from a contractor and set a repair budget you’re comfortable with. There are even some loan types designed to help pay for the work.

With a renovation loan, you can roll the cost of the work into your mortgage, so you don’t have to cover it all out of pocket once you move in. Here are a few options from FHA, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the VA (see visual below):

Each program has its own rules, and not every lender offers all of them. So, talk to a trusted lender to see which options are available to you and which make sense for how you plan to tackle updates and repairs over time.

Some cities even offer tax breaks to buyers who renovate a fixer-upper and raise its value. These programs vary by location, so check with your city or a tax professional to see what’s available where you want to live.

If you want to check for more information yourself, go to your local county or city official dot-gov website. Then, use the search bar and look for: [City or County Name] AND “home rehabilitation” OR “property tax incentive” OR “housing repair”

A local agent can also help you find fixer-uppers in the neighborhoods you have your heart set on.

#5577. Balance Theory acquires CISO decision intelligence platform VectorBlack

Cybersecurity investment management company Balance Theory Inc. today announced that it has acquired VectorBlack, a decision intelligence platform for chief information security officers developed by ThreatShare.ai, for an undisclosed sum.

Developed by Jason Lewis, Gerry Eaton and Wayne Schepens, VectorBlack is designed to provide CISOs with timely decision support on emerging threats, industry developments and market trends. The artificial intelligence-driven platform is aimed at anticipating the issues most likely to catch the attention of chief executives and boards, allowing security leaders to raise them before the questions are asked.

Rather than simply aggregating information, VectorBlack is said to show security leaders what has changed in the cybersecurity landscape and why it matters to their organization. Its focus as what the company calls a CISO Strategic Intelligence Platform was shaped by input from security executives, including Ryan Clarque, CISO at Black Rifle Coffee Co. Clarque said having a strategic view ahead of a renewal, budget decision or board discussion “can make all the difference.”

Lewis began developing the underlying technology before teaming up with Eaton, an industry analyst, and Schepens, a cybersecurity entrepreneur who founded public relations firm LaunchTech Communications in 2015.

As part of the deal, Schepens will join Balance Theory as chief cyber market analyst to help shape market strategy and product adoption. Lewis is taking on the role of principal data engineer, leading the continued development and integration of VectorBlack’s technology. Eaton will focus on applying the platform to targeted research and sector-specific intelligence for cybersecurity leaders.

At the core of Balance Theory’s offering is an AI-native platform for cybersecurity investment decisions and execution. Combining program context, proprietary market intelligence and AI agents, the platform is used by security teams to manage more than $1 billion in cybersecurity spending. It claims customers average a first-year return on investment of more than 300%.

VectorBlack’s technology will be integrated into the Balance Theory platform, adding to the market intelligence that already informs customer investment decisions. By tracking market developments, competitive dynamics, emerging technologies and real-world experience with security products, the combined teams are aiming to show CISOs how their own investments are performing, what others in the industry are seeing and where the market is headed.

“VectorBlack will take Balance Theory’s capabilities a step further by delivering tailored intelligence across the security product categories our customers invest in,” said Greg Baker, co-founder and chief executive of Balance Theory. “This creates a powerful new level of insight to inform smarter technology investments and long-term security strategy.”

The company said details on integration and availability will be announced at a later date.

Balance Theory is a venture capital-backed company that raised $19 million in a Series A round led by SYN Ventures in July, with existing investors DataTribe and the Maryland Technology Development Corp. also participating. The round coincided with Accuvant Inc. founder and former Optiv Security Inc. Chief Executive Dan Burns joining Balance Theory as executive chairman. Including a $3 million seed round in 2022, Balance Theory has raised $22 million to date.

#5576. 3 Housing Questions That Might Come Up at Your Next Family Dinner

This time of year usually means more time spent with family and friends. And in recent years, when everyone gets together, the conversation has a way of drifting to housing.

Your uncle is sure home prices are about to crash. Your cousin heard foreclosures are surging. And someone across the table brings up the word “recession.”

If you’ve wondered about any of this yourself, that makes sense. There’s a lot of noise out there. So let’s look at what the data actually shows, so you’ll have real answers the next time it comes up.

Let’s start with your uncle’s crash prediction. The short answer is no. Experts project home prices will keep climbing nationally in 2027.

On average, forecasters expect prices to rise about 1.4% next year (see graph below). That’s slower than the big jumps of a few years ago, but it’s still growth, not a crash.

Prices are dipping in some markets, though. It just depends on where you live. Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), explains why:

“Price declines are occurring mainly in southern states, where there has been robust new home construction in recent years. Given the region’s faster job growth, these price drops should be viewed as temporary and as a second-chance opportunity for those previously priced out of the market.”

So, the dips that are fueling all the social media chatter are limited to select areas, and experts think they’ll be short-lived. It doesn’t mean a crash is looming.

If you’re thinking about moving, look at the numbers for your area.

Then your cousin chimes in about foreclosures. They’ve ticked up lately, but here’s some important context. That’s compared to very low levels. They’re still below where they were before the pandemic, according to ATTOM.

So, why doesn’t today look like 2008? Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . we have had many recessions post-WWII but only one foreclosure crisis. That foreclosure crisis started with a massive credit boom from 2002-2005, and then a credit bust. . . none of that is happening now . . .“

Today’s homeowners also have something a lot of people didn’t have back then – equity. In every state, the average homeowner with a mortgage has more than $100,000 of it, according to Cotality (see map below):

If a homeowner hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house instead of facing foreclosure.

While someone in your family may be convinced a recession is coming, experts don’t agree. The average forecast from The Wall Street Journal’s survey of economists puts the odds at about 24%, so most experts aren’t expecting one. And that’s a good thing.

But even if one hits, history shows a recession doesn’t mean home prices will automatically fall. In 5 of the last 6 recessions, prices actually went up, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) (see graph below):

The one exception was 2008, the only one of these recessions that started in the housing market itself.

So, the next time your uncle predicts a crash or your cousin brings up 2008, you’ll know prices aren’t crashing, foreclosures are still low, and a recession doesn’t automatically spell trouble for housing. If a move in 2027 is on your mind, connect with a local real estate agent to look at what prices are doing in your neighborhood so you can plan with real local numbers, not scary headlines.

#5574. The ‘Twilight’ Home in Forks, WA, Is Hiring a Social Media Manager—and the Job Comes With Complimentary Stays

First, Robert Pattinson was announced as the next James Bond. And now, the original Swan House in Forks, WA, is offering a rare opportunity to work and stay in the storied property.

“We’re looking for someone who genuinely loves Twilight, understands the fandom, and is excited about sharing the story of this very special house and the town of Forks,” the home’s owner, Christine Haning, tells Realtor.com®.

The vacancy was first announced in a Nov. 17 job listing, which calls for a “creative, ‘Twilight’-loving social media manager to help grow Bella Swan House.” The post says the team is looking to hear from anyone who loves “creating Instagram Reels, keeping up with "Twilight" fandom news, dreaming up fun content ideas, and connecting with fellow fans.”

While they’re not necessarily looking for someone with an established platform of their own—or many years of experience—Haning hopes to find someone who shares the same passion for the now-iconic vampire stories. And the paid, part-time, remote opportunity comes along with a major perk: complimentary stays at the house for content creation.

“We’re actually almost completely booked for the next 12 months, and that’s only because we don’t open our calendar any further in advance!” Haning notes. “So, the complimentary stays are a pretty unique perk. Not just because they’re free, but because getting a reservation at the house can be difficult.”

The home is available to book directly on the Swan House website, or through Airbnb. Pricing begins at $400 a night.

Haning explains that certain dates are “intentionally” blocked off throughout the year for “maintenance, photography, and content creation.” These are the times the social media manager will be able to stay at the home and experience its magic firsthand.

“I think being able to actually spend time in the house and explore Forks is such a valuable part of creating authentic content that fans will connect with,” she says.

The historic farmhouse was built in 1905, and while it’s not the St. Helens, OR, home fans may recognize from the films, the Swan House’s connection to the franchise goes back much further.

“One thing I’ve realized since taking ownership of the house and running its social media account is how few people know the history behind the books versus the movies,” Haning adds. “Most fans are familiar with the house in Oregon where the first movie was filmed, but before the movies, there were the books!”

Haning confirmed the abode is the original home that inspired Bella and Charlie Swan’s dwelling in the books—a linkage that’s been recognized by the town of Forks since 2006.

“That literary connection is what makes it so special to me,” says Haning.

Haning says the house has “so much history and character.” She purchased it in June 2025, and has worked to create a “really special blend of the books and films” in the time since.

There’s a yellow kitchen, just like Bella mentions her mom, Renee Dwyer, painted in the books. Haning also decorated one of the three bedrooms with purple bedding and wall art to closely resemble Bella’s room in the films. There's even a cardboard cutout of Edward Cullen to watch you sleep.

Charlie’s dining table makes an appearance, too.

The home sleeps eight, and has a fully-equipped kitchen, as well as a gourmet coffee and tea bar with a waffle breakfast station.

It’s also stocked with all of the “Twilight” DVDs, as well as a record player with the saga’s complete soundtrack collection.

A recent addition includes a display featuring “all the different editions of the ‘Twilight’ books,” which Haning notes includes some “rare, hard-to-find editions and memorabilia.” She says she’s having lots of fun acquiring “little treasures” to add to the home.

“What I love is that it doesn’t feel like a movie set or a themed hotel,” she says. “It’s a real, historic home in the actual town of Forks, filled with little details that fans recognize and appreciate. It brings together the literary history, the visual nostalgia of the films,and the experience of actually being in the place where the story takes place. It’s really the best of both worlds.”

Given Forks’ major role in the series, the home’s central location in the town is a major plus. The Swan House is surrounded by the Olympic Peninsula’s stunning landscape.

“It’s honestly one of the most beautiful places I’ve ever been,” says Haning, adding that the entire town has embraced the world author Stephanie Meyer created.

There are stores with “Twilight” merchandise, the real Forks High School is nearby, and the hospital even has a reserved parking spot for Dr. Carlisle Cullen. And of course, the coastal community and Native American reservation of La Push is “just down the road.”

“It’s such an immersive experience. Sometimes when I’m there, I find myself getting a little bit lost in it all, and the story starts to feel surprisingly real,” Haning gushes. “I’d love to find someone who shares that excitement and can help us bring it to life through creative content.”

Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5573. 3 Things Sellers Need To Know About Pricing Today

If you’re getting ready to sell your house, you’ve probably heard how important it is to price it right. And that’s especially true right now.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from and they’re feeling pinched by today’s mortgage rates. That makes them more selective. And that means having the right pricing strategy matters more than ever.

That starts with understanding these three things. Because, with the right approach, you can still put your house in a great position to sell.

It’s natural to look at what your neighbor’s house sold for and think yours should sell for something similar. And those comparable sales (or comps) absolutely matter. But they only tell part of the story. Here’s why.

Buyers aren’t shopping against what sold three or even six months ago. They’re comparing your house to what’s available right now.

That’s why your agent will look at more than just recent sales. They’ll also consider the houses currently for sale, what’s going under contract, and how your house stacks up against those options to find the right price for your house.

The goal isn’t necessarily to price lower than everyone else. It’s to make sure buyers see the value in choosing your house over the competition.

As Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com explains:

“Pricing to today’s demand is helping homes move and keeping more transactions alive in a high-rate environment.”

Understanding how your house compares to what’s available today can help you feel more confident in your asking price.

Getting your asking price right puts you in a stronger position from the start. But when an offer comes in, remember that price is only one part of the equation.

Today’s buyers may still negotiate on things like money toward closing costs or repairs, even when a house is priced well – and that’s not necessarily a commentary on your price, it’s just the norm for negotiation in today’s market.

According to Redfin, 44.7% of home sales involve seller concessions. That’s just under half. And 15.8% had both a price reduction and a concession.

Now, that doesn’t mean you have to agree to everything a buyer asks for. But sometimes offering a closing-cost credit or helping with a mortgage rate buydown could be what seals the deal. Other times, holding firm is the better move. Your agent will help you decide.

The best advice? Look at the whole offer, including what you’ll actually walk away with, to decide what’s right for you.

Even with a competitive price, some houses take longer to sell than others. And if yours isn’t getting the attention or offers you expected, that doesn’t mean your sale is off track. It just means it’s time to take a closer look at what’s happening.

Your agent can help you use buyer feedback and local market activity to figure out what adjustments, if any, could make a difference.

Are buyers seeing your listing online but not scheduling showings? Maybe the photos or presentation aren’t doing your house justice.

Are people touring but not making offers? It could be the condition, the price, or how your house compares to others they’ve seen.

And if buyers are making offers, but the terms aren’t working for you, that may call for a different negotiation strategy altogether.

While you may worry that means you have to drop your price, that’s not always true. A price cut can help, but only if it addresses what’s keeping buyers from making a move.

That’s why feedback, local competition, and an agent who knows how to interpret both are so important.

Selling successfully today isn't about finding one magic number and hoping everything falls into place. #5572. Enterprises fear AI success more than failure, because success means lock-in they can’t escape

The supercomputing world built its reputation on scientific simulation, but the artificial intelligence infrastructure now filling the same data centers raises a harder question. When models turn data into revenue, control over that data and the intelligence it produces becomes a board-level concern few companies discuss publicly.

A new buyer’s guide sets out to measure that control provider by provider. Sovereignty is not a single checkbox but a stack of control layers that buyers have to examine one at a time, according to Amit Eyal Govrin (pictured), lead analyst for sovereign AI at theCUBE Research and chief executive officer of Agentcy Labs.

“When it comes to sovereignty, it’s all about control,” Govrin said. “And when we have to look at control, there’s a lot of layers to go into it. And the first one is, are you in fact comfortable … ceding that control to somebody else? Are you comfortable being in somebody else’s jurisdiction where they can potentially compel your data if ever required?”

Govrin spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how sovereignty pillars, the U.S. CLOUD Act and incoming European regulation are reshaping the way enterprises choose AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.)

The guide rests on five pillars — territorial, operational, technological, legal and financial. Territory, meaning where data centers sit and where data is hosted, is the pillar most providers get right easily, Govrin explained. The operational layer is murkier, and he pointed to Amazon Web Services Inc. as one example while noting that AWS does run a sovereign region in Brandenburg, Germany, covered by EU citizens.

“You’re in the AWS Frankfurt region as a German customer. Perfectly fine. Are you sovereign because you’re in that region?” Govrin said. “If that region goes down, that PagerDuty may not necessarily go to somebody out of Germany. It may go somewhere else. It may go into Seattle or to Hyderabad for all you know.”

To build the guide, Govrin and his team graded seven hyperscalers across 40 offerings and handed out 117 grades in five regions. The scoring framework uses 17 yes-or-no tests, with legal assessed separately because local laws make it a poor fit for pass or fail, drawing on more than 300 sources and hundreds of buyer interviews. Google LLC’s air-gapped offerings scored relatively well, but the finding that surprised Govrin most applied to every provider.

“No hyperscaler across the board had an answer to the U.S. CLOUD Act,” Govrin said. “Now imagine you’re a European entity or anywhere else outside the world, and now there’s a production order from a U.S. court system that states that this hyperscaler needs to turn over your data. At that point, there is no contest. Your data becomes Uncle Sam’s data.”

“When money’s on the table, you know what happens,” Furrier said. “Everyone fights for it or argues for it. So I think this is a tinderbox moment where one match could blow everything up.”

#5571. Oklahoma City, OK, Struggles With Low Starter Home Availability Compared to Other Cities

A recent metro-by-metro analysis by Realtor.com® reveals where buyers can still find a starter home. For many would-be homeowners, these options have felt increasingly scarce as rising prices and climbing mortgage rates compound affordability challenges.

Furthermore, research from economists supports this trend. Nationally, the share of starter homes in active inventory fell from 38.1% in August 2019 to 36.2% in August 2026. During that same period, starter home prices rose 30.8%, from roughly $260,000 to $340,000.

As a result, some markets like Oklahoma City have experienced a downturn in available starter homes in recent years.

A starter home is typically defined as a property priced at roughly 80% of a metro's median list price. This captures the relative affordability of homes at the lower end of a local market. These homes are generally smaller and less expensive, making them accessible to a first-time buyer or a household with an Income at or below the area median.

In Oklahoma City, OK, the share of starter homes has seen a steady decline. The portion of these homes was 34.8% in 2019, which then decreased to 33.1% in 2022. As of 2026, the share has fallen further to 31.4%.

Therefore, this represents a total decrease of 3.4 percentage points between 2019 and 2026. This trend indicates a shrinking market for entry-level homes in the area, presenting a challenge for new buyers.

For those weighing the decision of renting or buying, current data suggests that renting is the more financially prudent choice for now. A July Rent Report from Realtor.com found that the cost of buying a starter home in the 50 largest metros was $858 higher per month than renting one. This 50.6% premium on homeownership makes renting the more affordable option across all 50 of the largest metros.

In Oklahoma City, OK, this trend holds, offering a clear financial advantage to renters. The median rent for an apartment was $915 as of July 2026.

Moreover, the local rental market has seen prices decrease by 1.50% year-over-year, making it an even more attractive alternative to purchasing a home with a significant down payment. (A rent vs. buy calculator can help individuals assess their personal financial situation.)

#5570. Sovereignty is the AI story everyone mentions and few have planned for ahead of 2027

AI infrastructure economics are entering a more sober phase as enterprises move past standing up AI factories and start asking how to run them profitably. Durability, real demand and long-term value are now the tests separating lasting providers from the froth.

That shift rewards cloud providers with an operating track record rather than a single speculative wager. Vultr has extended its global cloud to AI with chips from Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. Enterprises are now making a flight to quality toward stable, cost-efficient platforms, according to Kevin Cochrane (pictured), chief marketing officer of Vultr.

“We’re seeing now not speculative bets in the buildout of AI infrastructure. We’re seeing real bets based on proven economics, proven ROI that people are looking to achieve,” Cochrane said. “What I think is going to wind up happening is a maturation of our industry leveraging this open stack.”

Cochrane spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI infrastructure economics favor a global footprint and why sovereignty requirements reach well beyond national governments. (* Disclosure below.)

Vultr now operates 34 cloud data center regions, the latest a new region in Chennai, India. That footprint was built to keep cloud-native applications close to users, and inference follows the same logic, Cochrane explained. Agents make fast turns back to reasoning models, so CPUs and GPUs must sit together near the edge, he noted.

“This is kind of what Vultr was built for, which is one global platform, not isolated islands of data centers that are serving a bespoke customer. It is a true global cloud platform,” Cochrane said.

Sovereignty adds another constraint, and it reaches well beyond national governments. A global insurer tuning an open-source model for credit risk needs training clusters in each country because the underlying data cannot cross borders, Cochrane noted. Regulators are already tightening the rules, as the U.S. Commerce Department’s new curbs on remote chip access show.

“The way you have to post-train a model for credit risk in the U.K. versus Germany versus Singapore versus the United States, it’s going to be different,” Cochrane said. “It uses different data.”

"Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" star Dorit Kemsley has revealed she has moved into a new property after she and her estranged husband, PK Kemsley, were "ordered" to list their longtime Los Angeles mansion following a prolonged legal dispute during which the businessman admitted they were experiencing a "financial crisis."

While attending the Maison D’Or cocktail launch at The Sun Rose West Hollywood, Dorit told Page Six that she and her children, Jagger, 12, and Phoenix, 10, have found a new place to call home.

“As everyone knows, we were going to court to be evicted by a certain date, which is pretty crummy, but I did find another house. The kids and I are moving into a new home imminently. Fresh beginnings, fresh start. We are all welcoming it," she told the outlet.

Dorit, 50, and PK, 58, are embroiled in a contentious divorce that has been exacerbated by significant monetary woes, including the looming threat of foreclosure on their $7 million Encino, CA, home.

In July, PK requested a judge allow him to sell the property while accusing the reality TV star of leaving their children with her parents in Florida—while providing no information about when she plans to return to the U.S., while he has been left to fight for their home alone.

PK alleged that Dorit was gone for a "minimum of three weeks," per court documents seen by the New York Post, stating that her "extended trip" demonstrates her "prioritization of personal travel over addressing the urgent financial crisis facing [their] family home."

In August, TMZ reported that PK's wish was granted after a judge ordered the sale of the six-bedroom, 10-bathroom Los Angeles abode, while noting that the TV personality had to move out by November.

According to the outlet, a hearing was held on Aug. 26, when PK alleged that Dorit had not been paying the mortgage on the home.

Meanwhile, Dorit, who is being represented by lawyer Samantha Spector, claimed that PK should be paying the bills, adding that he has enough money to cover the debt as well.

The back and forth between the acrimonious exes continued when PK accused Dorit of delaying the home's listing, while she alleged that he had refused to sign an agreement with celebrity real estate agent Zach Goldsmith of The Agency, whom Dorit said she hired to help market the property.

Goldsmith has loose ties to the "Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" world. Not only does he work for Kyle Richards' estranged husband, Mauricio Umansky, he is also expecting a baby with the reality TV star's daughter Farrah Aldjufrie.

Neither PK nor Dorit will be able to delay the sale any longer after a judge determined that the property must be listed, with Goldsmith as the agent, while also ruling that PK should become a manager of the LLC through which they bought the dwelling to ensure a swift sale.

The judge also ruled that Dorit will have to cover the cost of utilities, as well as the past-due amounts.

Meanwhile, PK was ordered to pay the mortgage until Dorit moves out. However, he will be reimbursed for all the payments made using any profits from the sale.

The businessman will also get back the funds he put into the home following their split. The judge denied his request for sanctions.

It marked the latest in what has been a very ugly separation battle between the two reality TV stars.

Just last month, Dorit came under fire from PK when she jetted off on a lavish European vacation, during which she celebrated her 50th birthday in true style, enjoying a lavish lunch alongside Hermès executive Michael Coste.

Dorit's European getaway infuriated her estranged spouse, who filed legal documents on July 13 in which he slammed his former partner for taking the trip while they are still going through a "financial crisis."

The home has come close to hitting the foreclosure auction block in recent months. However, each planned sale was postponed, according to reports—although PK's legal team noted in its filing that the risk of their losing the dwelling has "escalated" significantly.

He further claimed in the filing that he stopped the property from falling into foreclosure after splashing out $300,000.

PK alleged that Dorit has not made any mortgage payments, despite raking in a substantial income from "The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" and spending what he estimates to be $1 million on luxury getaways and designer clothing.

PK argued that she has put her travel plans ahead of the family's financial troubles, requesting that the court allow him to move forward with selling the property.

Dorit filed for divorce from PK in 2025 after 10 years of marriage, citing "irreconcilable differences."

At the time, she asked the judge to award her sole custody of their kids, in addition to spousal support.

The filing came just one day after PK was photographed sharing a kiss with Shana Wall.

One month after Dorit filed for divorce, PK requested joint custody of their children, while also waiving his right to spousal support and asking the court to do the same for Dorit's plea.

They announced their separation in May 2024 in a joint statement: "We have had our struggles over the last few years and continue to work through them as two people who love each other and share two amazing children together. They reduced their asking price to $7.99 million a few weeks later, before whipping the home off the market altogether.

#5568. Metano launches with $12M to help enterprises secure AI agents

Artificial intelligence agent security startup Metano Inc. today launched with $12 million in funding to help enterprises secure AI agents across endpoints, cloud infrastructure and software-as-a-service applications.

Metano’s platform is aimed at giving enterprises consistent visibility and control over AI agents, bringing together agent discovery, context-aware threat detection and real-time enforcement in a single layer.

It’s seeking to address the issue wherein security teams face a growing and fragmented attack surface as organizations deploy AI agents across devices, coding environments, cloud infrastructure and SaaS applications. Metano argues that existing security products protect individual infrastructure layers but lack the visibility and behavioral context needed to secure autonomous agents operating across them.

Making the problem harder is that AI agents, which often run with legitimate credentials and approved tools, can make decisions and take actions dynamically. Instructions, external content and operating conditions can all change how an agent behaves, according to Metano, introducing risks that may not be apparent during initial testing.

“Traditional security tools weren’t designed for AI agents that can make decisions and change their behavior as they operate,” Chief Executive Neelima Rustagi explained.

The first part of Metano’s offering is discovery, with the platform identifying approved and unapproved AI agents, Model Context Protocol servers, skills and software packages, along with their access privileges and potential security exposure.

The second part is Hive, Metano’s real-time context graph, which connects agent tasks, identities, tools, data access and actions. By analyzing activity across an entire session, Hive identifies suspicious behavior and determines whether an agent’s actions align with its intended purpose, allowing security teams to understand why an agent’s behavior may pose a risk.

Metano also offers enforcement as the third part of its platform, placing security controls wherever agents operate. Security teams are given centrally managed policies and guardrails to stop dangerous actions as they occur, even when an agent’s activity may bypass traditional network gateways.

The platform’s detections draw on research from MARS Labs, Metano’s own AI security research team. Malicious skills, compromised software dependencies and vulnerabilities in MCP connections are among the threats the group investigates. The company says its agent detections are mapped to MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications.

Rustagi co-founded the company with Chief Technology Officer Ratnesh Pandey. The Metano team also brings security experience from ServiceNow Inc., Zscaler Inc., Palo Alto Networks Inc., FireEye Inc. and Microsoft Corp.

Among the companies already using the platform is data engineering firm Streamvector Inc., which does business as Sigmoid. Srivatsa Ramarao, Sigmoid’s chief information security officer, said Metano has helped Sigmoid adopt AI securely while minimizing shadow risks, allowing it to “say yes to AI across the business.”

Sierra Ventures led the seed round, with Correlation Ventures, High Alpha and 360 ONE also participating. According to Mark Fernandes, managing partner at Sierra Ventures, every platform shift in security produces a few companies that “own the new control point,” with agents representing one of the biggest disruptions he has seen.

Metano’s platform is generally available now, and the company claims security teams can begin using it in under 30 minutes. Also on offer is a free Eval Edition, which provides 30 days of real-time agent scanning so security teams can identify agent activity, risky configurations and potential exposure in their own environments. Metano has completed a SOC 2 Type 2 examination and holds ISO 27001:2022 certification, along with a listing on Okta Inc.’s Okta Integration Network.

The LIT price took a hit on yesterday’s exploit news, dropping more than 20% to $2.50. However, the team’s response and USDC fund recovery have seen the price recover to just under $3, surging +10% over the past 24 hours.

On November 16, 2026, Lighter, the high-performance decentralized perpetuals exchange that settles on Ethereum with zero-knowledge proofs, activated Guardian mode and paused all withdrawals and new pool creation.

On-chain data showed roughly $10.39M in USDC leaving the platform’s Ethereum settlement contract in a single withdrawal. Some researchers put the total impact closer to $15.5M across two large market-maker accounts. The attacker used a leaked API key tied to a trader’s account. The root cause was insecure custom signing code that reused cryptographic nonces, allowing the attacker to reconstruct the private key from public signatures.

With the key, the attacker created a public pool from the compromised account, acquired most of its shares, moved the victim’s USDC into the pool, and redeemed it. Importantly, Lighter’s core protocol and smart contracts were never compromised; this was an account-level key compromise, not a smart-contract exploit. Funds were rapidly swapped into ETH, with portions routed to Hyperliquid. LIT initially dropped by 20% on the news before buyers stepped in.

Lighter moved fast. Within hours, the team publicly confirmed the cause, named the attacker wallet, and made clear that the protocol itself remained intact. The Security Council recovered approximately $5M in USDC and returned it to the affected trader. Guardian mode was deactivated the same day and withdrawals resumed. New safeguards followed immediately: wallet signatures are now required for transfers into public pools, API key signatures are non-public, IP allowlists are planned, per-key permission limits are in place, and automated monitoring for nonce reuse is active.

Users running custom or third-party signing software were strongly advised to rotate keys and switch to Lighter’s official SDKs. The message was clear: the platform treated the incident as a user-key hygiene issue and hardened the surrounding controls without ever having a core vulnerability.

That combination of transparent communication, partial recovery, rapid resumption of operations, and concrete security upgrades is exactly the kind of response that historically flips sentiment from fear to “they handled it cleanly.”

#5565. 2026 BCDA Merit: Ballston Duplex

At the outset of this project, Arlington County zoning permitted only single-family homes on the intended site, despite growing demand for missing middle housing in transit-rich, sought-after urban areas. The project would ultimately become a duplex with two stylish, fully independent homes.

The team at Teass \ Warren recognized the simultaneous opportunity for innovative design, while effecting meaningful change on a larger scale. The project proceeded through a complex approvals process that spanned two years.

#5563. Exclusive: Fig Security partners with Elastic to show how data changes affect detection coverage

Security operations startup Fig Security Inc. today announced an integration partnership with Elastic N.V. that it says gives security teams visibility into how data changes affect their detection coverage.

The partnership sees Fig’s capabilities for mapping detection dependencies now integrating with Elastic Security, the open security operations platform from Elastic. The platform offers prebuilt integrations and detection rules to establish coverage from day one, with Fig claimed to help security operations engineers safeguard that coverage as their environments evolve.

Detection rules are dependent on data arriving in the structure they expect, including the fields and values needed to identify suspicious activity. According to Fig, those dependencies can break when changes are made in tools that the security team does not own. The resulting problem, which Fig calls drift, leaves rules active while the data feeding them is missing the information needed to catch an attack.

Once connected through a read-only application programming interface key, Fig’s Security Data Lineage feature maps an Elastic environment’s sources through pipelines, mappings and fields to the detection rules that use them. Any change to a source, pipeline or mapping is said to have Fig identify the affected detections, along with a suggested repair.

“Elastic gives security teams control over their data, and Fig gives them control over the engineering around it,” said Gal Shafir, co-founder and chief executive of Fig, who previously led global security architecture for Google Cloud Security. Teams are able to test each change against their own environment, he said, before shipping it as code.

Environments “never stop changing,” according to Jamie Hynds, director of product at Elastic, who said Fig traces those changes to the detection rules that depend on them so that SecOps teams can maintain their coverage.

Fig also works alongside Elastic’s Automatic Import and AI Agent, two features designed to help teams build new integrations and custom rules as their requirements grow. Changes tested in Fig against the organization’s own data can then be shipped as code using continuous integration and continuous delivery, with version control and one-click rollback included.

The integration is also aimed at organizations moving to Elastic Security from another security information and event management platform. After Elastic’s Automatic Migration has translated their existing detection rules, Fig checks each translated rule against the data available in Elastic ahead of cutover. Rules that need rework are flagged, with a recommended fix for each.

Founded in 2025 by Shafir, Nir Loya Dahan and Roy Haimof, Fig launched in March with $38 million in seed and Series A funding from Team8 and Ten Eleven Ventures. The company added an AI agent and software-style deployment tools to its platform in July.

The Fig and Elastic integration is available now, with demonstrations offered through Fig’s website.

#5558. Florida Homes Are Flooding in the Dry Season—and Too Many Owners Are Unprepared

The Sunshine State is facing an unusual bout of heavy rain and flooding in the middle of its dry season, which usually begins in November.

The unexpected weather has put pressure on drainage systems and left standing water in many communities, particularly those in South Florida’s Broward County and along Central Florida’s Atlantic Coast in places like Daytona Beach and Cape Canaveral.

On Nov. 18, the western part of Broward County faced what meteorologists refer to as a “rain bomb.” In just 24 hours, West Hollywood received over 15 inches of rain, while surrounding neighborhoods saw about 10 inches.

Due to the severity of the situation, which has led to issues such as stranded cars and out-of-service traffic signals, Broward County and Hollywood declared states of emergency, with Hollywood officials encouraging residents to shelter in place and avoid unnecessary travel.

Forecasters expect additional rainfall through the end of this week as well as 2 to 4 inches across Eastern Florida, with about 4 to 8 inches from Miami to Jacksonville between Tuesday and Friday. Some areas may even get hit with up to 12 inches.

While the wet and windy conditions are expected to improve, the Southeast may see a cooler, rainier Thanksgiving this year. The rain could linger from the upper coast of Texas toward the southern Atlantic Coast throughout the holiday weekend.

“The dry season doesn’t mean your house is in the clear. Florida is currently showing us that heavy rain can flood homes miles from the beach,” says John Espenschied, owner at InsuranceBrokers.com in O'Fallon, MO.

If you’re a Florida homeowner, these unexpected weather conditions are a reminder that flooding may occur year-round—even outside of the traditional summer, hurricane season.

They can also give you a nudge to review your home insurance policy as it relates to flooding and take precautionary steps to protect your property and loved ones.

Florida’s current flooding is drawing attention to the fact that many homeowners do not have enough insurance coverage to recover from the damage.

The Realtor.com® 2026 Housing and Climate Risk Report highlights the financial consequences. It found that over 6% of U.S. homes face severe flood risk, representing almost $3.4 trillion in property value.

At the same time, the number of active flood insurance policies from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) fell by 4.5% between May 2025 and May 2026, decreasing from 3.62 million to 3.45 million.

And the issue goes beyond coastal communities.

Moody's U.S. flood risk analysis, which accounts for flooding from heavy rain and overflowing rivers rather than just coastal storms, found that potential uninsured residential flood losses could exceed $375 billion in a modeled 1-in-100-year flood scenario. This may result in a national insurance protection gap of 65%.

According to Chris Bacon, chief operating officer of Openly in Boston, there are four primary factors that explain why many homeowners are lacking adequate flood protection.

First, most homeowners do not live in the highest-risk flood zones, so they don’t consider it a significant peril. Second, the cost of flood insurance can be high, especially for homeowners in higher-risk flood zones.

“The additional cost can be a constraint of homeowners’ budgets, and thus they choose to not purchase the coverage,” explains Bacon.

Third, mortgage companies do not require flood coverage unless the home is located in a high flood risk zone, so homeowners simply skip it to save money. Finally, the coverage from the NFIP, which goes up to only $250,000, is often lower than what a consumer needs should there be a major loss.

While there are private flood providers that can cover higher limits, premiums can be significantly higher because pricing reflects each property’s individual flood risk.

“That’s why working with an independent insurance agent is so critical. They can provide the right coverage advice and show multiple options so you can make an informed decision for your unique situation,” Bacon adds.

If you own a home in Florida (or any other state where flooding may occur), take a close look at your home insurance coverage. Determine whether it covers water that rises from the street or yard. Unfortunately, most policies don’t.

In the event you don’t have flooding insurance, get quotes from both the NFIP and private insurers.

“The federal program caps building coverage at $250,000. You can buy up to $100,000 in separate coverage for your belongings. If your home would cost $400,000 to rebuild, ask what it would cost to insure the extra $150,000,” adds Espenschied

Don’t forget to compare deductibles and start dates, and remember that federal coverage usually takes 30 days to kick in.

John Dickson, president and CEO at Aon Edge, a private flood insurance provider based in Kalispell, MT, points out that deciding whether to purchase flood insurance is a question of values.

“When you get a picture of how much you can lose, choosing to purchase flood insurance becomes an easy decision,” Dickson explains.

Fortunately, there are a number of precautions you can take to reduce the risk of serious flood damage on your property.

“Keep gutters clear of debris, and remove or clear debris blocking nearby storm drains and install a sewer backflow check valve,” says Bacon.

If you have a basement, elevate HVAC equipment, electrical panels, and water heaters above expected flood levels where possible.

Outside of your home, grade soil away from the foundation and extend downspouts to improve drainage. Finally, keep sandbags or flood barriers on hand, and know your evacuation routes.

If you have a swimming pool, proper pool preparation is key. Avoid draining the pool completely, as hydrostatic pressure from waterlogged soil can cause the pool shell to pop out of the ground.

“Instead, lower the water level slightly (no more than 1 to 2 feet) to allow room for heavy rainfall, turn off power to the pool equipment at the breaker, and secure or store loose pool furniture and equipment inside to prevent severe damage,” Bacon explains.

To protect personal property, particularly high-value, irreplaceable, and sentimental items, move them off ground-level floors and store them on upper levels or high shelves. Keep important documents, family heirlooms, and electronics in sealed, waterproof containers, and create digital backups of critical financial and personal records.

For furniture or heavier items that must remain on the ground level, use blocks or risers to elevate them above potential floodwater lines before severe weather arrives.

“None of these steps eliminates risk, but together they reduce damage and help lead to faster recovery,” adds Bacon.

#5557. Nodal Networks raises $11.3M to solve global shipping bottlenecks

Nodal Networks Inc., a company that builds artificial intelligence decision networks to manage the world’s shipping container terminals, announced today that it has raised $11.3 million in seed funding to help port and rail hubs reduce congestion and move more cargo.

Freight networks move more than a billion shipping containers per year. They carry everything from clothing, electronics, furniture, raw materials for construction and perishable goods – the things that people rely on every day.

However, according to Sea-Intelligence Pte. Ltd., a Copenhagen-based shipping consulting and data analytics company, in September only half of the world’s container ships arrived on time and the late ones were a week behind. Oftentimes, ships can spend nearly half their time at port not working cargo.

Nodal Networks believes the solution is better management, not new infrastructure, which will be key to providing better terminal capacity.

“Watching ports through Earth-observation satellites, I started to see transport as a physical internet: Containers are the data packets, ports and rail yards are the routers, and congestion is the lag,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Paul Albert-Lebrun. “So, we went looking for the routers. We spent eight months in ports, terminals and rail yards, and even sailed the North Sea aboard a container ship, learning the work from the people who do it.”

Albert-Lebrun worked in satellite operations and later led product at Kepler Communications Inc., a space telecom company. Co-founder and Chief Commercial Officer Nic Westgate, by contrast, comes from mining engineering, approaching the problem from the opposite end.

Together, they combined their expertise in Malcom, the company’s AI-powered platform for improving terminal operations, named after Malcom McLean, a North Carolina truck driver turned entrepreneur who pioneered modern container shipping.

The AI platform combines agents with specialized forecasting models that can see, understand and predict incoming shipments, timing and offloading metrics to follow congestion, track lost productivity and make better-informed decisions about container placement, equipment allocation and loading operations. The company said it’s already deployed in terminals across three continents but did not provide details on which locations.

“There’s a lot of noise about AI in our industry right now, and I see a new company pitching terminals almost every week,” said Peter Levesque, an adviser to Nodal and former president of Ports America Inc. and CEO of CMA CGM North America LLC. “Most bring a general-purpose tool and look for somewhere to apply it, and few can answer the question every operator asks: what’s the return? Nodal got into the details, surrounded itself with the right people and kept the customer’s bottom line at the center of everything.”

Levesque added that Nodal has proven itself in terminal after terminal by showing measurable results.

According to Nodal, Malcom has already reduced truck time by one-half in one terminal after operators reassigned yard equipment. At another terminal, ship loading and unloading speeded up by 5% after the team pinpointed what kept cranes waiting for containers. In both cases, the company said Malcom helped operators identify which decisions would have the greatest impact.

The company said it would use the new funding to expand Malcom’s reach to more terminals within the groups Nodal already works with, support new customers and advance product development. It also intends to extend Malcom beyond the terminal, adding planning for shipping lines, railroads and trucking companies, becoming support for transportation networks where operators work together to exchange information.

#5556. Resident of Collapsed Brooklyn Building Sues for Negligence After Losing $100K Record Collection

The first of what is likely to be several lawsuits was filed in Kings County Superior Court on Monday, alleging widespread negligence by a host of landlords, construction companies, and contractors in last week's deadly Brooklyn building collapse.

Dengane Omari Jack lived at 1321 Flatbush Ave., which collapsed last Wednesday, tragically killing eight people and wounding 18 more. Jack was at work at the time of the collapse, but he rushed home to see if his extensive reggae vinyl record collection, valued at $100,000, might be salvaged. It was a total loss.

"He was one of the lucky ones," a friend wrote on a GoFundMe campaign to support Jack. "But surviving came at an unimaginable cost: in a matter of seconds, he lost his home, everything he owned, and a lifetime's worth of memories and work."

Now, Jack is suing his landlord and management company, as well as a half-dozen companies affiliated with 2625 Bedford Ave., the lot adjacent to his Flatbush building. None of those entities has filed a response to the complaint yet in court.

The suit alleges the building's owner, Isolag Realty Group, and the property manager, Olufemi Falade, failed to take action after he pointed out cracks in the facade of 1321 Flatbush Ave. earlier this year.

According to the lawsuit: “During October 2026, Plaintiff observed cracks at or near the Building's entrance, photographed those cracks, and reported the condition to the landlord or management responsible for the Building.”

The suit goes on to allege that Falade “personally received or responded to the report of the cracks on behalf of the Building's ownership or management. Plaintiff was falsely told, in substance, that the condition was not the landlord's fault or could not be fixed.”

Falade has appeared on the city's "Worst Landlord" watch list, put out by the city's Public Advocate office, six times in the past decade.

Jack’s suit also names several entities tied to 2625 Bedford Ave., the adjacent lot where excavation work was taking place at the time of the building collapse.

Those defendants include general contractor Townhouse Builders, d/b/a Promont; New Jersey–based LMW Engineering Group and its president, Jieming Wang; W6 Facility X, an LLC affiliated with Robert Fischman; and LLCs affiliated with lot owners Faigy Fischman and Judy Swimer.

The suit points to a pre-construction survey commissioned by the builders, which documented that the facade of 1321 Flatbush Ave. was in "poor" condition prior to the excavation.

"The Defendants, who were responsible for excavation, design, supervision, inspections and monitoring received, or in the exercise of reasonable care, should have obtained and considered, the Pre-Construction Survey to evaluate all relevant Pre-Construction Site Conditions and, in particular, the Building's condition and its need for support and protection before proceeding with work at the Construction Site," the suit alleges.

Furthermore, the suit says the defendants "had actual notice through the surveys, reports, observations or complaints applicable to their respective work, or constructive notice because the conditions were discoverable through the inspections and monitoring they were required to perform."

The suit also claims that "the excavation, inadequate structural protection, negligent engineering orinspection services, and failure to address the Building's developing dangerous conditionproximately and/or substantially caused the Building to collapse, causing Plaintiff's losses."

The 2625 Bedford Ave. construction project had a history of safety violations noted by the Department of Buildings. The demolition of a building that had previously been on the site was halted in March of this year after demolition contractor N Tech Design of America had failed to take proper safety precautions, including installing netting and putting up sidewalk shields, records show.

A month later, inspectors returned to the site and found that the demolition had gone ahead anyway, in defiance of the stop-work order, according to city records. A $10,000 fine was issued.

In May, a city inspector issued additional citations and another stop-work order against the contractors for allegedly failing to ensure adequate protections of neighboring buildings and for deviating from approved construction plans. Within a week, the city lifted that stop-work order.

Jack is suing for compensatory damages, rent relief, and punitive and exemplary damages.

In an interview with Gothamist, he valued his lost record collection at more than $100,000.

“ Nobody has contacted me from the city for, like, ‘We found some stuff that is still usable.’ I didn't hear anything like that,” Jack told the outlet. “And I don't know who to reach out to either.”

Thankfully, he'd been transferring many of his vinyl treasures into digital files prior to the collapse and had his hard drive with him at work when the building fell.

“ Every single day I was just backing up stuff. I don't know if it's intuition was telling me to do this. But I was doing it every day for the past week,” he added.

The GoFundMe to support Jack, who DJs under the name Roots Outernational, has raised more than $12,000 so far.

Last week, hours after the collapse, Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez opened a criminal inquiry into the collapse. No charges have been filed yet.

In a statement late Wednesday, DOB Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said that the department was working with law enforcement in the ongoing investigation.

"The Department of Buildings is doing everything we can to understand exactly how this collapse occurred, so that the responsible parties can be held to account," said Tigani.

Tigani also revealed that neighboring 1323 Flatbush Ave., which was heavily damaged in the collapse, was unsalvageable and would have to be brought down in a controlled demolition.

Realtor.com® has reached out to Townhouse Builders, LMW Engineering, Jack, and Jack's lawfirm, Antin, Ehrlich & Epstein LLP, for comment. Isolag Realty Group and Falade were not immediately reachable for comment.

#5554. How Will Amendment 3 Affect Florida Real Estate Sales? Experts Weigh in

(TNS)—Sweeping property tax cuts are on the horizon for some Florida homeowners following the passage of Amendment 3.

The measure will raise the statewide homestead exemption to $250,000 over the next two years. It will also place stricter limits on tax increases for all other properties.

But will it give Florida’s real estate market a leg up during tough economic times? Industry leaders are divided, with most taking a wait-and-see approach.

The total number of homes sold in the Tampa Bay metro area is down about 5.2% compared to this time last year. That’s according to the latest statistics from the Suncoast Tampa Association of Realtors.

Related: Before the election, data showed there was not a strong case for either the measure passing or failing.

Some real estate agents are urging out-of-state buyers to move before the end of the year to lock in tax savings. Anyone who moves after 2026 will have to wait five years to receive the full homestead exemption.

Corina Lessa Silva, president of the Suncoast Tampa Association of Realtors, said she’s not expecting a dramatic bump in sales over the next couple of months. You don’t have to buy a home to establish residency, she said; renting works, too.

Still, “If a big piece of that monthly payment—which is property tax—is going to be lowered…it could help more people get into homes in the long term,” Lessa Silva said.

Savings will vary widely. The nonpartisan nonprofit Florida Tax Watch estimates that by 2028, homestead property owners could save an average of $1,133 in Hillsborough County, $956 in Pinellas and $1,150 in Pasco.

For renters trying to break into the housing market, those savings probably aren’t enough to make up for the other costs of homeownership, said Lei Wedge, an assistant professor of finance at the University of South Florida’s Muma College of Business.

Freddie Mac pegs the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at a steep 7.18%. The median price for a home in Tampa Bay is about $400,000, according to the Suncoast Tampa Association of Realtors.

“Just because your future property tax will be cheaper, it does not help you with your down payment right now,” said Wedge.

Though most of the focus has been on single-family homeowners, commercial property owners are bracing for major changes, too.

Bowen Arnold, principal of Tampa-based DDA Development, said in the past 3 or 4 years, he’s seen the taxes on commercial properties he owns shoot up more than 10% in some cases.

Under the new rules, local property appraisers cannot increase the assessed value of non-homestead properties by more than 5% per year.

But don’t expect to see a spike in commercial sales as a result, said Andrew Frey, a managing director at the commercial real estate firm JLL.

“This will be of zero benefit for the buyers, it’s just a windfall for the current owners,” he said.

The biggest question hanging in the air is how local governments will fill major funding gaps caused by these tax cuts.

One solution might be by increasing the millage rate used to calculate our tax bills. That would end up canceling out some of the savings promised to homesteaded property owners, while raising everyone else’s taxes in the process, Wedge said.

Developers could also end up shouldering greater costs if cities decide to charge higher impact fees or raise the cost of construction permits, said Arnold.

All this uncertainty could put a damper on commercial markets, said Frey. “Investors like predictability. It could cause investors to push pause for a while until these things are sorted out.”
