#5483. Coinbase Brings ChatGPT Into Crypto Trading as Pancake Rebrand Signals Binance Rivalry

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Coinbase is bringing crypto trading directly into ChatGPT as competition for AI-powered financial services intensifies. Meanwhile, PancakeSwap has dropped “Swap” from its name, expanding beyond decentralized trading. The two developments show how Coinbase and Binance-linked crypto projects are positioning themselves for the next phase of digital finance.

Coinbase announced its ChatGPT integration yesterday, allowing users to connect accounts and manage portfolios. Users can check balances, analyze holdings, and place eligible trades using everyday language. And every order requires explicit approval before execution.

The timing coincides with Pancake’s attempt to reposition itself beyond its original decentralized exchange business.

Trade Base assets from ChatGPT@ChatGPT now connects to your Coinbase account, so you can trade Base assets in chat pic.twitter.com/tg9r2Iv3Qe

The Coinbase plugin allows eligible users to trade crypto and equities without leaving ChatGPT. Users can request market or limit orders through conversational instructions.

Before execution, ChatGPT displays an interactive confirmation card showing order details. Users must approve the transaction before Coinbase processes it through its Advanced Trade platform. Standard trading fees, eligibility requirements, and account limits still apply.

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong described the integration as another step toward an emerging agentic economy. The idea involves AI assistants handling increasingly complex financial tasks for users. But Coinbase still keeps humans responsible for approving individual trades for now.

To decentralize AI and preserve freedom, we need a coordination layer: a market economy where agents communicate and cooperate through prices.Teams of specialized open-weight models can outperform frontier models, just as a team of skilled people can outperform any single…

The integration also builds on Coinbase’s AI infrastructure. Its Coinbase for Agents toolkit provides developers with connections to trading accounts and market data. The ChatGPT launch brings those capabilities into a more accessible consumer interface.

As of today, the official integration currently remains limited to eligible U.S. Coinbase users. It also depends on ChatGPT account and workspace availability.

new brand, who dis?PancakeSwap is now Pancake 🥞6 years ago we were known for one thing. Today, we’re More Than a Swap. Let us reintroduce ourselves 👇 pic.twitter.com/J3P7Mocu2P

While Coinbase expands through ChatGPT, Pancake is changing how users perceive its decentralized trading ecosystem. Formerly known as PancakeSwap, the platform announced its rebrand today. The new identity reflects six years of expansion beyond its original token-swapping business.

Pancake now operates across more than 11 blockchain networks. The platform reports over 208 million users and more than $4.4 trillion in cumulative trading volume.

Its services now include perpetual contracts, tokenized stocks, ETFs, yield products, and developer infrastructure. The project is also preparing a dedicated mobile application. Its CAKE ticker and contract address remain unchanged, with existing staking positions unaffected.

Pancake’s relationship with Binance makes this rebrand interesting. Binance Labs announced a strategic investment in CAKE in June 2022. The investment supported the decentralized exchange’s development within the BNB Chain ecosystem.

The rivalry becomes clearer when looking beyond the latest announcements. Binance has already introduced its own AI infrastructure through Binance Agent OS. Launched in August 2026, the platform connects compatible AI applications with Binance trading, market data, wallet, and payment capabilities.

Its Model Context Protocol server supports compatible AI agents, including ChatGPT. Developers can build applications that access supported Binance services through user-controlled permissions.

Pancake is also developing its position in this emerging market. In July, the platform partnered with BNB Chain’s Agent Studio to help developers deploy autonomous agents.

These agents can interact with Pancake’s liquidity pools, rebalance positions, and execute trading strategies. Its AI tools also include portfolio planning and assistance across DeFi products.

This creates an interesting contrast between the two ecosystems. Coinbase is bringing AI-powered trading directly to consumers through ChatGPT. Binance is building infrastructure that allows developers and AI agents to interact with its services. Pancake adds a decentralized execution layer to the wider BNB Chain ecosystem.

The next battle in crypto may not be about which exchange attracts the most human traders. It could be about which infrastructure becomes the preferred destination for AI-powered financial activity.

#5482. Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

Turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

Most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to plan. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

For years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

We recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

We eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

Not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

What I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:

“Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

If you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a new closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

There’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5481. Ampace Highlights AIDC Battery Safety and Semi-Solid-State Technology for AI Data Centres

At Data Centre World Paris, Ampace showcased its PU200 UPS battery system, built with semi-solid-state cells. Recent large-scale fire testing of the PU100 provides evidence of the company's approach to system safety.

PARIS, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- At Data Centre World Paris 2026, Ampace showcased how it designs batteries for a critical moment in an AI data centre: when the mains supply fails and the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) must immediately carry the load. Its PU200 battery system combines high-rate discharge capability with a compact cabinet for facilities where space for backup power is limited.

Ampace develops the cells, modules and complete battery systems used in its data centre portfolio. Its engineers work from the requirements of the installation back to the cell itself. The power a UPS must deliver guides cell design, the heat generated during discharge informs thermal management, and the space available in the facility shapes the cabinet. Safety and reliability are design priorities at each stage.

Battery safety, from cell design to large-scale fire testing

A UPS battery can spend long periods on standby before it is called on to deliver high power within seconds. Ampace designs its cells with low internal resistance to limit heat generation during high-rate discharge and support reliable power delivery until an alternative supply takes over.

To assess how a complete battery system behaves under fire conditions, Ampace subjected its PU100 UPS battery system to large-scale fire testing under the sixth edition of UL 9540A. The PU100 met the applicable test criteria. For data centre operators evaluating battery fire risk, the results provide evidence of how the tested system performed under those conditions.

Semi-solid-state cells for high-power backup

The PU200 brings Ampace's semi-solid-state lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cell technology into a UPS battery cabinet. Its cells support the short, high-power discharge required during a supply interruption, while the compact cabinet gives operators more flexibility when allocating floor space in an existing facility or planning a new modular data centre. A detachable battery management system simplifies access for servicing.

Ampace's AIDC Battery Solutions White Paper explores the evolving role of UPS batteries in AI data centre power architectures beyond traditional backup power. Ampace will continue to work with European data centre operators and industry partners to support power infrastructure needs.

#5480. A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he said.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A big part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively new sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he said, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

What you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he said.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

Often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré said. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

But that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

And when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré said; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

#5478. Intuit sells Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68B, less than a third of what it paid

Financial software company Intuit Inc. today announced that it has agreed to sell its Mailchimp email marketing business to Italian technology holding company Bending Spoons S.p.A. for about $3.68 billion.

Coming five years after Intuit agreed to acquire Mailchimp for $12 billion, the sale price is less than a third of what the company paid. The 2021 purchase was the largest in Intuit’s history at the time.

Although Bending Spoons describes the transaction as all-cash, Intuit will reinvest $368 million of its proceeds in newly issued Bending Spoons shares. That leaves Intuit with $3.31 billion in cash from the sale, according to the companies. Included in the deal is The Rocket Science Group LLC, the legal entity behind Mailchimp. Closing is expected in early 2027, subject to regulatory approvals.

Selling Mailchimp is said to sharpen Intuit’s focus on the artificial intelligence-native tools it has built to help businesses win new customers, manage their pipeline and grow. Once the deal closes, Intuit intends to use the cash proceeds to buy back its own shares before the end of fiscal 2027.

Jack Tam, a senior vice president at Intuit, said the company is confident Bending Spoons “will lead Mailchimp to continued success in this next chapter.”

Growth at Mailchimp has stalled in recent quarters. Revenue from the business fell 1% to $313 million in the quarter ended Oct. 31. Intuit’s full-year guidance has Mailchimp revenue coming in flat to down 1%. In November 2024, Chief Financial Officer Sandeep Aujla told analysts that Intuit was seeing higher churn from smaller Mailchimp customers.

“Mailchimp is a powerful brand, built over two decades of reshaping the email marketing category and redefining how companies grow their audiences,” said Luca Ferrari, co-founder and chief executive of Bending Spoons. “We’re honored to welcome it to Bending Spoons and excited about what we can accomplish together.”

Ferrari added that Bending Spoons plans to invest substantially in Mailchimp after closing. According to Bending Spoons, the transformation of a business it acquires is typically deep, entailing reorganized teams, overhauled technology and redesigned user interfaces.

Founded in 2013, Bending Spoons has built a portfolio of digital businesses that includes AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Tractive, Vimeo and WeTransfer. Since listing on the Nasdaq in July, the company has also completed acquisitions of Airtable Inc. for $1.285 billion and whiteboard platform Miro for $1.355 billion.

Intuit announced the sale alongside its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results. For the quarter, it reported adjusted earnings per share of $2.91, up 56% from $1.87 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $4.35 billion, up 12% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting adjusted earnings of $2.70 per share on revenue of $4.31 billion.

For its fiscal second quarter, Intuit expects adjusted earnings per share of $3.17 to $3.22 on revenue of $4.93 billion to $4.95 billion. Intuit lowered its full-year revenue guidance to between $23.08 billion and $23.37 billion.

Behind the cut is Credit Karma, the company’s personal finance and credit score service, which is now forecast to grow 3% to 7% this fiscal year, down from 11% to 13% previously. Intuit reiterated its full-year adjusted earnings guidance of $22.88 to $23.12 per share. None of the guidance includes the effect of the Mailchimp sale.

Intuit shares fell more than 10% in after-hours trading.

#5477. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5475. Exclusive: ICE Mortgage Technology appoints AI strategy, product leaders

ICE Mortgage Technology appointed Kiran Sahota as vice president of AI strategy and Leslie Peeler as vice president of product.  AI Summary

ICE Mortgage Technology has appointed Kiran Sahota as vice president of AI strategy and Leslie Peeler as vice president of product, the company announced Thursday.

The two executives will help guide how ICE applies artificial intelligence, automation and other technology across its mortgage platforms, including origination, servicing, and data and analytics. The leadership moves come as lenders and servicers face persistent pressure to reduce costs while managing rising compliance and performance requirements.

“Kiran and Leslie have been at the forefront of major technology and operational change in our industry,” Bob Hart, president of ICE Mortgage Technology, said in a statement. “They have applied emerging technologies to some of the toughest challenges facing lenders and servicers, and their expertise will be instrumental as we continue investing in technology that helps our customers succeed.”Peeler joins ICE from mortgage subservicer Cenlar, where she most recently served as executive vice president and chief operating officer. Cenlar is in the process of being acquired by Pennymac. Her background also includes senior leadership roles at IBM and a stint as senior vice president of credit portfolio management at Fannie Mae.

At ICE, Peeler will oversee servicing product development, including the MSP loan servicing system.

“Mortgage servicing is no longer just about administering loans. It’s about helping clients adapt to changing market conditions, operate more intelligently and build stronger relationships with homeowners,” Peeler said.Sahota will lead the application of AI and intelligent automation across ICE’s mortgage technology business. Her role will focus on identifying high-impact use cases where AI can address operational and customer experience challenges for lenders and servicers.

She previously served as chief information officer at Freedom Mortgage and later as president of Xpanse, a mortgage technology company launched by the founders of Freedom. Earlier in her career, Sahota held vice president roles at Rocket Mortgage and Rock Ventures.

“Having worked on the lender and servicer side has given me a deep understanding of the challenges they face every day,” Sahota said. “The question shouldn’t be where we can add AI, but what problems matter most and whether AI is the best way to solve them.”

#5473. Zoning reform is remaking parking lots into a housing paradise

Parking lot redevelopment is gaining momentum as zoning reforms expand by-right and ministerial approvals on commercial land. The tradeoffs include labor and affordability rules, tighter lending, and continued lawsuits over eligibility and process.  AI Summary

Developers across the country paved over paradise to put up a parking lot. But changes to zoning laws to increase housing supply now have developers paving over parking lots to create a housing paradise.

In California, a series of state laws has made that easier. Florida lawmakers have gone after the same land. San Diego suburb National City took matters into its own hands. Because of its high housing costs, California has been the leading model for how reforms can work. But the Golden State is also a model for how neighborhood advocates and cities fight the reforms, often rendering them worth less than the paper they’re written on.

Much of the zoning reform push across the country focuses on where ground-up developers could build residential density, particularly infill in urban areas. The pressure is on land.

Underused parking lots are one option. The median share of downtown land used only for parking is about 26% in U.S. cities with more than 500,000 people, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation.

California’s Assembly Bill 2011 created a ministerial approval path, exempt from environmental review, for apartments on sites where office, retail or parking is a principal use. AB 2243 expanded those tools for commercially zoned property when it took effect last year.

Florida’s Live Local Act requires cities and counties to allow multifamily rentals by right on commercial, industrial and mixed-use land when a share of the units is affordable. Lawmakers have amended the law multiple times, including this year, since enactment in 2023.

National City shows how the local action can work. The city loosened height limits in its mixed-use zones last year, making underused lots more workable for housing.

National City Investment Group has broken ground on Market View, a 120-unit workforce housing project that will replace a parking lot beside Manolo Farmers Market in National City. This small grocery chain has locations in San Diego, where leaders have instituted reforms that have faced neighborhood challenges and lawsuits that new state law quashes.

Opponents still turn to the courts, even though reforms were meant to curtail or preclude lawsuits. And they are getting more inventive.

In San Francisco, neighbors are suing over an 848-unit project at 15 Marina Blvd. The towers would replace the Safeway’s parking lot and rise above a newly built store. They say the city wrongly ruled it eligible for AB 2011 and denied them a hearing.

To get the case into federal court, local opponents invoked an 1871 law, commonly known as the Ku Klux Klan Act. The developer wants the federal court to dismiss the case.

In Los Angeles, the fight is over habitat. Planners rejected 398 homes at the Woodland Hills Country Club in August, citing mountain lions. The state Department of Housing and Community Development said the city violated AB 2011. Pro-housing groups have sued the city while the developer threatens its own lawsuit for damages that could exceed $20 million.

Under AB 2011, a qualifying project gets ministerial approval, which means municipal staff checks it against objective standards and no hearing is required. Residents lose the chance to comment on the project or its environmental effects, said Sheri Bonstelle, a land-use attorney at Greenberg Lusker who represents developers, told HousingWire TBD.

“Neighbors are really upset that they no longer have a voice at all,” Bonstelle said.

Developers will also pay for the faster path. AB 2011 projects must meet labor standards, including prevailing wage. Bonstelle said that can add roughly 30% to construction costs, which developers weigh against discretionary review and the risk of a lawsuit under the California Environmental Quality Act.

“It’s literally a monetary analysis,” Bonstelle said.

The math has worked for some of her clients, she said. They’ll trade off higher costs for the elimination of entitlement risk and confidence that a project can be built. Bonstelle said lenders also favor the ministerial path. That’s especially crucial now, given the tight lending environment.

How much access neighbors get depends on the city. Los Angeles has a detailed AB 2011 application, Bonstelle said, so developers must file substantial information that neighbors can request and review. The city knew these projects were coming and was thorough about what had to be filed. Smaller cities are the bigger problem, she said.

“It’s more of an issue with the smaller cities that haven’t had the projects come through yet,” Bonstelle said.

Some cities hand developers a checklist meant for a building permit, she said. Her firm then goes through item by item with city attorneys to explain that most of those materials are not due at the planning stage of ministerial review.

Other cities believe state law should not apply to them and decline to process applications, Bonstelle said. In one case, her firm is working with a small city that has been “incredibly difficult.” The firm is asking the state Department of Housing and Community Development for a technical assistance letter explaining what the law requires.

Florida’s Live Local Act addresses similar commercial land. Cities and counties must approve multifamily rentals administratively on commercial, industrial and mixed-use land, with no rezoning or public hearing, if at least 40% of units are affordable for 30 years. Lawmakers have amended the law three times since 2023, most recently in 2026.

The law covers parking lots zoned for those uses, Patrick Chopson, an Atlanta architect and co-founder of Cove, told HousingWire TBD. “That’s a big deal,” Chopson said. Cove, which has a proprietary AI platform, recently acquired Deerfield Beach, Fla., architectural firm Gallo Herbert Architects. The firm has done a lot of work statewide in affordable housing.

The act also funds projects. In St. Petersburg, Nashville-based Elmington Capital Group plans Skyway Flats, a 174-unit affordable apartment building on surface parking next to an assisted living facility in the city’s Skyway Marina District.

The five-story building will have 28 one-bedroom, 100 two-bedroom and 46 three-bedroom apartments. All will target households earning 30% to 80% of the area median income, and 18 will go to young adults aging out of foster care.

Pinellas County commissioners unanimously approved $6 million in March to buy the land. The county will require affordability for 99 years. The $77 million project also draws on federal tax credit equity, tax-exempt bonds and a state loan through the Live Local Act.

Skyway Flats is in predevelopment. Elmington expects financial closing and a construction start in early 2027.

Similar to Pinellas County officials, National City planners acted on their own. They changed zoning to allow more density on parking lots. The change fits within the California law context. San Diego County alone needs more than 171,000 homes, regional officials say.

The city’s planning commission began reforming the code in July 2025 to allow four stories. Previously, the code capped buildings at three.

That cap limited how many units a project could hold, Andrew Regenberg of Gafcon, the firm working with the owner, told the commission in a public hearing. Chris Dallo, who heads the investment group, backed the change.

“We believe that more housing means more opportunity not just for our market, but for local businesses,” Dallo told the commission.

Market View is scheduled for completion in the first quarter of 2028. It will have three buildings, mostly studios, one-bedrooms and two-bedrooms, linked by open space and the market. RDC designed it, and R.D. Olson Construction is the general contractor.

Councilmember Ditas Yamane, who represents the district, said the groundbreaking followed a long review.

“This milestone is the result of a long, thoughtful process and extensive due diligence to bring this vision to life,” Yamane said.

#5472. Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”

#5471. Wiz ties Microsoft Agent Framework package compromise to release pipeline certificate

Microsoft Corp.’s official Python package for its Agent Framework artificial intelligence agent toolkit was compromised earlier this week, as an attacker published two malicious versions to the Python Package Index that were designed to steal cloud and developer credentials.

The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published on Tuesday through Microsoft’s own publisher account, giving them the appearance of a routine update to a package that sees close to 200,000 downloads a month. Both versions were pulled from PyPI within about an hour, but anyone who installed them in that window is at risk.

Researchers at cloud security company Wiz Inc. have since found that the attacker appears to have gained publishing access using a client certificate and private key for Microsoft’s Engineering System Release Pipeline, an internal service the company uses to sign and publish packages. Address filtering on the service blocked the attacker’s first attempt from Amazon Web Services, according to Wiz, though the attacker was able to publish on a second try from Microsoft-owned address space.

How the attacker obtained the credentials is not known. Microsoft had not responded to a request for comment from BleepingComputer as of Wednesday.

The researchers also observed part of the operation, as the attacker’s tooling was reporting its progress to the same public webhook it was using to collect stolen data. The tooling identified itself as Cairn, an open-source penetration-testing framework that uses AI.

The malware itself is delivered through a .pth file added to both releases, a type of file Python runs every time it starts, meaning the credential stealer runs even if the framework itself is never imported. The two versions also kept the genuine agent-framework-core 1.26.0 as a dependency, so the framework continued to work normally while the malware ran in the background.

Once running, the malware collects secrets from environment variables and from other running processes, along with credential files for services such as Azure, npm, Git, Docker and Hugging Face. It also requests Azure managed identity tokens for 12 resources, according to application security company Endor Labs Inc., with the second version adding requests for GitHub Actions tokens. The stolen data is then compressed, encoded and sent to a webhook.site address controlled by the attacker.

Researchers at malware tracking site OpenSourceMalware described the malware as a “focused credential and token stealer, not a remote access trojan,” noting that it does not install any persistence on infected systems.

Wiz’s analysis suggests the number of victims may be small, though it covers only the 50 requests the attacker’s free webhook.site account retained. Of those, 17 represented only three unique successful thefts of victim data, with the rest coming from the attacker’s own machines and from sandbox and security vendor scanning.

The incident is not the first this year involving an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Microsoft’s durabletask package was hijacked after its PyPI token was stolen in an attack that has been linked to TeamPCP, the group also behind the compromise of LiteLLM. Wiz says it has not linked the two incidents.

Anyone who installed either of the malicious versions is being urged to treat it as a credential compromise, according to researchers, who recommend rebuilding from version 1.26.0 and rotating any secrets the affected systems could access.

“A list of dependencies in production might show no trace of the framework, while a build runner could have installed it and been shut down before the alert arrived,” James Matchett, head of security at software supply chain security company Cloudsmith Ltd., told SiliconANGLE.

“If that runner had access to a deployment token, the team needs to know which version it installed and what the token could access,” he added.

#5469. Mortgage delinquencies rise to 4.42% in Q3 2026

Mortgage delinquencies increased in Q3 2026 to 4.42%, MBA reported, with serious delinquencies rising to 2.12% without accounting for seasonality. FHA and VA foreclosure rates reached 1.89% and 1.06%, respectively, their highest levels since 2017 and 2016.   AI Summary

Mortgage delinquencies increased in the third quarter of 2026, with the share of loans at least one payment past due rising to 4.42%. That’s according to the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA)’s National Delinquency Survey, released Thursday.

The seasonally adjusted delinquency rate for one- to four-unit residential properties was up 5 basis points from the second quarter and 43 bps from a year earlier.

Foreclosure starts also increased, with the share of loans entering the foreclosure process rising 1 basis point from the previous quarter to 0.21%. The percentage of loans already in foreclosure reached 0.71%, up 4 bps quarterly and 21 bps year over year.

“Loans 90 days or more late or in foreclosure increased for the fifth consecutive quarter and are 51 basis points higher than the third quarter of 2025,” said Marina Walsh, MBA’s vice president and head of industry analysis.

Walsh said the deterioration in government-backed loans is contributing to higher foreclosure activity. The Federal Housing Administration (FHA) foreclosure rate reached 1.89%, its highest level since the first quarter of 2017, while the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) foreclosure rate climbed to 1.06%, its highest since Q4 2016.

By delinquency stage, the 30-day rate increased 4 basis points from the previous quarter to 2.25%, while the 60-day rate rose 1 bps to 0.74%. The 90-day delinquency rate remained unchanged at 1.43%.

Performance varied by loan type. The conventional mortgage delinquency rate increased by 1 basis point from the second quarter to 2.73%, while the FHA rate declined 5 bps to 11.74%. The VA delinquency rate rose 11 bps to 5%.

All three loan categories posted annual increases. Conventional delinquencies were up 11 bps from a year earlier, while FHA delinquencies increased 96 bps and VA delinquencies rose 50 bps.

The seriously delinquent rate, which includes loans at least 90 days past due or in the foreclosure process, reached 2.12% on a nonseasonally adjusted basis. That was up 6 basis points from the second quarter and 51 bps year over year.

FHA loans recorded the largest annual deterioration in serious delinquencies, with the rate rising 197 basis points. The rate increased 13 basis points for conventional loans and 60 basis points for VA loans.

The five states with the largest quarterly increases in overall mortgage delinquencies were Wyoming, up 72 basis points, followed by West Virginia and Louisiana, both up 32 basis points. Arkansas saw its rate increase by 31 basis points, while Kentucky’s rose by 27 bps.

Walsh said the overall mortgage delinquency rate closely tracks the national unemployment rate, which stood at 4.1% in October.

Although the labor market has remained resilient, Walsh pointed to several pressures on household finances, including wage growth lagging inflation, declining personal savings, and rising balances on credit cards, auto loans and student loans.

Borrowers who took out mortgages in recent years at higher interest rates may also face affordability challenges that make timely payments more difficult, Walsh said. Changes to mortgage relief programs over the past year, including the removal of some COVID-era flexibilities, could be adding to financial pressures for some homeowners.

#5467. Why Compass wants the MLS antitrust dispute out of New York

Seven MLSs are urging an SDNY judge to retain their declaratory judgment case against Compass over MLS cooperation and listing submission rules. Compass argues the filing was anticipatory and seeks dismissal or severance and transfer to multiple home districts.  AI Summary

Compass International Holdings and a group of seven MLS plaintiffs are asking a federal judge in New York to decide if and where their antitrust battle over MLS cooperation and listing submission rules should proceed. The parties filed dueling letters earlier this month laying out competing narratives on forum shopping, efficiency and control over nationwide litigation.

In a Nov. 13 letter, Compass said it will seek to dismiss a consolidated declaratory judgment action filed by seven multiple listing services headquartered in Arizona, California, Colorado and North Carolina, or, alternatively, to sever and transfer each MLS’s claims to the district where Compass has brought its own antitrust case against that MLS.

The lawsuit was filed in the Southern District of New York (SDNY) by Arizona Regional MLS (ARMLS), OneKey MLS, MLSListings, Bridge MLS, Canopy MLS, Recolorado, Hive MLS and Doorify MLS after Compass sent letters to MLSs across the country in September demanding that they stop fining agents for publicly marketing office exclusive listings.

The MLSs are seeking declarations that their rules comply with Section 1 of the Sherman Act and state antitrust statutes, and an injunction preventing Compass from “bringing or pursuing any claim” against them over those rules, according to the amended complaint.

Compass told the court the MLSs’ consolidated suit is an “improper anticipatory filing” under the Declaratory Judgment Act. Citing prior legal precedent, Compass argued that courts may decline jurisdiction when declaratory relief is used “for procedural fencing.” The company pointed to its September demand letters, the sue‑by deadlines it set, and a series of deadline extensions it granted as part of what it characterizes as a good‑faith attempt to resolve the dispute short of litigation.

In the letter, Compass said counsel for ARMLS, Doorify MLS and Hive MLS requested a draft release and then sought additional time, citing illness and scheduling constraints, before filing this lawsuit in New York without substantively responding to the demands. Other MLSs, including MLSListings, BridgeMLS, REcolorado and Canopy MLS, also requested extensions to respond to the demand letter, Compass said.

Compass alleges the MLSs used those extensions to prepare the SDNY filing and then sued the day after certain extended deadlines expired. Compass also emphasized that it has since filed “home‑district” actions against each MLS in its own federal district, along with additional suits against other MLSs.

Since those damages claims cannot be resolved by declaratory relief alone and involve additional parties and provisions, Compass argued in its letter that the SDNY case would not “settle the controversy.”

However, as an alternative to dismissal, Compass is asking the court to sever each MLS’s claims and transfer them to the districts where the company’s separate antitrust suits are pending: Arizona, Northern California, Colorado and the Western and Eastern Districts of North Carolina.

Compass said the MLSs themselves allege they act “independently,” operate in distinct regional markets, have different governing boards and maintain non‑identical rules. Having a shared adversary in Compass and a similar form demand letter do not make their policies a single transaction or occurrence, the company told the court.

In a response letter sent on Wednesday, counsel for the MLS plaintiffs urged the court to keep the case and deny Compass’s anticipated motions. The MLSs argue that the SDNY suit is a textbook use of the Declaratory Judgment Act and that Compass, from its New York headquarters, orchestrated a “nationwide campaign” against cooperation rules that should be resolved in a single forum.

The MLSs characterize Compass’s pre‑suit communications differently, saying the company presented only two options: abandon their cooperation rules entirely in exchange for what they describe as a “toothless” release that left them under a “perpetual threat” of future litigation, or face antitrust lawsuits without clarity as to timing or venue.

The MLSs also dispute Compass’s forum‑shopping argument, emphasizing that they sued the brokerage in its home district and in the same court where Compass chose to litigate a separate cooperation‑rule case against Zillow.

By contrast, they say Compass’s 15-case strategy across 11 districts invites inconsistent outcomes and “massive inefficiencies.”

The MLS plaintiffs also pushed back on Compass’s bid to sever and transfer their claims. They argue their joinder meets federal procedure rules because each MLS plaintiff faces the same type of challenge from a single defendant over listing-submission rules that, while not identical, share common structure and legal issues.

Regarding the possibility of transferring the case, the MLSs say Compass cannot meet its burden to show, by clear and convincing evidence, that moving the case would serve the convenience of parties and witnesses and the interests of justice. They feel that their choice of Compass’s home forum is entitled to substantial deference, particularly because Compass’s executives and documents are in New York.

It remains to be seen how the court will rule on this issue. However, the ruling will help determine where and how quickly federal courts address the legality of MLS rules that require brokers to share publicly marketed listings with other brokers through the cooperative database of the MLS.

#5465. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”

#5464. Etherscan Warns of Support System Access Attempts as Security Scares Hit Crypto and Banks

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Another day, another security scare. This time, Etherscan is warning users after detecting attempts to gain unauthorized access to its customer support system. But the timing could hardly be worse for an industry already dealing with a growing list of cyberattacks.

The warning comes just days after hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely, injecting malicious code into websites operated by 178 organizations. The affected names included HSBC, BBC, Ledger, IKEA, Salesforce, Zoom, and CNN.

Meanwhile, crypto platforms have faced separate attacks involving compromised API keys, protocol vulnerabilities, and stolen customer information. Traditional banking has not escaped either, with a French bank recently losing approximately €100 million to hackers.

So what kind of security era are we entering? The problem is no longer confined to crypto exchanges or experimental DeFi protocols. Banks, technology companies, payment providers and blockchain businesses are increasingly exposed to the same interconnected digital infrastructure.

Etherscan disclosed earlier today that attackers had attempted to gain unauthorized access to its Freshworks customer support and ticketing system. The company is investigating and has introduced precautionary measures. It has not confirmed that customer records were successfully accessed, but warned users about suspicious support communications, unexpected links, and requests for sensitive information.

Security Notice: Reminder Regarding Etherscan Support CommunicationsEarlier today, we detected attempts to gain unauthorized access to our customer support and ticketing system (Freshworks).We are currently investigating the situation and taking precautionary measures.In…

The concern is particularly relevant because support impersonation remains an effective way to steal users’ crypto and money. An attacker posing as an Etherscan representative could exploit a user’s existing support request to make a phishing message appear legitimate.

But Etherscan is hardly the only name facing security questions this week. Just two days ago, hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation signup process. They injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects, allowing the code to run on websites using the affected software.

Optimizely confirmed the vulnerability and said it had removed the injected code and fixed the flaw. Its November 17 incident report said the unauthorized party exploited the signup process rather than stealing customer administrator passwords.

The financial damage remains unclear. It is reported that investigators could not establish how many visitors were affected or whether the attempted thefts succeeded.

The uncomfortable takeaway is that attackers did not need to breach 178 separate companies. They exploited one software provider whose code was embedded across hundreds of websites.

Crypto’s security problems extend beyond Etherscan and the Optimizely incident. DeFiLlama’s hack tracker recorded several attacks during the week, including a $10.39 million incident involving Lighter Perps on November 16. The attacker exploited a compromised trader API key, enabling unauthorized withdrawals.

Lighter said its protocol and smart contracts were not compromised. It temporarily suspended withdrawals and activated Guardian mode to prevent further unauthorized activity.

Another incident hit MORE Markets, where an attacker exploited a lending mechanism to drain approximately $308,000 in WFLOW. B18 TimeBank also suffered an exploit on November 17, losing $404,540 in USDC through its reward voucher redemption mechanism.

These incidents show different weaknesses across crypto infrastructure. Not every loss comes from a broken smart contract. Compromised credentials, vulnerable applications and flawed authorization mechanisms can be equally damaging.

Traditional finance faces its own problems. French lender Crédit Mutuel Arkéa disclosed a cyber heist earlier in November, with hackers stealing approximately €100 million through fraudulent transactions originating from the bank’s own accounts. The bank said customer assets were not affected, although some transactions were temporarily suspended.

Deutsche Bank also made headlines on November 17 after confidential internal documents surfaced through an international journalistic investigation. It was a document leak, not a confirmed breach of its current banking systems.

Deutsche Bank said security testing found no indication that its current IT environment, account information, login credentials, or payment data had been compromised. Still, the leak could have wider geopolitical repercussions.

Banking institutions are not immune to major security incidents simply because they operate under traditional financial regulations.

Crypto has suffered enormous losses. The October Binance incident alone involved $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, making it one of the largest cryptocurrency heists on record. Yet, traditional finance also faces attacks involving payment infrastructure, third-party service providers, and internal transaction systems.

The Optimizely incident is particularly revealing. Both HSBC and Ledger appeared among the affected organizations. The vulnerability did not care whether visitors were interacting with a traditional financial institution or a crypto company.

Neither system offers complete protection. The real question is whether companies can secure the increasingly complex infrastructure connecting their services. A single compromised vendor can expose hundreds of organizations, while one stolen credential can bypass otherwise sophisticated security systems.

Crypto users have every reason to demand stronger protections. But traditional banking customers should not mistake regulation and familiar branding for immunity.

With Etherscan investigating attempted unauthorized access, the data provider is now joining the growing list of companies dealing with security incidents.

#5463. Broker Action Coalition pushes for QM change on compensation cap

The Broker Action Coalition wants lender-paid broker compensation excluded from QM points and fees, aligning with retail LO pay. BAC says the current treatment harms small-balance and rural loans, citing 2026 wholesale data and prior CFPB findings.  AI Summary

The Broker Action Coalition (BAC) is proposing a change to federal mortgage rules that would exclude lender-paid mortgage broker compensation from the Qualified Mortgage (QM) points-and-fees calculation, aligning its treatment with compensation paid to retail lenders’ employee loan officers.

In a white paper recently released by BAC, the coalition argues that the current rules create an uneven playing field between independent mortgage brokers and retail lenders, particularly on smaller-balance loans.

Under the Ability-to-Repay/Qualified Mortgage rule, points and fees generally cannot exceed 3% of a loan amount for loans of $137,958 or more in 2026. Smaller loans are subject to graduated percentage and dollar limits.

Currently, compensation paid by a wholesale lender to an independent mortgage broker counts toward that limit, while compensation paid by a retail lender to its own employee loan officer is excluded.

The coalition argues that both types of compensation are often funded through the interest rate and are indistinguishable from the borrower’s perspective. The difference can leave brokers with less room to cover other fees that count toward the cap, potentially causing otherwise qualifying loans to exceed the limit while losing QM status and its associated liability protections.

The disparity is particularly pronounced on smaller loans, where the dollar limits leave less room for additional charges. The coalition said small-balance and rural loans are particularly vulnerable because fixed-dollar charges consume a larger share of the available cap.

The white paper also points to a decline in small-dollar mortgage lending. The share of home purchase loans under $70,000 fell from more than 11% in 2011 to less than 4% in 2020, citing research from Pew Charitable Trusts, the Urban Institute and the Department of Housing and Urban Development.

In rural and lower-cost markets, the group argues, the restrictions can make it harder for brokers to compete for loans that are already less financially attractive to originate.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau‘s 2013 rulemaking established the distinction between employee and broker compensation. At the time, the bureau said including broker compensation in the calculation could help reduce the risk of mortgage brokers steering borrowers toward more expensive transactions.

The coalition acknowledges that consumer protection concern but argues that subsequent regulations addressing loan originator compensation and steering have made the points-and-fees restriction a less targeted way to address the issue.

Specifically, the group points to existing rules that prohibit loan originator compensation from varying based on a loan’s interest rate or other terms, as well as a separate prohibition on steering borrowers toward transactions that provide greater compensation.

The proposed reform would take two approaches: The primary proposal is a statutory amendment to the Truth in Lending Act that would exclude rate-funded creditor-to-broker compensation from the points-and-fees definition when it is paid under a compliant loan originator compensation agreement.

The parallel regulatory proposal would ask the CFPB to amend Regulation Z to create the same exclusion.

“The proposed reform would remove an inequitable regulatory constraint without changing the competitive forces that influence compensation today,” the paper reads. “While individual brokerages may adjust their compensation arrangements, there is little evidence to suggest that the reform would materially diminish the wholesale channel‘s overall pricing competitiveness.”

Under the proposed language, the exclusion would apply only when compensation is funded through the interest rate, is not paid directly by the borrower or financed into the loan amount, and is established through a standing agreement between the creditor and broker that does not vary based on individual loan terms.

The coalition said the proposed requirements would prevent brokers from adjusting compensation on individual loans to circumvent the cap. The change would leave the 3% limit and existing compensation and anti-steering rules intact, with borrower-paid compensation and other fees still subject to the cap.

Data from two wholesale lenders representing $13.4 billion in combined 2026 production showed that loans with 2.75% broker compensation accounted for 14.53% of units and 12.41% of volume. BAC said the figures indicate most brokered loans close with lower compensation.

The group also argued that the CFPB has authority under the Truth in Lending Act to make the change to preserve access to affordable mortgage credit. It cited the bureau’s 2019 assessment of the Ability-to-Repay and Qualified Mortgage rule, which documented fee waivers and other challenges affecting smaller brokered loans.
