#5461. Resolve AI’s SRE-1 model finds root causes of production alerts as AI agents go on call

Incident remediation company Resolve AI Inc. has announced the launch of SRE-1, a new model that has been trained to find the root cause of production alerts, and Primary On-call, a new service that puts its artificial intelligence agents on call ahead of human engineers.

The new model, announced Wednesday, reflects the company’s argument that while AI has transformed how software gets written, it has barely touched how software gets run. According to Resolve AI, production has no public training corpus to match the published code that models learned from, as incidents at each company stay private.

SRE-1 is a 27 billion-parameter model built on open weights and trained by a team of 16 AI researchers over a final run of 7.4 days on up to 512 graphics processing units. Measured on the same incidents before and after training, which used reinforcement learning alone, the pass rate for a single investigation rose from 6.9% to 38.8%.

Resolve AI used Snowflake Inc.’s Cortex Training, a serverless service for customizing open-weight models, to build SRE-1. Snowflake Senior Vice President of Engineering Vivek Raghunathan said Resolve AI was the first design partner for the service.

In testing on 49 difficult live production cases, each run five times, an ensemble of five SRE-1 investigations matched the strongest frontier model tested at a lower cost, according to the company. Resolve AI also benchmarked its complete system on 178 production alert investigations, solving about twice as many incidents as general-purpose coding agents.

Primary On-call puts that research to work on the critical path. Each page is investigated across telemetry, infrastructure, code and operational knowledge, according to the company. Depending on what it finds, the agent can close the alert, mitigate the problem where a team’s policies permit or escalate to a human. Once it has acted, the agent checks the fix against the production baseline, monitoring it until recovery holds.

The agent also links related alerts and investigations into a shared view of each underlying problem. For teams wary of handing over the pager straight away, Resolve AI offers a shadow mode that records the call the agent would have made on each page.

Up to 80% of paged alerts in production are said to be handled by Primary On-call without escalation. Customers have reported a tenfold improvement in mean time to resolution, along with root-cause accuracy of up to 95%, according to Resolve AI.

Salesforce Inc. is among the early users. Bhupesh Patel, a software engineering principal architect at Salesforce, said that in the first few weeks of dark launch testing, the agent closed more than 70% of the CRM Analytics team’s paging alerts “without waking an engineer.”

“No engineering team can keep up with how fast code and patches land in production,” said Resolve AI Chief Executive Spiros Xanthos. “The answer is agents that are accurate and fast enough to sit on the critical path, and that takes a model built for production.”

Primary On-call is now generally available. Access to SRE-1 is limited to Resolve AI’s own platform.

Resolve AI is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised more than $190 million to date, including a $40 million extension to its Series A round in April, led by DST Global and Salesforce Ventures, that valued the company at $1.5 billion. Notable customers include Coinbase Global Inc., DoorDash Inc., Figma Inc., MSCI Inc., Nasdaq Inc., SAP SE and Zscaler Inc.

#5460. NAR’s latest data, must-have AI tools, Compass’ 15 new lawsuits

Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

That opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is currently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this big news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

#5459. Senate committee advances Matt Jones’ nomination as FHA commissioner

The Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs voted 13-11 to advance Matt Jones’ nomination as HUD assistant secretary for housing and FHA commissioner, sending it to the full Senate.  AI Summary

Matt Jones’ nomination to serve as assistant secretary for housing at the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and as Federal Housing Administration (FHA) commissioner advanced in the Senate on Thursday, moving through committee on a narrow vote.

The Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs approved his nomination 13-11, sending it to the full Senate for consideration. Jones would permanently fill the vacancy left by Frank Cassidy in June and succeed Joseph Gormley, who has been serving in the role on an acting basis.

Committee chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said Jones’ mix of public- and private-sector experience is central to his support. According to Scott, housing affordability remains one of the biggest challenges facing families across America, but if confirmed, Jones “will play an important role in implementing the 21st Century Road to Housing Act and helping more families achieve the American dream of home ownership.”

Jones currently serves as HUD’s deputy assistant secretary for single-family housing. He previously was associate vice president of government housing finance at the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), senior adviser for capital markets at Amerifirst Home Mortgage, and senior counsel for the Senate’s Finance and Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs committees.The 13-11 vote reflected partisan divisions over the direction of federal housing policy and FHA’s role in addressing affordability and ownership gaps.

Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the committee’s ranking member, voted against the nomination, saying Jones’ office has “cut resources for first-time homebuyers and proposed weak rules for keeping foreclosed homes in the hands of families instead of corporations.”

“We should vote to make life more affordable for American families. But these nominees will do the opposite, accelerating the Trump administration‘s disastrous economic policies,” Warren said. If confirmed, Jones would oversee FHA’s single-family, multifamily and health care mortgage insurance portfolios. FHA currently insures roughly $2 trillion in mortgages.

The FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund posted a strong financial performance in fiscal year 2026, even as its capital ratio declined from 2025 levels. The results have renewed industry pressure on FHA to cut annual mortgage insurance premiums to ease costs for first-time and lower-income borrowers.

Jones would also inherit an agency that has seen a series of policy adjustments under HUD Secretary Scott Turner, including efforts to revise servicing standards and modernize technology infrastructure.

MBA president and CEO Bob Broeksmit said the trade group supports the nomination due to Jones’ “extensive mortgage industry experience, deep understanding of government housing finance, and leadership of FHA’s single-family operations.”

“We urge the full Senate to confirm Matt Jones before the 119th Congress adjourns and look forward to working with him and HUD to continue modernizing FHA programs and to improve affordability for owning and renting a home,” Broeksmit said.

#5457. Housing groups urge FHFA to delay condo reserve rule until 2028

Five housing and mortgage trade groups urged FHFA to delay a planned condo reserve requirement increase from 10% to 15% until Jan. 4, 2028. They cited budget cycle constraints, unclear implementation details and potential GSE financing disruptions.  AI Summary

Five housing and mortgage industry trade groups are asking the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) to delay a planned increase in condominium association reserve requirements by one year, citing implementation challenges and potential financing disruptions.

In a Nov. 19 letter sent to FHFA Director Bill Pulte, the organizations asked the agency to direct Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to postpone the changes from Jan. 4, 2027, to Jan. 4, 2028.

The new requirement would increase the minimum reserve allocation for applicable condominium project reviews from 10% to 15% of annual budgeted assessment income.

The letter was signed by the Community Associations Institute, Community Association Roundtable, Community Home Lenders of America (CHLA), Housing Policy Council and National Association of Mortgage Brokers (NAMB).

The groups said they support adequately funded condominium reserves but argued that associations, lenders and homeowners need more time to prepare for the change.

Some have asked for change before. In June, NAMB asked the FHFA to delay upcoming Fannie and Freddie condo review and insurance standards by 12 months. But Fannie Mae retired its limited review process for condominium projects on Aug. 3.

“Condominium project eligibility has already declined following recent changes to project review requirements, including the elimination of Limited Review options,” the groups wrote.

The coalition identified three primary concerns with the planned increase, stating that “the change could have unintended consequences for condominium financing and housing availability.”

First, many condominium associations operate on annual budget cycles and cannot easily adjust their funding midyear. Some may also need updated reserve studies, board approvals or homeowner consultations before changing their funding practices.

The groups also said questions remain about how the new requirement will apply to existing budgets, recently completed reserve studies, major capital improvement projects and alternative funding arrangements.

Lenders, servicers and condo management companies will also need time to update their systems, underwriting procedures and project reviews.

Second, the groups warned that associations unable to meet the higher reserve requirement or qualify under an alternative reserve study provision could lose eligibility for conventional financing through the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs). The groups raised concerns that this could reduce the pool of potential buyers, make it more difficult for existing homeowners to sell or refinance, and put pressure on condo resale values.

The impact could be particularly pronounced in older buildings, smaller communities and associations with more “modest-income” homeowners, the letter stated. Projects that lose conventional financing eligibility could become more reliant on nonagency or portfolio loans, which may be more expensive or less readily available.

Lastly, the coalition said higher reserve contributions could add to housing costs at a time when homeowners are already facing elevated mortgage payments, property taxes, insurance premiums, maintenance expenses and association fees.

Fannie Mae has estimated that the higher reserve requirement could add an average of $13 to $14 per month to condominium owners’ costs, but the actual increase would vary by association, according to the coalition. Its accompanying analysis illustrated how the additional five percentage points could affect homeowners if the entire increase were funded through regular assessments.

As part of the proposed one-year extension, the coalition urged FHFA to convene industry stakeholders to evaluate the financial and operational effects of the change, clarify how existing reserve studies and funding arrangements will be treated, and develop transition provisions for associations working toward adequate reserve funding.

“We believe that strengthening condominium financial health and maintaining housing affordability should be complementary objectives,” the letter said.

#5456. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

License under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”

#5455. Huawei Unveils Financial AI Scaling Capabilities at Singapore FinTech Festival 2026

Powered by Open Hybrid AI Infrastructure and Three Intelligent Factories, Huawei Helps Global Financial Institutions Build Differentiated Competitive Advantages

SINGAPORE, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- At SFF 2026, Huawei shared insights on "Accelerating Financial AI at Scale, Advancing Agentic Finance" with global financial institutions and industry partners, showcasing its technologies and solutions.

Jason Cao, CEO of Huawei Digital Finance, and Alvin Feng, President of Huawei International Financial BU, delivered keynotes on the Festival Stage and Frontier Stage. Huawei showcased solutions for resilient infrastructure, application modernization, insurance, securities, and central banks, plus joint solutions under the RONGHAI Financial Partner Program and achievements from its 4-Win ecosystem collaboration.

To Move from AI Adoption to AI at Scale, Financial Institutions Must Build Their Own AI Capabilities

The competitive focus in financial AI is shifting from model performance to enterprise-grade system capabilities. Financial institutions must be able to independently select, securely operate, replicate at scale, and continuously evolve their AI capabilities.

Jason Cao shared lessons from China's AI journey: an open ecosystem makes AI affordable; extreme engineering makes it effective; and commercialization at scale makes AI deeply integrated and reliable in business. He identified four characteristics among China's financial institutions: ongoing application modernization (Zero Legacy); hybrid infrastructure combining on-premises deployment and public cloud; enterprise-grade AI architecture for centralized development and management; and AI in core business workflows such as mobile banking, credit, and risk control, reshaping business processes to enhance competitiveness.

As AI evolves to understand intent, plan, and act proactively, customers and employees will rely on their own AI agents. Banks must ensure their financial services can be understood, connected, and invoked by these agents, while building an AI flywheel linking data, execution, learning, and feedback toward Customer-AI-Friendly Finance.

Huawei is exploring a "Two Super Agents, Multiple Specialized Agents" architecture. The Customer Super Agent and Employee Super Agent understand user intent, deliver personalized services, and flexibly invoke specialized banking capabilities. Multiple Specialized Agents support domains such as credit, marketing, risk management, and wealth management through human-AI and multi-agent collaboration. Banks can turn expertise in compliance rules, credit judgment, marketing strategies, and risk management into invokable, reusable, continuously evolving AI capabilities. Through the Two Super Agents and Multiple Specialized Agents, Huawei helps banks connect customers and employees, coordinate business tasks, and continuously capture and refine expert intelligence to build self-evolving, enterprise-grade systems.

Cao said scaling AI for business growth requires hybrid infrastructure combining on-premises deployment and public cloud for flexible options, open architecture for technical agility, standardized engineering to build and replicate AI efficiently, and proven knowledge, skills, and agent capabilities as shared assets for reuse across teams and scenarios. He stressed that financial institutions must own their data, knowledge, and business logicâthe core assets underpinning differentiated competitivenessâand integrate them deeply with business processes to create financial-grade AI capabilities.

Three Intelligent Factories on Open Hybrid AI Infrastructure Accelerate Production-Grade Deployment of Financial Agents

On the Frontier Stage, Alvin Feng delivered a keynote titled "Owning Your AI, Advancing Agentic Finance" and unveiled Huawei's Fintelligent AI Solution. He outlined an enterprise-grade framework to address security, sustainability, and scalability: open architecture for flexibility and continuous technological evolution; standardized engineering for mass production of AI agents; and shared assets for reuse across teams and scenarios.

Built on open hybrid AI infrastructure, the solution brings these capabilities together through three intelligent factories: the Agent Factory for agent development and governance; the Token Factory for full-lifecycle token operations; and the Data&Knowledge Factory for continuous, high-quality data and knowledge supply.

At the Huawei Finance Exhibition Area, Huawei showcased its capabilities and partner practices for scaling AI worldwide. With 16 years in finance, Huawei has served more than 7,100 financial customers, including 54 of the world's top 100 banks.

#5454. Why some regional brokerages are avoiding ancillary services

Large national brokerages are expanding into mortgage, title, and servicing to offset thin margins. Several regional firms are opting out, leaning on lender relationships and advertising partnerships while others call ancillaries essential for control and profitability.  AI Summary

It’s no secret that the U.S. housing market may see fewer than 4 million existing home sales in 2027. In an attempt to boost ever-tightening margins and claim a larger slice of the transaction pie, many large national brokerages have spent the past year doubling down on ancillary services.

From new mortgage joint ventures to diving into mortgage servicing, companies from eXp Realty to HomeServices of America are looking to further integrate the disparate parts of a real estate transaction into one vertical platform. While this may be the way some of the nation’s largest brokerage companies are thinking about the future, many regional brokerages with strong market share in their states or metros are taking a different tack.

“Our company has been around for 153 years and our strategy has always been to be masters of our craft and not to chase every adjacent revenue stream,” Matt Leone, the chief marketing officer at Brown Harris Stevens (BHS), a RealTrends Verified brokerage, said. “I think that we are a residential resale, new development and property management brokerage. Mortgage and title may offer additional income, but our greatest opportunity is to stay relentlessly focused on real estate and be the best at that. I think, when you venture into other arenas, your core gets saturated and your eyes come off the prize.”

Like BHS, Linda O’Koniewski’s RealTrends Verified firm, Leading Edge Real Estate, is also staying out of ancillary services.

“While margins are critically thin for brokerages, and the income would be welcome, we have given it all up,” O’Koniewski said, noting that her company had previously had partnerships with insurance and mortgage companies. “What our clients need is the best loan officer and product. They need a super-responsive insurance agent. We are dedicating ourselves to developing processes and strategies that pre-resolve preventable problems in a transaction and create the best outcomes for our clients.”

O’Koniewski added that her firm’s in-house legal counsel has also suggested homing in on real estate as industries like mortgage and title are not their primary area of expertise.

Although firms like Leading Edge and BHS may not own or have ancillary services joint ventures, this doesn’t mean they lack relationships with lenders or title companies.

At BHS, instead of offering mortgage or title services directly or through a joint venture, the company works with trusted mortgage or title professionals to contribute to the company’s blog, sponsor its podcasts and participate in educational panel discussions.

Leone said BHS works to establish relationships with the top mortgage and title professionals through a “massive in-house commitment to marketing and content creation,” bringing voices from ancillary services industries that BHS feels are the most aligned with its culture and mission.

“They’re providing their expertise to our audience that follows us, as well as providing advertising support to expand the audience that views our 18-plus podcasts and in-house created episodic series shows,” he said. “It is legitimate advertising and earned media exposure at fair market value that allows us to get their expertise to broadcast that to our client base and it also allows us to have an ancillary source of legitimate income.”

Through these posts and marketing material, Leone said BHS is looking to educate its agents and clients, which is why the brokerage likes to partner with creative and experienced ancillary services providers through the program.

“We’re bringing experienced professionals that have seen it all before, and we like to bring those individuals in to get their insights,” Leone said. “Hopefully it allows everyone to stay informed and that is our goal when we’re creating content.”

While not yet as advanced as BHS’s marketing machine, this is what Peter Voss is looking to do with the in-house video production and editing segment he and his team have launched at 3% Listing Co.

“Agents can schedule a time with the in-house video team whenever they want and work with our director on a script and then get in front of the camera and record. We take care of all the editing and produce the video,” Voss said.

Voss said, for his firm, the video production started as a way to provide services to their agents that are beneficial to their business, but also something his firm could afford without significantly increasing overhead costs.

“It is a way to help our agents get their branding out and hopefully generate more transactions, which helps them but also helps our business,” he said.

In the future, Voss said they are looking to expand this service beyond just 3% Listing Co agents, allowing the company to have an additional revenue stream similar to BHS’s operation.

While brokerages like BHS, 3% Listing Co. and Leading Edge may not feel the need to go all-in on ancillary services, Michele Harrington, at First Team Real Estate, a RealTrends Verified firm, sees them as a must-have.

“It is kind of a no-brainer. The profit margins in the real estate brokerage business are just so tiny, so any little bump in the market or a downturn in the market is really going to hurt,” Harrington, a HousingWire Woman of Influence, said.

This is why Harrington believes anyone who owns a brokerage should be exploring ancillary services. Even prior to opening First Team, Harrington, who previously led a 300-agent company based in Southern California, had her own escrow and mortgage companies.

At First Team, Harrington runs an escrow company and a mortgage brokerage operation. She previously had mortgage joint ventures, but said she preferred going the owned mortgage operation route in order to maximize margins.

“The joint venture business isn’t my favorite type of mortgage operation because it is hard to be competitive and have good rates for consumers when everyone involved is trying to make a profit,” she said. “So, your best bet is being a broker where you can go directly to the banks or Rocket or United Wholesale Mortgage and broker the loan. It makes you way more competitive.”

By owning ancillary services, not only can you boost your profit margins, Harrington also feels it enables brokers to provide even better service to consumers.

“It gives you more control. If something goes wrong with escrow or mortgage, the agent calls me, and I tell the president that they need to fix it. That level of control is a nice perk for the agents,” Harrington said.

Beyond providing her agents with more control over transactions, Harrington said having ancillary businesses within her company also helps First Team be more competitive as a brokerage.

“If I want to be more competitive in my splits or be more competitive by offering signing bonuses, I can do those things because ancillary services increase my margins,” she said.

While Voss sees the value of having ancillary services operations, especially when it comes to revenue opportunities, he still doesn’t believe the juice is necessarily worth the squeeze.

“We have talked about bringing mortgage in-house, but what we have found is that in-house operations can be a turn off to a lot of agents,” Voss said. “They feel like it is kind of forced on them to have to send their clients to their firm’s mortgage lender. We are really focused on recruitment right now, so that is why we have shied away from this.”

Leone agrees, telling HousingWire that in-house mortgage or title operations often feel like a “forced option” that agents have to suggest to their clients.

“We don’t want to get in between the relationship of the client and our agent and the agents understand who is best for their client and who is best for that transaction,” he said. “Different lenders make sense for different neighborhoods, price points and scenarios and we don’t want to get in the middle of that.”

Instead Leone and Voss feel that their companies can generate more revenue by focusing on being the best at helping buyers and sellers transact real estate.

“We really focus on our relationships with mortgage lenders and title companies and making sure that we make their jobs easier so that they may be more open to sending business to us and our agents because they know we will get the job done,” Voss said.

#5453. Despite posting a solid earnings beat, Elastic sees its stock slide on rough guidance

Elastic N.V.’s stock was trending lower in late trading today after the enterprise search software firm reported earnings and revenue that beat Wall Street’s expectations but disappointed with guidance that came in below forecasts.

The company reported second-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of 94 cents per share, easily beating the analyst consensus estimate of 81 cents. Revenue rose 17%, to $496 million, surpassing the Street’s target of $487 million.

The results helped Elastic bounce back into profitability. Its net income for the quarter came to $171 million, rebounding from a loss of $51.3 million in the same period one year ago.

However, investors were less than impressed with the company’s guidance. For the quarter in progress, Elastic said it’s looking for earnings of between 90 cents and 92 cents per share on sales of $507.5 million to $508.5 million. That’s some way below the Street’s targets of 95 cents in earnings and $517.6 million in revenue. The company is not helped by the weak Euro, with currency conversions likely to cause a $4.5 million headwind on revenue in the quarter.

The full-year picture is not much better, as Elastic forecast annual sales of between $2 billion and $2.01 billion compared with the Street’s model of $2.01 billion.

Netherlands-based Elastic is one of Europe’s most successful software companies. It’s the developer of the popular open-source enterprise search platform Elasticsearch, which is used by thousands of businesses all over the world. The base platform is free to download and use, with Elastic making money by selling a special cloud-hosted version that ships with premium features not available in the open edition. The company also sells application observability and security tools.

In the last couple of years, Elastic has tried to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom by positioning Elasticsearch as a useful cog in the wheel that feeds real-time data into large language models to provide them with business context. A key capability is Elastic Context Engine, which gathers, structures, and serves business-specific context to AI agents so they can make accurate decisions with fewer tokens and lower latency.

More recently, the company has built AI-native products including AlertZero, which enables enterprises to orchestrate teams of autonomous security agents that automate tasks around data protection and threat hunting.

Elastic Chief Executive Ash Kulkarni (pictured) said he’s excited about the potential of those new capabilities to drive significant revenue over time. “Elastic delivered another strong quarter, beating guidance across all key metrics,” he said. “Our strong results reflect expanding customer adoption and position us well to continue our strong execution in the back half of fiscal 2027.”

Unfortunately for Kulkarni, investors didn’t seem to share his enthusiasm. The market was clearly expecting trouble on the horizon in the hours before the company published its report, as its stock declined 8% during regular trading. Once the results were out, it fell another 8% after-hours. That means Elastic’s stock is now up just over 1% in the year to date.

Elastic’s stock had rallied more than 150% between April and October, but virtually all of those gains have now been erased. Prior to today, the shares had already lost more than 20% this month amid broader concerns about the AI industry. Some investors continue to worry about the potential of AI technology to challenge the business models of software companies.

Built with leading asset managers and already live with their investors, Anduin Investor Portal delivers a fully white-labeled experience that connects fundraising, onboarding, reporting, and ongoing communications, supported by AI-powered workflows.

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Anduin today opened its Investor Portal to all. Developed with leading asset managers and already live with their investors, the fully white-labeled portal connects fundraising, onboarding, reporting, and ongoing servicing in one experience, supported by AI-powered workflows.

"By putting AI to work across connected data and workflows, we're helping firms reduce manual work, deliver best-in-class investor experiences, and scale their operations without adding complexity."

Anduin's migration experts use a programmatic approach to transfer investor data and documents from legacy portals accurately and efficiently, reducing the burden on internal teams. The portal has supported the migration of more than 50,000 investor records and documents. It also connects with existing infrastructure through APIs, including CRM systems such as DealCloud and Salesforce.

#5451. New CEO at Villa eyes manufactured housing, ADU opportunity

Villa hired former Century Communities CFO David Messenger as CEO to scale its ADU and manufactured housing lines. Since 2019, Villa has delivered 425-plus homes and is building projects in Santa Rosa, CA, Altadena, CA and Westminster, CO.  AI Summary

Offsite construction, one of the housing affordability crisis’s hidden-in-plain-sight solutions, gained a blast of momentum this summer when the ROAD Act called for removing the permanent chassis requirement for manufactured homes. Now, some builders are preparing to capitalize on that growing buzz.

Villa, which operates in California and Colorado, is among them.

Since launching in 2019, the company has delivered more than 425 homes across three core verticals: manufactured single-family communities, ADUs on single-family lots, and ADUs within multifamily communities.

The builder originally focused exclusively on ADUs, but has since expanded into primary homes, delivering its first batch of manufactured single-family houses in Northern California earlier this year. The company is currently building 25 homes in Santa Rosa, California and 14 duplexes in Westminster, Colorado, while also helping rebuild housing for victims of the 2025 Eaton Fire in Altadena, California.

The goal now is to scale both the ADU and manufactured housing businesses, with plans for larger single-family communities of up to about 100 lots. To support that growth, Villa announced earlier this week that it hired David Messenger, former CFO of Century Communities, as its next CEO.

For Messenger, moving from one of the country’s largest production homebuilders to an offsite builder focused on ADUs and infill development is quite a pivot. But it also represents an opportunity to focus more on attainable housing in the high-cost areas where Villa operates.

For example, in Santa Rosa, a city of about 180,000 north of San Francisco, the average home price is about $705,000. Comparatively, homes in Villa’s new community, Acacia Village, start at $620,000

“I’ve been drawn to affordable, attainable housing. I think it’s something that the country needs,” Messenger said in an interview with HousingWire TBD.

Beyond the opportunity to deliver attainable housing where it’s badly needed, Messenger sees room for growth across all of Villa’s verticals.

“We’ve got three verticals already established. I think all three can continue to grow,” he said.

Villa’s ADU business has plenty of room to grow, Messenger said. Homeowners in California and Colorado are driving strong and growing demand, while California multifamily operators are increasingly building ADUs on open or underutilized land to generate extra rental income.

“More and more multifamily operators see [ADUs] as a way to increase their rental income…at a relatively low cost to their overall project,” Messenger said.

The other growth opportunity is in Villa’s new manufactured home communities. Messenger sees an opening to partner with land developers to build larger communities, potentially with up to around 100 lots. Instead of taking on the expense and risk of acquiring, entitling and developing land themselves, Villa plans to purchase fully entitled and developed land.

“There is an opportunity to work with land developers who, as they’re developing land, are looking for a takeout. The land developers don’t necessarily want to own the land long term. I think if we can provide them a takeout when it’s finished, that is an attractive option for both of us, as we can buy a finished lot. I don’t think that Villa is going to be in the game of developing land, and we’re not looking to take on entitlement risk,” Messenger explained.

Messenger also plans to draw on his experience at Century Communities to help Villa build a more scalable operation. Although the companies operate differently, he believes many of the same production homebuilding principles can apply.

“Having spent 10 years at a production homebuilder, you learn how to establish repeatable processes. Homebuilding involves unpredictable issues every day, so the goal is to make those issues more predictable. Offsite construction lends itself to that because a significant portion of the home is built in a factory, making the process more predictable. It’s about establishing standardized processes that can be repeated for every unit and every lot,” Messenger said.

“Once we get those processes working like a machine, that’s what makes the business scalable,” he added.

As Villa scales, Messenger doesn’t expect production capacity to be an issue. Instead of owning and operating its own factories, the company contracts with reputable, third-party production facilities to build its homes and ADUs.

“We’ve partnered with different factories all over the state of California. We partner with factories in Colorado, Nebraska and Albuquerque for dealing with those projects. We are developing an extensive array of relationships to make sure that we don’t get hamstrung by a capacity problem,” he said.

The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law in July, included a provision that removed the decades-long requirement that manufactured homes be built with a permanent steel chassis. The change has received a lot of attention, leading The New York Times to name chassis as its word of the day on November 11.

Manufacturers cite two main benefits of this rule change, which the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development is now finalizing. First, removing the steel chassis gives manufactured homebuilders greater design flexibility, allowing them to build larger, multi-story and more aesthetically appealing homes that more closely resemble traditional site-built housing.

“If you actually walk through a manufactured home product today and look at the finishes being delivered, it’s a completely different product from what people actually think about. If we can do some marketing and outreach and get people in the door to see what these homes look like, I think they’ll be amazed at what they see,” Messenger said.

That added design flexibility could help the industry shed longstanding stigmas and gain acceptance in communities where zoning restrictions historically thwarted manufactured housing, which is typically a more affordable alternative to traditional stick-built homes.

Manufacturers also see an opportunity to expand into high-cost urban and suburban infill markets, where multi-story designs can make higher-density development more economically feasible. Villa, which operates in high-cost cities with limited developable land, is among the homebuilders positioned to benefit from this rule change.

“As we’re evaluating communities, not having a chassis requirement should open up more lots and communities where we can build on,” Messenger said. “I think it provides additional opportunities for us.”

#5449. Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am

The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.

A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.

Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

The window is closing. Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

Competitors are everywhere. AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”

The data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each new model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

The data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

Momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.

Learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

Jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its big commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

At AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”

Finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook says Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”

Prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick important problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”

Swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

Farecast, the airfare prediction company I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments company whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.

Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, said it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”

So pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one big shot once you have it.

Chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

To repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one says, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.

In AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.

#5448. Rate’s Jesse Allen: Reverse mortgage lenders should plan for the ‘down case,’ not FHA relief

Jesse Allen of Rate said lenders should expand reverse mortgage product menus to reduce reliance on FHA-backed HECMs. He said proprietary reverse is about 40% of Rate originations and that Rate is also growing its HECM volume year over year.  AI Summary

With mortgage lenders continuing to cut expenses, including personnel, as the originations forecast for 2027 dims, Jesse Allen said the reverse mortgage business at Rate is still growing and he isn’t waiting for federal housing leaders to offer help.

At last week’s National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association Annual Meeting & Expo, Allen said he’s planning for the “down case” on Federal Housing Administration policy regarding upfront mortgage insurance premiums (MIP) for Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs). Allen’s comments came not long after Ginnie Mae President Joe Gormley said the Trump administration is “very comfortable” with current MIP structures for FHA-insured single-family home loans and reverse mortgages.

“In an uncertain environment, you have to plan and execute to your down case scenarios, and then when something better than down case happens, you’re that much better,” Allen said.

Allen, the president of the 55+ lending division at Rate and a NRMLA board member for 2026-27, sat down with HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily at NRMLA Annual to discuss some of the hot topics of interest for industry professionals. He said that lenders should look to expand their product menus to insulate themselves from any obstacles to federally insured loans, and he pitched responsible home equity release as the next big opportunity for the wider mortgage industry.

NRMLA and other trade groups have spent the past year arguing that the FHA could lower the upfront mortgage insurance premium for certain borrowers. Allen said that cutting some fees would pull more people into the FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund, which he called “basic insurance economics.” NRMLA has also laid out the math to lower premiums for borrowers who utilize less of their HECM proceeds while lobbying to eliminate second appraisals.

But with the political transition underway after the recent midterm elections, Allen does not expect quick action. “I’m not building my business model or business case around that,” he said. “If positive things happen, it’s wind in the sails.”

Still, a lower upfront MIP could be “powerful for older homeowners” who want to access their equity responsibly, he said, as they might tap 30% to 40% of their available line of credit now while saving the rest for later in retirement.

When asked whether he thinks a more balanced Congress is coming in 2027, Allen said everyone’s definition of balanced differs. But he also believes that if Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) takes over the Senate banking committee, “we’re going to see more regulatory interest.” Allen’s approach, he added, is to operate daily as though auditors are showing up, which should be the standard for a business that serves a protected class of senior homeowners.

Allen clarified that Rate is a nondelegated correspondent lender for proprietary reverse mortgage products and is fully delegated on FHA-backed HECM products. Proprietary loans make up about 40% of Rate’s reverse mortgage originations, he said, and he estimated them at 55% to 65% of its volume based on their typically larger loan sizes.

Similar to the industry at large, private-label loans are where growth is happening at Rate, although its HECM volume is rising too, Allen said, with the company outpacing the industry year over year. According to data compiled by Reverse Market Insight, Rate was the 13th-largest HECM lender in the country through the first nine months of the year, with its 228 endorsements up 41% compared to the same period in 2025.

Proprietary loans often serve borrowers that FHA products can’t, including owners of high-value homes and those who want to pay off consumer debt without it counting against them in qualification — a guideline NRMLA has pushed to change. But Allen said his team spends time reminding loan officers that the HECM is “still an awesome product.”

Compared with a traditional home equity line of credit, he said, a HECM line of credit mitigates the risk that falling home values lead to frozen lines, leaving borrowers without access when “they need their equity the most.” HECM lines of credit can grow for the life of the loan if the borrower doesn’t exhaust funds and meets requirements like property tax and insurance payments. Proprietary lines of credit typically stop growing after seven to 10 years, Allen added.

Allen pointed to reverse for purchase financing as a tool for addressing affordability. He said that one of Rate’s top loan officers recently closed a reverse for purchase for the parent of one of his real estate agent partners. The LO had a couple of reverse mortgages under his belt but had never done a purchase deal, and he worked with one of the company’s specialists to get it done.

“Specialty lending in general is a big priority for most mortgage companies today,” Allen said, naming non-QM and builder programs alongside reverse.

Allen thinks that today’s retirees are less willing to sacrifice their lifestyles. Reverse mortgage proceeds can fund a variety of uses — from family vacations to in-home care that eases the load on adult children, or even a move into a 55-plus community without draining savings.

“That’s why I love this business, because it’s infinitely customizable,” he said. “Every client is unique, every situation is unique, and we have this expanding suite of products to really help deliver for the clients … so that they can get the joy out of the transaction.”

#5446. XRP Price Was Worth Less Than a Penny When GTA 5 Launched: Could GTA 6 See It Hit $100?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP price was trading below one cent when Grand Theft Auto V arrived in September 2013. Thirteen years later, Rockstar is preparing to release GTA 6, while XRP has grown into one of the largest cryptos. XRP is a financial giant today.

The comparison is striking. On September 17, 2013, the day GTA V launched, XRP was trading at $0.009613. Today, XRP trades near $0.95, representing a price gain of almost 100 times from that launch-day price.

But can XRP deliver another extraordinary rally as GTA 6 arrives? A $100 price target would turn a relatively small crypto investment into a fortune, but it would also require XRP to reach a market valuation never seen before in the crypto industry.

When GTA V introduced players to Los Santos in 2013, XRP was still largely flying under the radar. Its price sat below one cent, and its market cap was ranging around $75 million. Then the following years changed everything.

XRP broke above $0.10 in May 2017 before accelerating during the historic crypto bull market. By December 2017, the token had crossed $1 and continued climbing toward its January 2018 all-time high of $3.84.

That is an extraordinary transformation from its GTA V launch-day price. A $1,000 investment at $0.009613 would have purchased more than 100,000 XRP. At $3.84, that position would have been worth nearly $400,000. Something that only crypto can do.

However, XRP’s journey was far from smooth. The token endured successive bear markets, regulatory uncertainty, and the SEC’s lawsuit against Ripple in December 2020. Its recovery eventually pushed XRP back toward record territory in 2025, when it reached $3.65.

Now, XRP is trading around $0.95, substantially below its previous peaks. Will another major recovery begin before GTA 6 is released?

Rockstar’s GTA 6 arrives more than 13 years after GTA V, creating an interesting milestone for XRP investors. XRP has experienced multiple market cycles during the same period, transforming from a sub-penny asset into a major digital currency.

XRP currently has 63.5 billion tokens in circulation. At $100 per token, its market capitalization would reach $6.35 trillion. That would put XRP among the most valuable financial assets in the world, exceeding the market capitalization of most publicly traded companies.

The bullish argument rests on XRP’s potential to capture a much larger share of institutional payments, cross-border settlements, and digital asset liquidity. Ripple has spent years building financial infrastructure around the XRP Ledger, while institutional interest in crypto investment products continues to develop.

A stronger crypto market could also provide the liquidity needed for another substantial XRP rally. But XRP would need considerably more capital, adoption, and sustained demand to justify a multi-trillion-dollar valuation.

The historical comparison remains fascinating. XRP went from less than a penny when GTA V launched to several dollars during subsequent crypto cycles. Few people back then would have believed XRP could get to where it is now.

#5445. Google adds computer use capabilities to Gemini’s Mac app

Google LLC today released a new version of Gemini’s Mac client that can interact with other apps on the user’s computer.

The feature is available in the U.S. on launch. It requires a Google AI subscription, which equips consumer Google accounts with a broader lineup of artificial intelligence tools. The offering also includes additional storage space and certain other features.

Users can instruct Gemini to launch a local app by including the command “@Computer use” in their prompts. For example, a designer could upload a sketch of a vehicle and ask the AI assistant to turn it into a three-dimensional animation. Gemini finds the local app that is needed for the task, creates a project plan and carries out the work step by step.

The assistant supports tasks that comprise dozens of actions. Furthermore, consumers can use the output of a newly completed Gemini workflow to launch follow-up projects. A user could have the assistant generate a visual asset in a design tool and then turn it into a mini-app with Visual Studio Code.

Gemini can interact with not only local apps but also web services. That means it can load data from webpages into programs that run on the user’s machine, as well as move data in the opposite direction and between cloud services.

The AI carries out its work in a background window. As a result, users don’t have to pause their work while the assistant is running. They can track Gemini workflows via a preview pane built into the Mac client’s chat window. Additionally, Google has included controls that make it possible to give Gemini feedback mid-task.

The Mac version of Muse, Meta Platforms Inc.’s recently launched AI agent, can also interact with local apps and data. Furthermore, a cloud-based virtual machine enables it to perform tasks even when the user’s computer is offline. Dots, a competing service from OpenAI Group PBC, offers a similar capability.

Google may seek to match its rivals’ cloud-based workflow hosting features in the future. The company can also extend Gemini in other ways. Notably, it could bring Gemini’s computer use mode to additional operating systems and add features for business users. OpenAI’s Dots already includes capabilities designed to automate business workflows such as procurement.

#5444. Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Update, Tuesday Nov. 17: ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests Vulcan’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff. Read our follow-up story for details. This story has been updated with ULA’s preliminary findings.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit Sunday, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased.

ULA said Sunday that it didn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it would work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as quickly as possible.

Amazon Leo said in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to reach orbit. The Centaur, powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris, appears to have started normally and couldn’t make up for the shortfall. ULA appears to have lost telemetry and the mission about 10 minutes into the flight.

Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t said what caused the shortfall.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

In June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security launches after February.

ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the New Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight, CBS News reported.

ULA is also under new leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

#5443. Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am

It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).

Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows users are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS.”

Instead, the Copilot as “a new OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

Microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

Many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.

The high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

Operating systems like Windows provide users with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the new Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

The New OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

Currently, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the new Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as New OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

If you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business plan and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, users don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

“We increasingly think of all our apps together as a new operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” said Nadella in his letter to shareholders, published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.

The end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella said.

The Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race: In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.

Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.

#5441. What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am

Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.

That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.

According to the report, the attempts to recover were further complicated by a second problem: servers that engineers restarted were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again, a phenomenon known as a “thundering herd.”

Microsoft says active service disruptions lasted nearly 24 hours. Delayed email continued to be delivered after service returned Friday morning, and the company posted its public all-clear on X late Friday night, nearly 38 hours after the outage began.

The underlying flaw dates to July, when Microsoft began rolling out a fix to the software that handles incoming connections on its networking gateway, the servers that sit in front of Outlook and many other Microsoft 365 services.

Microsoft hasn’t said what the fix was meant to address. It ran worldwide for more than three months without problems, according to the report.

Under heavy load, however, parts of that software could get stuck waiting on one another, using up the servers’ processing power and memory until they froze.

That’s what happened last week. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved Teams traffic onto the same servers that handle Outlook email, adding to their load, according to the report. Microsoft called the switch part of normal operations but didn’t say what prompted it.

Complicating matters, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already out of service because of an unrelated problem, which also isn’t detailed in the report.

When traffic peaked during the U.S. workday, that was enough to trigger the outage.

Two things stand out as likely areas of scrutiny:

Microsoft’s testing didn’t catch the bug. Its labs mostly used less powerful machines with fewer processing cores, running a different mix of traffic, while the problem was worst on the newer servers handling real customer load.

The fix also passed through Microsoft’s standard staged rollout, spreading worldwide over several weeks without any sign of trouble, according to the report.

The company certainly has the means to test on the hardware it actually runs. It spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its most recent quarter, much of it on AI infrastructure.

The safeguards meant to contain the damage didn’t hold. Walls between regions failed because of what the report calls “a separate issue,” which it doesn’t explain, so the outage went global.

The gateway is made up of thousands of “capacity units” grouped into regions, with walls between them meant to keep a failure in one place. Microsoft also runs a second, independent gateway so services can switch over during a disruption.

Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps made that switch, which is why Teams chats and meetings mostly kept working. Exchange couldn’t, “for scale reasons,” as the company put it, so email stayed down.

Microsoft’s own tools added to the problem. Its automated recovery “was not designed” for a fleet that was almost entirely unresponsive, according to the report, and its usual ways of rolling back a bad change couldn’t quickly undo one that was months old.

The company’s systems automatically shifted traffic from unresponsive servers to healthy ones, and the extra load triggered the same bug on those servers, too. About 10 hours in, engineers turned off some of that automatic rerouting.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, posted an abridged version of the report on X late Sunday. “We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” he wrote.

Lamanna had previewed the findings Friday afternoon, blaming “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” for the slow recovery, as GeekWire reported when Microsoft declared the outage over.

Microsoft says it has rolled back the defective code, added server capacity and monitoring, and put new limits on how traffic is redistributed to avoid another cascade. A final report with a full list of repairs is due Nov. 20.

It may also answer the biggest question the preliminary report leaves open: why the walls between regions didn’t stop the outage from spreading worldwide. Microsoft blames that on “a separate issue,” apart from the July bug, but hasn’t said what it was.
