#5439. Amazon picks its Bond: Robert Pattinson to play 007, ending years of speculation over coveted role

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 16, 2026 at 8:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 8:32 am

Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media, “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson.

The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series. He takes over from Daniel Craig, whose fifth and last Bond film, “No Time to Die,” came out in 2021.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond films when it bought MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, and it took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Fans and bookmakers had been guessing about Craig’s successor since he said in 2019 he was leaving the role.

Over the years, the rumored contenders included Idris Elba, Tom Hardy, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Holland and Henry Cavill. By the end, there were five finalists. Pattinson beat out Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner after screen tests in London in late October, according to The New York Times. Casting director Nina Gold ran the tests, which covered stunts, dialogue and camera presence.

Bond is one of the most valuable properties Amazon got in the MGM deal, its second-largest acquisition ever behind Whole Foods. The franchise has earned nearly $7 billion at the domestic box office, adjusted for inflation, since “Dr. No” in 1962. Now Amazon is running it without the Broccoli family, whose stewardship over six decades built it into one of Hollywood’s biggest moneymakers.

Pattinson’s casting is the most visible move yet in Amazon’s plans for Bond. As the Times noted, the 2025 deal followed years of behind-the-scenes friction over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe beyond the films. The Times also pointed out that Amazon has to win over a generation of moviegoers who grew up during the franchise’s long hiatus and gravitated toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Amazon is already putting the back catalog to work. Alongside Monday’s announcement, it published a guide to streaming the 007 films on Prime Video.

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk

To lead the next film, Amazon brought in producers Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman, and David Heyman, who produced all eight “Harry Potter” movies. Denis Villeneuve (“Dune”) is directing from an original screenplay by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight. No release date has been set, and the Times reports that a theatrical release before 2028 is unlikely.

“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond,” Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said in a statement. Hopkins said Pattinson’s “remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice” to carry on the 007 legacy.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

Some longtime fans have worried that under Amazon, Bond will lose his distinctly British character and become more corporate and American, the Times reported. Pascal and Heyman, in a joint statement, called the English actor “the perfect Bond for our times.”

Bezos had yet to weigh back in on social media about Amazon’s pick, but Amazon CEO Andy Jassy did in a LinkedIn post, writing that he was “excited” to have Pattinson in the role, calling him “one of the most versatile actors of his generation, who consistently makes fearless choices, and keeps surprising people with his performances.”

Fans online were split. Some posted images of Elba or Cavill, calling Pattinson as 007 a “huge miss.” Others said the actor was on a “generational run” right now with the roles he’s landing. Others shared GIFs of Sean Connery, saying there will only ever be one Bond.

I checked in with my mom, a longtime Bond lover and the biggest movie fan I know. She quickly responded via text.

“No way … not sexy enough for me,” she wrote of Pattinson. “I really liked Daniel Craig, but Sean Connery has always been a favorite.”

#5438. Industrial monitoring startup BrightAI closes $97M investment

BrightAI Inc., a startup that helps industrial companies detect malfunctioning equipment, has raised $97 million in funding.

Smith Point Capital led the Series A round. BrightAI said in its Wednesday announcement of the deal that a number of other venture capital firms contributed as well. They were joined by GE Vernova Inc., an energy equipment company that emerged from the 2024 split-up of General Electric Co.

Many industrial machinery malfunctions affect internal components that aren’t visible to an outside observer. As a result, issues often go unnoticed until they cause a major disruption. Palo Alto, California-based BrightAI develops hardware and software tools that help customers spot issues earlier.

The first component of the company’s product portfolio is a collection of sensors called State Stickers. They’re small, rectangular devices with a ruggedized case and a long battery life. Technicians can attach them to industrial equipment to monitor for issues that can’t be detected visually.

The motion of a machine’s internal components produces noise and  vibrations that tend to follow a specific pattern. If an industrial fan’s blades rotate 30 times per minute, it might give off a whooshing sound every two seconds. BrightAI’s State Stickers can detect when a machine diverges from its usual operating pattern.

The sensors wirelessly transmit their measurements to a device called the Stateful AI Hub. It runs artificial intelligence models that analyze the data for signs of hardware failures. According to the company, its models become more accurate as the number of sensors deployed at a site grows.

BrightAI offers software that enables companies to augment the data from its sensors with drone footage. A utility, for  example, could use a BrightAI-powered drone to detect erosion at the top of an electric pole. The company’s AI models automatically draw a square around damaged components to spare technicians the hassle of manually analyzing footage.

The company says that its software can also collect maintenance data in other ways. A BrightAI-powered drone can read the meters that are attached to assets such as data center coolant tanks to check their internal pressure. Furthermore, built-in support for infrared cameras enables the software to spot overheating equipment.

The third core component of BrightAI’s product portfolio is an AI wearable. The Stateful Wearable, as it’s called, provides technicians with troubleshooting advice in the field. It also checks whether they follow safety guidelines during inspections and automatically turns maintenance data into reports.

“Our infrastructure is under more strain than it has ever been, and Physical AI has finally become reliable enough to work in the field,” said founder and Chief Executive Alex Hawkinson. “Bringing those two facts together is a once-in-a-generation opportunity.”

BrightAI says that its products monitor hundreds of thousands of industrial assets across 50,000 sites. Investor GE Vernova, which is also a customer, plans to expand its use of the company’s technology in connection with this week’s funding round. BrightAI, for its part, will use the capital to grow its international presence.

#5437. Study: 403 U.S. data centers rival Denmark’s carbon emissions; Oregon ranked No. 2 in power use

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 17, 2026 at 3:48 pm

A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

The research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, said in a statement.

Guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

The research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability and explored in an associated website, comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions.

In the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.

Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

The researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

Nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

The study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group.

All three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for new clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.

“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July.

Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the company to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

“So that is a real challenge,” Hurst said in September, “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”

At the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. Amazon has agreed to become the anchor tenant of a massive planned data center campus with proposed natural gas and nuclear power generation, according to the Financial Times.

“Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers” published in Nature Sustainability and researchers from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, University of Pisa, IMT School of Advanced Studies, Aurora Energy Research, Environmental Systems Research Institute, Baxtel and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

#5435. Former UW AI researchers Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin raise $110M for AI startup Noeri

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:37 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:14 pm

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a company’s own work.

Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Noeri’s software studies a company’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company said.

It works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the company said.

The pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin said at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”

Noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

Choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

Noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

#5433. Portland startup Fairly raises $22M to pair local caretakers with AI for vacation rentals

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:58 pm

Fairly, a Portland, Ore.-based vacation rental startup led by Vacasa founder Eric Breon, raised a $22.4 million Series A round, the company announced Tuesday.

Oregon Venture Fund led the round, with participation from Elevate Capital and Breon.

Fairly pairs vacation rental owners with local caretakers who look after the homes. Its software handles pricing, bookings and scheduling, and uses AI to draft routine guest messages and flag maintenance problems.

Guests booked more than $66 million in reservations through Fairly over the past year, up from about $5 million the year before, the company said. Nearly 900 caretakers now manage about 2,000 homes across 47 states, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Owners pay a single 20% fee, which Fairly splits with the caretaker, compared with the 25% to 40% the company says other managers typically charge. Fairly also says it doesn’t tack extra fees onto guest bills, so guests pay less overall.

“At Vacasa, I led a 7,000-person team, and delivering quality, individualized care at that scale is not an easy task,” Breon said in a statement. “At Fairly, we take a completely different approach: we empower dedicated, hyperlocal caretakers to care for homes, and our systems do the heavy lifting around them.”

Breon founded Vacasa in Portland in 2009 and spent more than a decade there. The company went public via a SPAC deal in 2021 and was acquired in May 2025 by Phoenix-based Casago, a vacation rental manager.

Fairly, founded in 2023, emerged from stealth in December 2024 with $10.1 million in pre-seed funding. The company has now raised $32.5 million in total.

Fairly now employs 106 people, up from 25 at its launch in 2024. Co-founder Subechya Person remains chief product officer; co-founder and former CTO Jeff Flitton left the company in February.

#5431. Radian Aerospace plans to make its own composite materials for space plane (and for other companies, too)

by Alan Boyle on Nov 17, 2026 at 4:00 amNovember 17, 2026 at 4:11 am

On the way to building a space plane, Seattle-based Radian Aerospace is planning a factory to make the advanced materials it’ll need — and it plans to sell those materials to other companies as well.

Radian CEO Richard Humphrey said he envisions the factory, known as Foundry 1, as a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility with a footprint spanning “just under 100,000 square feet.” Six to 12 sites around the country — including sites in the Pacific Northwest — are currently under consideration, with late 2027 as the target for starting production, he said.

Foundry 1 is meant to produce ceramic matrix composites, or CMCs — not only for Radian’s space plane, but also for other applications ranging from gas-turbine components to high-performance braking systems.

“Each of these industries has a bottleneck that’s being driven by a lack of an industrial base to really build these next-gen materials,” Humphrey told GeekWire.

Humphrey and his teammates ran into that bottleneck while developing Radian One, a reusable rocket-powered plane that’s meant to transport cargo and crew to and from low Earth orbit. Securing a reliable supply chain for the required materials proved so challenging that Radian decided to produce its own.

“Defense and space programs need these materials at costs and production rates that today’s supply base cannot deliver,” Humphrey said today in a news release. “Foundry 1 unlocks a substantial commercial opportunity for Radian and a more direct path to revenue. It positions us to supply customers across these industries while advancing the technology that will make Radian One possible.”

Ceramic matrix composites embed reinforcing fibers, such as carbon or silicon carbide, within a lightweight ceramic material. The ceramic provides resistance to extreme heat, while the fibers help the material carry loads and resist damage from cracking.

Carbon-fiber composites have been around for decades, but turning them into products is typically labor-intensive and expensive. To drive down the cost while improving quality, Radian is developing an automated system for producing CMCs. The company says it’s targeting a 50% reduction in CMC manufacturing costs by cutting manual labor, shortening processing cycles and minimizing waste.

Artificial intelligence will play a role as well, Humphrey said. “We see an AI-native base where we can actually learn from each individual piece while digital-twinning them, so each piece ends up with a digital passport,” he said. “We know exactly where every fiber is, the angle of each fiber to the fiber next to it, and then we do in-process CT screening.”

Greg Scofield, an adviser to Radian and former director of the Purdue Hypersonics Laboratory, said Radian is taking an integrated approach to the challenges surrounding CMC production. “Designing fiber placement, thermal processing and inspection together creates an opportunity to improve cost and quality throughout the production line, with benefits for customers across defense and space,” he said.

The payoff could be huge: A report from Polaris Market Research suggests the global market for advanced composites could rise to $126 billion by 2034.

In partnership with NASA’s Glenn Research Center, Radian has already tested a patent-pending composite material called Dur-E-Therm at temperatures exceeding 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit (1,480 degrees Celsius) under conditions that simulate hypersonic flight.

Radian’s next steps are to select the site for Foundry 1 and begin construction while continuing CMC development at partner facilities. That’s a tall order for a small company.

Humphrey said the company currently has about 20 employees working at locations including the University of Washington’s Advanced Composites Center. Back in 2022, Radian announced a $27.5 million funding round that brought total investment to $32 million at the time. Humphrey said Radian has raised additional funding since then, but he wasn’t ready to share updated figures.

So, how much will Foundry 1 cost? “We’re not quite ready to put a pin in the number,” Humphrey said. “It’s fair to say it’s sub — not a lot less, but it’s sub $100 million in terms of total capital to stand this up for what we’re doing.”

He acknowledged that following through on the plan for Foundry 1 will require raising more capital. “It is part of what we do, and we have a really super group of investors that have been behind us for a long time,” he said.

Humphrey said the Radian One space plane remains the focus of the company’s long-term vision — but for now, the company is devoting all of its resources and capital to Foundry 1.

“It’s the bottleneck to Radian One being successful,” he said. “We think that by applying all of our attention to that, it serves the broader market but also serves advancing Radian One. Both of those are hard things, so we’re going to focus on one hard thing at a time.”

Is Radian becoming an advanced materials and aerospace company? Humphrey said that’s “a good way to think about it,” but he emphasized that aerospace still gets top billing.

“I’d rather be launching today than just be building CMCs,” he said. “But building CMCs is what gets us to flying tomorrow. By advancing materials, it’s our single best way to be ready for Space 3.0, if you want to call it that. … At times we have to be adaptable to really move the project forward, and sometimes it goes a little sideways before you go forward. It’s just the way I’ve come to accept it.”

#5430. Lawmakers form bipartisan caucus to create meaningful AI safety legislation

A bipartisan group of more than two dozen congressional lawmakers said today they’re forming a new AI Safety and Innovation Caucus to tackle the growing security risks posed by the advances in sophisticated artificial intelligence models.

The lawmakers cited the July hack of Hugging Face Inc.’s servers by a team of autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI Group PBC, which broke out of an isolated sandbox environment, as an example of these risks. They also pointed to another incident involving the now-public Anthropic PBC, which also reported that its agents escaped their testing environments to access third-party systems.

These incidents have “underscored the need for Congress to better understand these risks and develop policy solutions,” said Representative George Whitesides (D-California), a co-chair of the caucus. “As AI capabilities accelerate, so do the potential consequences of catastrophic misuse, loss of control over advanced systems and threats to national security.”

Whitesides (pictured) is co-chairing the caucus alongside Representatives Nathanial Moran (R-TX) and Don Beyer (D-Virginia). In a post on X, they stressed the need for bipartisan collaboration to create the basic policy guardrails for AI safety, citing the growing concerns of the American public.

Does it feel like there's a new tech or AI crisis every day? Recent headlines are raising serious concerns about our digital safety and security.

Today, I'm joining @RepDonBeyer, @RepNateMoran, and over 20 of our colleagues to launch the bipartisan AI Safety and Innovation… pic.twitter.com/bhMyygy1J6

— Rep. George Whitesides (@Rep_Whitesides) November 19, 2026

The 26-member caucus includes seven Republicans, which is a surprising number given that the White House administration under President Donald Trump has strongly opposed any heavy-handed regulation of the AI industry. The goal of the caucus is to identify “targeted solutions” that ensure AI remains under control without derailing innovation and threatening America’s lead in the industry.

Whitesides said the lawmakers will focus on two things: proposing legislation to augment AI safety, and responding quickly to high-profile security incidents by gathering developers, independent experts and government officials to brief lawmakers and come up with solutions.

“We want to be a conduit through which effective, responsible legislation can be refined and brought to the floor of the House,” Whitesides told Politico in an interview. He said the group will work together to propose, provide feedback and endorse new AI legislation. He believes there’s an urgent need for this, because most other groups within the House are more focused on educating members or creating legislation within their own parties, he said.

Another thing the caucus intends to do is to pursue relationships with outside AI experts who can help lawmakers to navigate complex policy decisions. It also wants to help raise public awareness around AI and its safety issues, and ensure members outside of relevant committees have the tools they need to contribute to new legislation and debate.

In the recent midterm elections, Americans made it clear that AI is becoming a major issue for governance. Moreover, a recent survey revealed that 43% of Americans don’t trust either of the two major political parties to properly get a grip on AI safety, according to a one-pager that accompanied the press release.

“Artificial intelligence affects every American, and it should not be a partisan issue,” Moran said. “This caucus gives us a place to find the areas of consensus, set partisanship aside and put smart, targeted policies in place so we can innovate while we keep people safe. Congress needs to be prepared.”

#5429. Target’s turnaround is paying off, with operating profit up 76%, helped by a $301 million tariff windfall

After years of declining sales and dwindling store traffic, Target’s turnaround plan under CEO Michael Fiddelke is showing gains. The retail giant reported $26.45 billion in Q3 merchandise sales for the three months ending Oct. 31, up 6.9% from last year and beating analysts’ expectations of $25.96 billion. Operating profit was $1.67 billion, up 76% from last year and beating analysts’ expectations of $1.3 billion.

But there’s a wrinkle: $301 million of that profit came from refunds of President Donald Trump’s tariffs, about 18% of the total, according to Target’s Q3 filing released on Nov. 18. Over the first nine months of this year, Target recognized $1.3 billion in tariff refunds following the Supreme Court’s ruling in February that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not give the president authority to impose tariffs.

Still, even without that windfall, Target seems to be recovering. Excluding the $301 million, Target would have reported about $1.37 billion in operating profit, still higher than the $948 million it recorded a year earlier. Neil Saunders, managing director of GlobalData Retail, told Fortune it’s a sign Target is genuinely gaining with consumers.

“Tariff refunds are certainly very helpful to Target, and they have provided a very nice boost to the bottom line,” Saunders said. “That said, even if you take the tariff gain out, Target is still up on the prior year, and I think that really reflects the fact that the business does have some momentum on the consumer side.”

He said Target’s investments in revamped stores and new products are helping it compete with other retailers beyond price point, saying “the recovery has multiple dimensions to it.” Target had earmarked $5 billion for this year to upgrade its physical stores. It also introduced nearly 3,000 new beauty products from 60 brands and added 3,000 food items earlier this year. On Sept. 10, it launched Target Beauty Studio, bringing 90 prestige and international brands to shelves, including French nailcare and Korean cosmetics, with two-thirds of those brands being new to Target. Those categories are Target’s strongest Q3 performers, with more than 9% growth in beauty and nearly 7% growth in food and beverage year over year. Overall comparable sales increased 5.6%, supported by a 5% increase in customer traffic.

This follows a tough 2025, where Target saw comparable sales falling 2.6% as shoppers pulled back on discretionary purchases. It faced growing competition from Amazon and Walmart and boycotts over its DEI rollbacks. Saunders said Target is trying to recapture itself as an “interesting place to go and discover things” so that consumers, already feeling squeezed by the cost of living, are more willing to open their wallets for “Tarzhay,” its chic-at-affordable-prices brand identity.

“If consumers are spending a little bit more on something, they want that extra expenditure to be justified, and the only way you can really justify it is by having really nice products or really interesting products that people want to buy,” he said.

#5428. NEWWAVE Unveils New Brand Identity and Strategic Positioning as a Trusted Technology Partner at 15

HANOI, Vietnam, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Marking its 15th anniversary, NEWWAVE announces a new brand identity and strategic positioning as a Trusted Technology Partner, building on its engineering expertise and evolving capabilities to address changing business needs in an era of AI and rapid technological advancement.

The announcement reflects the Vietnam-based company's commitment to moving beyond software execution toward a more consultative, end-to-end partnership, helping global clients navigate technology complexity, make informed decisions, and implement reliable solutions that deliver lasting business value.

As AI, cloud technologies, and increasingly interconnected systems reshape business operations, enterprise technology decisions involve greater complexity. Beyond technical execution, businesses need partners who understand operational priorities, navigate integration challenges, and maintain reliable systems over time.

For NEWWAVE, this evolution aligns with lessons drawn from 15 years of international delivery. Its renewed positioning emphasizes a business-oriented approach that connects technology decisions with practical needs, from identifying challenges and shaping solutions to implementation and ongoing support.

"As technology decisions become increasingly connected to business outcomes, our priority is to work alongside clients with a deep understanding of their challenges, clear accountability, and long-term commitment to the solutions we build," said To Quang Duy, CEO of NEWWAVE.

Fifteen Years of Engineering Excellence and Global Ambition

Founded in 2011, NEWWAVE began with a small engineering team navigating limited resources and diverse client requirements. Engineers often took on multiple responsibilities, learning new technologies while solving practical delivery challenges.

As projects grew more complex, so did the team's understanding of what reliable software development demands: business context, cross-functional collaboration, and accountability throughout delivery.

Today, NEWWAVE brings together more than 300 engineers and specialists, has served over 200 clients worldwide, and has delivered more than 800 projects. Its commitment to reliable delivery is supported by ISO 9001:2015 for quality management and ISO/IEC 27001:2022 information security management certifications. These foundations have shaped a company that views technical expertise, consistent delivery, and client trust as interconnected responsibilities.

NEWWAVE's strategic direction brings together five core capabilities: Digital Consulting, Software Engineering, Cloud & DevOps, Data & AI, and Application Services.

These capabilities can be combined to address different stages of a client's technology journey, from assessing business needs and developing solutions to modernizing existing systems, integrating technologies, and supporting ongoing operations.

Depending on business objectives and project scope, clients can engage NEWWAVE for specific technology requirements or broader initiatives involving multiple capabilities. This flexible approach reflects its commitment to delivering solutions suited to each organization's needs rather than applying a single delivery model.

The new identity represents both the experience NEWWAVE has built over 15 years and its ambition to deepen relationships with global clients through technical expertise, responsible delivery, and lasting partnership.

#5427. Booking Holdings’ travel startup Vayo starts booking trips with AI agents, even on rival Expedia

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:20 amNovember 17, 2026 at 6:21 am

Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup launched by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel plans — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of users in its invite-only beta.

That includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group. Vayo confirmed that its AI agents book there by navigating Expedia’s website, without a direct integration or partnership for those bookings.

The company says Vayo recommends the best option for the traveler, wherever that option is booked, not just through its parent company’s brands.

Vayo is led by Mike Fridgen, a longtime Seattle entrepreneur with deep roots in travel. Booking Holdings, the parent of Booking.com, Priceline, Kayak and OpenTable, said last month that it plans to invest $100 million in Vayo, depending on its progress and market conditions.

Companies are still working out how to handle AI agents that use their sites on behalf of customers. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com, saying the agent didn’t identify itself.

When Vayo launched last month, Fridgen said it was relying on APIs and direct partnerships with travel companies, in part to avoid the risk of being blocked. Vayo says no site has blocked its bookings so far.

How the bookings work: Vayo’s new booking features work in two ways. It can book hotels, rental cars and activities through a direct connection with sister company Booking.com, and it has similar links to OpenTable for restaurants and SeatGeek for event tickets.

For flights and other bookings, its AI agents navigate the booking websites, signing in to the traveler’s existing accounts where needed and completing the purchase. Every booking requires the traveler’s approval, the company says.

If a site doesn’t allow AI agents, Vayo leaves that booking to the traveler.

Vayo uses 1Password to sign in to travelers’ accounts and, on sites other than Booking.com, Stripe’s Link agent wallet to pay, without seeing their passwords or card details, the company says. It reports a reservation as confirmed only after the supplier confirms it.

Payments and pricing: Travelers pay whichever company they book with, and Vayo is not the merchant of record. The company declined to share details on commissions, saying its partner arrangements are still taking shape and won’t factor into its recommendations.

When Booking.com has the best option, Vayo users get Genius Level 3 pricing, Booking.com’s top loyalty tier, with discounts of up to 20% on select stays.

The service is free to use during the invite-only beta. Responding to GeekWire’s questions, Vayo didn’t say how many people are using it or how many have completed a booking.

Who’s behind Vayo: Fridgen, the Vayo co-founder and CEO, was on the founding team of Expedia’s vacation-package business, led Alaska Airlines’ digital business and was founding head of product at airfare-prediction startup Farecast, before leading Decide.com and Madrona Venture Labs.

His co-founder and CTO is Allen Chen, the former CTO of Fanatics Collectibles, who previously co-founded Seattle software startups CloudPress and DataBlade. Ian Fliflet, OfferUp’s former chief growth officer, is head of growth. Vayo had about 20 employees, all working in downtown Seattle, when it launched last month.

Next on its product roadmap, the company says it plans to work inside the messaging apps people already use, and to let groups of travelers plan trips together.

#5426. ‘Strict cell phone bans seem to plug about half of that leak’: Harvard economist finds locking up students’ phones adds 1–2 weeks of learning a year

Making students lock their phones in pouches during the school day adds one to two weeks of learning a year, according to a national study released Tuesday.

The study, from Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research, with researchers at Dartmouth and the testing nonprofit NWEA, found that schools that required students to store their phones in pouches experienced an annual boost in achievement growth of 0.01 standard deviations—equivalent to one to two weeks of additional learning per year (or restoring two minutes per hour of class time). The team followed 3.3 million students at 4,600 schools across 49 states and Washington, D.C., from the 2021–22 through 2025–26 school years.

The gains are small, but they last. Achievement gains begin in the first year of the ban and appear to continue three years later, and the effect held across elementary, middle and high schools, and across rich and poor ones.

The result breaks with the last big study of school phone bans, which found in May that they did close to nothing for test scores. The argument has money riding on it: New York and 16 other states put bell-to-bell bans in place last school year, with the cost of a pouch at about $25 a student, according to Tom Kane, an economist and education professor who serves as the director of Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research.

That matters because of how far students have fallen. Kane released an education scorecard that traced a “learning recession” back to 2013, years before the pandemic. Between 2013 and 2024, eighth-grade math and reading achievement fell by roughly one grade equivalent. The slide lines up with the spread of smartphones: In 2011, fewer than a quarter of teen students had access to smartphones. By 2018, 95% did.

“Strict cell phone bans seem to plug about half of that leak,” Kane said in a statement.

As for the other half, Kane told Fortune: “The two main suspects are declining test-based accountability following the replacement of the No Child Left Behind Act and out-of-school social media use.” He added: “One of the big mysteries our study did not explain is the precipitous drop for the lowest achieving students. The abandonment of test-based accountability and out-of-school social media use could be most costly for them.”

A National Bureau of Economic Research study found in May that strict bans had close to zero effect on test scores. That team did find statistically significant gains with Yondr pouches in high school math, but those gains were offset by ban-related learning losses in middle school.

Tom Dee, a Stanford professor and coauthor of that study, told NPR he considers the early results on phone bans “largely disappointing.” Neither study has been published in a peer-reviewed journal. The two also measured different things: The NBER study pooled school-level mean test scores at several thousand Yondr-adopting schools, while the Harvard study used student-level scores at 844 schools that use both Yondr pouches and tests administered by NWEA.

Kane said the Harvard study, which is not a randomized trial, compared achievement growth at “roughly 800 Yondr-adopting schools before and after adoption against the achievement growth of 3,800 matched comparison schools over the same time period.” He added: “The fact that the two groups of schools seemed to [be] following similar trends in the years before adoption made us more confident.”

The Harvard team flags its own limits, too. It found signs that state-mandated bans in 22 states raised reading and math scores last year, but researchers cautioned that these findings might be confounded by preexisting trends in the states implementing bans.

“Given the difference in post-pandemic recovery in the states with and without bans, it will be hard for anyone—not just us—to discern the effect of the bans by comparing across states,” Kane said. A better test, he said, would compare schools that already had strict bans of their own with schools in the same state that adopted bans only after the state law passed.

Kane’s pitch to districts is about money: “$25 is a small price to pay for an additional one to two weeks of instruction per student,” he said.

Advocates say the study confirms what schools have already seen. “Anecdotal evidence has already demonstrated that schools making the transition have the ability to change their school culture and bring face-to-face interaction back to the classroom and common areas like the cafeteria,” Ashwin Verghese, communications director at the children’s advocacy nonprofit Fairplay, told Fortune. “Now, the Harvard study is backing that up with evidence of steady educational gains.”

Julie Scelfo, a mother and the founder and executive director of Mothers Against Media Addiction, said the gains matter more than they sound. “It’s easy to forget that education is sequential, meaning that basic building blocks must be established before a child can go on to higher orders of learning,” she told Fortune. “So a week or two may not sound like much, but it actually adds up to quite a lot across a child’s K–12 education.” The benefit isn’t only academic, she added, but includes “the ability to focus and develop other executive functioning skills that are critical to every area of a child’s life.”

Scelfo acknowledged the study “doesn’t say much about phone and social media use after school,” but said the rise of smartphones and social media among young people tracks with what pediatric groups have declared a national emergency in child and adolescent mental health. “Parents should do everything possible to delay access to these products until safeguards are in place,” she said. She pointed to state laws such as the Age-Appropriate Design Code and New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act as models for other states.

New York City has banned, unbanned, and rebanned phones in schools. The city’s ban dated to the late 1980s, but Mayor Michael Bloomberg started strongly enforcing it in 2006. A small industry grew up around the ban: Storage trucks outside schools charged students about $1 a day to hold their phones. One van owner in Far Rockaway told DNAinfo he netted around $160 to $170 per day. ​

In 2015, Mayor Bill de Blasio scrapped the ban, calling it “simply out of touch with the realities of modern-day parenting,” according to CBS New York. He also called it unfair, because the ban was enforced mostly at schools with metal detectors in low-income neighborhoods.

A decade later, the city reversed course again. When Gov. Kathy Hochul signed the 2026 state budget into law on May 9, 2025, she made New York the largest state in the nation to restrict smartphones and other internet-enabled personal devices throughout the entire school day. New York was one of 17 states that adopted bell-to-bell bans for last school year.

The pouches at the center of the study weren’t built for classrooms. Graham Dugoni, a former professional soccer player, founded Yondr in 2014. He found early success with live performers, including comedian Dave Chappelle, who used the pouches to keep audiences from filming performances starting in 2015. A California high school was using them as early as 2019. More than 3,300 schools nationwide began using the pouches between the 2019–20 and 2025–26 school years.

The researchers say the bigger unknown is what students do with their phones outside school. They point to Meta’s $17 billion settlement with state attorneys general, which requires a block on app access between midnight and 6 a.m. and muted notifications during school hours (8 a.m. to 3 p.m.), save for direct messages. The Harvard team wants states to encourage other platforms used by youth—YouTube, TikTok, Snapchat, etc.—to adopt similar restrictions so students don’t simply switch apps.

Verghese said other platforms “should absolutely adopt the same limits, but they can’t stop there.” Fairplay was disappointed that the settlement does not turn off by default “recommendation algorithms that connect kids to predators and send young people down dangerous rabbit holes,” he said, and he argued it was “too focused on offering parents tools rather than restricting harmful features.” He added: “Even if other companies adopted these restrictions, two hours per day on four or five different platforms adds up to far too much time.

“What families really need is for Congress to pass comprehensive legislation that will force companies like Meta to stop designing for addiction and make their products safer by default,” Verghese said, calling on lawmakers to pass the Kids Online Safety Act in the coming weeks.

Teodora Pavkovic, director of well-being and parent advocacy at Qustodio and Aura Parents, which make parental-control apps, told Fortune that a school-day ban “only addresses a fraction of students’ digital lives, leaving the hours outside school largely untouched.” Aura Parents’ 2026 State of the Youth Report found that sleep is the single strongest predictor of a teen’s digital well-being. “Teens with low well-being spend three times more time on their devices overnight, pick up their phones seven times more often, and take twice as long to disengage after bedtime,” Pavkovic said.

Kids don’t fully make up for lost screen time after school, Pavkovic said, “but they do pack their social lives into those hours.” Among nearly 30,000 children ages 7 to 17 in Aura’s data, about a third use their devices during school hours. By 3 p.m., more than 60% do. “School phone bans are a helpful starting point, but they need to be paired with healthy boundaries at home, like keeping phones out of bedrooms at night,” she said.

Kane says he now wants to study students’ smartphone and social media use outside of school.

#5425. LIVE – Bitcoin Price, Gold and Oil Fall: Should the US Repeat Its $2.2T 2020 Rescue?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price is getting hammered in the aftermath of the FOMC minutes. Gold isn’t doing much better; oil and stocks have joined the sell-off. The markets are already nervous about the Federal Reserve’s next decision, and yesterday’s FOMC minutes gave us another reason to worry: policymakers are still talking about raising interest rates.

Almost all officials saw further hikes as appropriate under their baseline outlook. Two even floated the possibility of a bigger increase if inflation refuses to cool.

This is a nasty combination for markets. Bitcoin fell around 3.2% over 24 hours, gold futures dropped more than 3%, and WTI crude lost around 3%. The dollar climbed to a 19-month high. Wall Street was mixed, though, with the Nasdaq finishing higher while the Dow and S&P 500 slipped.

Here’s the comparison. In March 2020, the Fed was slashing rates, buying bonds and throwing emergency liquidity at a financial system under immense pressure. Congress approved a $2.2 trillion rescue package to keep households and businesses afloat.

Today, we are watching markets fall while the Fed is possibly making money more expensive.

October’s FOMC minutes weren’t exactly what markets wanted to hear. The Fed held rates at 3.75%–4% during its October meeting, but almost all participants believed further increases would likely be appropriate. Two officials also said a hike larger than the usual 25 basis points could be considered if inflation data came in hotter than expected.

And there was more in those minutes than just interest rates. Officials raised concerns about hedge fund leverage and the growing debt tied to artificial intelligence investments. Some financing arrangements could become a problem if investors start questioning enormous AI spending, and whether it will generate the returns companies expect.

The risk is forced selling. Leveraged funds facing losses or investor withdrawals may have to dump assets quickly, potentially pushing prices down further.

Gold has its own problem. A stronger dollar and higher interest rates make it less attractive to investors who can earn a return elsewhere. Bitcoin price, meanwhile, remains vulnerable when traders cut exposure to speculative assets.

The Fed hasn’t declared a financial emergency. Its minutes actually describe the banking system as resilient. But officials are clearly paying attention to risks that could amplify a market shock.

March 2020 was brutal. COVID-19 lockdowns brought businesses to a standstill. Investors rushed for cash, stocks collapsed, and Bitcoin briefly slipped below $4,000 after sitting near $10,000 just weeks earlier.

The Federal Reserve didn’t wait around. It cut rates by 50 basis points on March 3, then delivered another 100-basis-point cut on March 15. The federal funds target range dropped to 0%–0.25%.

On March 23, the Fed announced unlimited purchases of Treasury securities and mortgage-backed securities, promising to buy whatever amounts were necessary to support market functioning. It also introduced emergency lending programmes to keep credit flowing.

President Donald Trump signed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act on March 27. The package included direct payments to eligible Americans, expanded unemployment benefits, and assistance for businesses struggling to survive lockdowns. The Paycheck Protection Program gave small businesses access to loans designed to help them keep employees on payroll.

The response was enormous, but the economy was facing an extraordinary shutdown. Millions of Americans had lost their jobs, businesses were closing, and normal economic activity had practically disappeared.

Markets eventually bounced back. The S&P 500 recovered its pre-pandemic record by August 2020. Bitcoin climbed above $12,000 during the same month.

The current US economy isn’t in the same position as it was during the pandemic. Inflation remains above the Fed’s 2% target, and policymakers are discussing rate increases rather than cuts.

Slashing rates to zero and flooding markets with liquidity might help asset prices. It could also make inflation worse. Another multitrillion-dollar spending package would face an entirely different argument in Congress, especially without a pandemic-style economic shutdown.

The Fed doesn’t have to choose between doing nothing and repeating the 2020 rescue. If banks struggle to fund themselves or credit markets start freezing, it can step in with emergency lending and liquidity operations. That’s a much narrower response than another round of unlimited bond purchases.

The Fed’s concerns about leveraged hedge funds and AI financing could become more relevant if investors start selling indiscriminately. A market correction is one thing. Forced selling spreading through the financial system is another.

At the moment, there’s no evidence that we’re facing another March 2020. The banking system remains resilient, and falling Bitcoin prices alone won’t trigger a government bailout.

But the Fed has a problem that didn’t exist in quite the same way during the pandemic. It may need to protect financial stability without giving up its fight against inflation. In 2020, Washington opened the taps. This time, we wait and see, and Bitcoin price will survive.

#5424. Seattle fleet tracking company Zonar names Atlanta-based CEO, who says HQ is staying put

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am

Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking company, has a new CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.

Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no plans to change that.” He said he visits the company’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.

Consoli succeeds Charles Kriete, who led GPS Trackit when the Florida-based company acquired Zonar from German auto supplier Continental in late 2024. Kriete ran the combined company, which is backed by private equity firm Inverness Graham, until September and is now a board advisor.

Consoli previously held revenue chief roles at legal software company Assembly Software, Skuid and Liaison Technologies, which OpenText acquired for $310 million in 2018. He also led North American sales at asset-tracking company I.D. Systems, and started his career as an aerospace engineer at General Dynamics.

Zonar sells GPS tracking hardware, cameras and software that fleet operators use to monitor vehicle location, fuel use and driver behavior, and says it has more than 400,000 active units installed.

Its biggest market is student transportation. Consoli said Zonar serves about half of the school bus market, and its customers also include trucking and delivery fleets such as US Foods, utilities and small businesses.

Zonar’s Seattle-area customers include the Kirkland Police Department, which in 2024 became the first agency to roll out Zonar’s mobile inspection app and GPS asset trackers in its patrol fleet after a pilot program. Officers use the app to complete a digital inspection of their patrol car before each shift, checking tire pressure, emergency equipment such as defibrillators and the rear enclosure used to transport suspects. Each inspection takes two to four minutes, according to the company.

Zonar has 409 employees after combining with GPS Trackit, including 70 in Seattle, more than in any other state. Consoli declined to share revenue figures but said Zonar has “more than doubled our profitability in the last 10 months,” helped by new pricing, a reorganized sales team, renegotiated hardware contracts and cost cuts.

Zonar has added 1,000 new customers so far this year, a spokesperson said. Sales to existing customers are running at 118% of the company’s 2026 plan, while new customer wins are at 97%.

“We’re a very attractive asset in this market right now,” Consoli said.

Zonar competes with larger players including Samsara, Motive and Geotab. Consoli said Zonar sets itself apart through customer service and flexibility. It offers Zonar One, a turnkey system that customers can install the day after ordering, and Zonar Flex, which is customized for large enterprise fleets.

He said those customers are “not going to get that level of tailoring and customization from any of the big players.”

Consoli also wants to lean further into AI. The goal is to send customers proactive alerts instead of making fleet managers dig through dashboards after the fact: a driver running stop signs, a truck off its route, or a school bus running late. Zonar already lets school districts notify parents through an app when a bus is delayed.

“Fleet operators today are really focused on outcomes,” Consoli said. “They want to know that compliance is handled, safety is improved.”

Founded in Seattle in 2001, Zonar was majority-owned by Continental from 2016 until the 2024 sale. The company cut 57 jobs in August 2024, when it had more than 300 employees, and made more layoffs after the acquisition.

#5423. Glenn Kelman’s next act: Former Redfin CEO takes on health care with stealthy startup Sojourn

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 9:41 am

Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.

The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.

“Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software company, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site.

His co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen, an internist who co-founded digital health company Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation.

This is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the company filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health plans that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management.

Kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words, confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their plans “after we’ve built our product.”

But after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health.

Searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.”

From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com, which sketches out the plan.

Why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story.

“Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care.

“The choices were all terrible,” it says.

Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost.

As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site says, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.”

Kelman, by his own account, is new to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now.

“I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote.

The team: In a LinkedIn post last week, Kelman said the founding team also includes Jennifer Chao and Ben Baker, with Sasha Aickin “adding some part-time magic.” He promised that “the mission is good and the ambition is vast.”

The lineup draws on Kelman’s past and the health insurance world:

Chao and Aickin both worked with Kelman at Plumtree Software, the enterprise software company he co-founded in 1996, before following him to Redfin. Sojourn’s recruiting page nods to the pattern: “We’re honored by the old friends who have worked with us from company to company, but we’re also eager to bring in new blood.”

The Sojourn site says the company is likely to have engineering hubs in Seattle for the member experience, San Francisco for the clinical platform, and Austin for the claims system.

AI all the way down: Sojourn is hiring software engineers and product managers “at every level of the organization.” The first thing on its list of qualifications: experience using frontier AI tools “to generate reliable, high-scale production code.”

That fits with his guest column. A recruiter told him Seattle’s startup scene was “dead,” he wrote, and a friend described CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at companies with old code. Kelman wrote that “the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.”

What we don’t know: The website doesn’t say when Sojourn plans to launch or where it will offer coverage first, although Chen’s bio suggests employers will be key customers, describing a care model “designed around the member and the employer who pays for it.”

A new health plan typically requires state insurance licenses and significant capital reserves, and the company hasn’t disclosed any funding. Kelman wrote in his column that he “met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea,” but he didn’t name them, and a search of SEC filings for Sojourn Health and Silica Health found no record of a fundraise.

In June, he joined venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence, saying at the time that he was still looking to start a new mission-driven enterprise, a process that involved “exploring ideas that are never going to work and howling at the moon.” It’s not clear whether Greylock is among his backers.

Kelman stepped down as Redfin CEO in January, six months after Rocket Companies completed its $1.75 billion acquisition of the Seattle brokerage. He said at the time that he wanted to find “another mission-driven enterprise outside of real estate.”

He appears to have found one. Whether health care is more or less screwed up than real estate is a question that will have to wait until he’s ready to chat.

#5422. I Built an AI Chatbot for $0. Here’s the Exact Stack.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

You don’t need money to ship a real, production-grade AI chatbot. You need to know which free tiers to stack. Here’s the exact toolchain.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’m an AI engineer and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds. I also built Rune Score, a sports analytics chatbot, and it cost me $0.

From the outside, it looks like a simple chatbot. Under the hood, it’s a distributed system that has to handle the freshness of sports data, user rephrasing, extraction failures, LLM call costs, streaming, memory, fallbacks and security. Here’s the stack I actually used to build it layer by layer, what I did with each tool and what’s free about it.

Before writing a line of code, a chatbot needs a face. I used Figma to generate the chatbot’s logo straight from a text prompt describing the style and mood I wanted, then iterated on it a few times inside Figma itself rather than handing it to a designer. Figma’s own free plan covers individual use with unlimited file storage.

The whole project lives in a GitHub repository, private while the chatbot was still rough, and it’s the same repo both Claude and Codex connect to. GitHub’s free plan gives unlimited private repositories with a limited feature set and 2,000 minutes a month of Actions included on GitHub Free for standard runners on private repos, enough to run tests and basic automation without hitting a wall. Standard runners on public repositories stay free no matter how much you use them.

Claude Code did the actual building, the chatbot’s backend and the AI agents running inside it. I kept it connected directly to the GitHub repository and never let it touch the main branch directly: every task ran on its own branch, and nothing merged until I’d reviewed the diff myself and approved the pull request. The genuine free route in is a Guest Pass: if someone you know already pays for Claude Max, they can send you one, and it unlocks a full week of free Pro-level access.

I gave Codex a different job, connected to the same repository but never writing production code itself. It reviewed what Claude had actually shipped, acting as an independent judge on pull requests, and I also used it to draft the next development prompt I’d hand back to Claude, effectively having one model plan the work and another execute it. Codex has a genuine free plan at $0 a month. Free accounts run on GPT-5.6 Terra, OpenAI’s cost-efficient model for that tier. The free plan is capped at a usage limit rather than a time limit, which is exactly the size of job a reviewer role needs.

I bought the chatbot’s domain name through Cloudflare, where registration is usually cheap since Cloudflare sells at cost with no markup, and kept the DNS in the same place rather than splitting it across providers. From there I used Cloudflare’s free security layer to protect the domain, including rate limiting rules to stop any single source from hammering the chatbot’s endpoints. Cloudflare’s WAF documentation covers exactly this kind of rule, and the core protections, DNS, DDoS protection, and basic security features, are included on the free plan.

I used Railway for both the backend and the frontend, with a separate test environment so I could ship changes quickly without risking the live version. New accounts get a one-time free credit grant before any card is required, and unlike some free hosts, Railway doesn’t put your service to sleep by default the way its own documentation describes for its optional Serverless feature, so there’s no cold start tax on the free tier unless you turn that behavior on yourself.

Users sign up and log in through Clerk, and I built the whole flow using Clerk’s own test environment first, so I could try edge cases without creating real accounts or sending real emails. The free plan covers up to 50,000 monthly active users at no cost, which is more than enough room to move from testing into a real launch on the same setup.

Conversations, users and application data all sit in Neon, a serverless Postgres database that scales down to zero and stops costing anything the moment nobody’s using it. The free tier includes enough storage and monthly compute hours for a real early product, with no credit card required to start.

Once the chatbot’s AI agents were actually running, I needed to see what they were doing under the hood: which prompts fired, where they failed, and what they cost. Langfuse traces all of that, and its free Hobby plan includes a healthy monthly allowance of tracing events, enough to debug and monitor a real chatbot without paying anything.

I wired Exa and Firecrawl directly into the AI agents responsible for research inside the chatbot’s runtime, so the chatbot itself can decide when it needs to look something up. Exa handles the search, finding relevant pages for a given question, and its free tier hands new accounts starting credit plus a recurring monthly allowance with no payment method required. It also ships a playground where you can test a search query directly in the browser before wiring it into your agent. Firecrawl handles what comes next, turning a page Exa found into clean text the agent can actually read, and its own free plan includes a monthly credit allowance with no card needed either.

Before committing to a specific model for the chatbot’s agents, I used NVIDIA’s API Catalog to try several without paying per token. NVIDIA gives any developer free credits to test a wide range of hosted models through its own endpoints, which made it easy to compare options before locking in whichever one actually powers the chatbot in production.

The chatbot talks back, not just types, so I used Azure AI Speech for text to speech, letting the chatbot switch between a female or male neural voice depending on the setup. The free tier includes a real monthly allowance of neural voice characters at no cost, enough for genuine daily conversations before you’d ever see a bill.

I’m an AI engineer and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds. I also built Rune Score, a sports analytics chatbot, and it cost me $0.

From the outside, it looks like a simple chatbot. Under the hood, it’s a distributed system that has to handle the freshness of sports data, user rephrasing, extraction failures, LLM call costs, streaming, memory, fallbacks and security. Here’s the stack I actually used to build it layer by layer, what I did with each tool and what’s free about it.

Before writing a line of code, a chatbot needs a face. I used Figma to generate the chatbot’s logo straight from a text prompt describing the style and mood I wanted, then iterated on it a few times inside Figma itself rather than handing it to a designer. Figma’s own free plan covers individual use with unlimited file storage.

#5421. Britain and the Pentagon told people to get ready in October. Now Costco is selling out of generators, and billionaires have ‘apocalypse insurance’

Costco shoppers are “pantry-loading” again. As of Sunday night, 21 of the 26 high-ticket generators on Costco’s website were sold out, according to Mizuho Securities analyst David Bellinger. One of the sold-out models, a Kohler, runs about $7,000.

The last time Costco members bought like this was March 2020, when then-CFO Richard Galanti told investors the buying was “off the charts” across the U.S. On March 12 of that year, U.S. toilet paper sales were up 734% from the same day a year earlier.

This time the buying picked up after a run of tech failures that has kept people out of their email, grounded flights, and left bank customers unable to move money, and households are now spending to get ready for the next one. Bellinger told clients that consumer anxiety after the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stop for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up on social media is behind the buying. He raised his Costco price target to $1,150 from $1,100 and said Walmart and Sam’s Club could see similar “pantry-loading lifts.”

Costco CFO Gary Millerchip told Bloomberg that stronger sales of rice, canned goods, water, paper products, generators, and batteries came toward the end of October. Mizuho says Home Depot and Lowe’s could sell more generators, too.

Smaller sellers are seeing the same thing. Survival Frog, which sells emergency food, radios, and other survival gear, saw sales jump 450% between Oct. 27 and Nov. 16 compared with prior weeks, founder and CEO Byron Walker told Axios. Most of the recent buyers were new customers, and food, led by canned meats, is the top seller, followed by radios, solar generators, battery packs, and water filters. Competitors saw similar trends, Walker said.

“You can’t turn on the news without hearing about a new cyberattack or a tech meltdown,” he said.

Costco’s reported sales don’t show the spike yet. U.S. comparable sales excluding gas rose 8.1% in the four weeks ended Nov. 1, according to Costco, the same pace as the first nine weeks of its fiscal year. Mizuho estimates U.S. growth sped up to 11% to 12% in the last week of October and into early November, and holiday shopping may be part of that.

The Federal Reserve’s cash data covers only the week before the bank outages. Currency in circulation averaged about $2.5 trillion in the week ended Nov. 11, roughly 3% more than a year earlier, according to the Fed’s weekly H.4.1 release. The next reading, covering the week of the Chase outage, comes out Thursday afternoon.

The stockpiling began more than two weeks before Microsoft 365 went down on Nov. 12 and the FAA’s nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, which halted departures for more than four hours, the longest in 25 years. In late October, governments sent the warnings. On Oct. 21, CISA said critical PHP vulnerabilities required immediate patching; PHP runs nearly 70% of websites. The next day, the U.K. launched its “Be Ready” campaign, urging families to stockpile three days of water, shelf-stable food, and cash. Within days came reports that the Pentagon wants every major base in the lower 48 states able to run on its own for at least 90 days. All of it landed during what was dubbed “Black October,” a month of cyberattacks on hundreds of companies and institutions.

Walker credits his sales boom to exactly those warnings: the U.K. and EU urging households to keep three days of supplies, and the Pentagon’s 90-day plan for bases, which fed rumors online of a 90-day U.S. “blackout.”

The ultrawealthy got there first. Reid Hoffman told The New Yorker in 2017 that he believed more than half of Silicon Valley’s billionaires had invested in “apocalypse insurance.” For everyone else, apparently, there’s Costco.

A few years ago, the Costco hedge was gold. The warehouse club’s one-ounce bars sold out within hours after their 2023 launch, and Costco capped how many bars each member could buy. That trade has cooled. U.S. Mint sales of gold bullion coins fell 34% in the first 10 months of 2026 from a year earlier, to 185,500 ounces, and October’s 11,000 ounces were down 58% from October 2025. North America was the only region to see outflows from gold ETFs in October, $512 million, according to the World Gold Council. Gold fell 6.3% for the month and fell to about $3,693 an ounce on Thursday, its lowest since September 2025. Costco members who bought bars in September are down about $700 apiece, by 24/7 Wall St.’s math.

Officials keep saying the outages aren’t connected to one another. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday there’s “zero evidence” linking them. “The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA,” he said. Vice President JD Vance told Fox News’ Laura Ingraham that friends have asked him whether they should be “preparing to build a bunker” or stock up on food and water. “And my answer to that is no,” he said. “We do not see some crisis coming down.”

Part of the problem is the cleanup from October. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Fox Business that patching after last month’s PHP alert left some systems, including at the NSA, that would “not come back up.” Microsoft blamed a “latent defect” in a network fix deployed over the summer. The FAA is switching off its new routers and leaning on 25-year-old equipment, and the White House is starting to admit AI is part of the story.

In the Axios Behind the Curtain column, Jim VandeHei and Mike Allen wrote that government officials and AI experts expect the disruption to last for months, under a catchphrase gaining currency: “Software Beirut.” They told readers to keep more cash on hand in case their bank is down for a day or two, the same advice Britain gave in October.

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.
