#5420. Early data points to Vulcan’s first stage in launch failure that cost Amazon 40 Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA said Tuesday.

In its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit.

That stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA said it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete.

The Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA said. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally.

The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes.

What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn.

ULA said Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based company hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning.

“It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and New Glenn for our return to flight.”

Impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on New Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight.

Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites.

Amazon has said it plans to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

#5419. Anthropic’s $81 Billion IPO Is the Biggest Ever — Here’s Who’s Getting Rich and Who Missed Out

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude is now a $2 trillion public company. Not everyone is happy.

Anthropic, the company behind the popular AI chatbot, surged more than 30% in its Nasdaq debut today after the largest IPO in history. It sold more than 980 million shares at $83 apiece for $81.3 billion, topping the then-record $75 billion SpaceX raised in June, according to The New York Times. Shares opened at $111.50 under the ticker “ANT,” valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion.

The biggest winners of the Anthropic IPO are the company’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, president Daniela Amodei. Each holds a stake that could be worth $20 billion or more, according to the Times. On the VC side, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Iconiq hold stakes worth more than $25 billion at the IPO price, The Wall Street Journal reports. Menlo Ventures’ stake is worth roughly $22.5 billion. Amazon, Google and Gulf sovereign wealth funds are also in line for huge paydays.

Then there’s Sam Bankman-Fried. The FTX founder led Anthropic’s $580 million Series B in 2022. After FTX collapsed, its bankruptcy estate sold the $500 million stake in 2024 for about $1.3 billion. At the IPO price, those shares would be worth roughly $37 billion today. China was also locked out of the offering.

#5418. Anthropic stock pops 30% to $2 trillion market cap in mega IPO

Anthropic’s stock surged more than 30% in its first minutes as a public company, a roaring debut that crowned the AI company—at least briefly—with a stunning, $2 trillion market cap.

Shares of Anthropic opened at $111.50 per share on Thursday, up 34% from the $83 IPO price. The stock pop began to moderate as the trading day continued, and Anthropic finished its first day as a public company up 17%, at $97.17 per share.

The strong demand for Anthropic shares came as the broader market was under pressure, with the Nasdaq down 550 points and the Dow Jones industrial average down 1101 points at the close of market.

At its $97 closing price, Anthropic’s market cap was just shy of $1.8 trillion—an astounding Wall Street debut that instantly puts the five-year-old AI company in the elite club of trillion-dollar public companies, alongside giants such as Alphabet, Apple, and Amazon. (Some calculations use a lower share count that excludes potential dilution from restricted stock, convertible notes, and other items, giving Anthropic a roughly $1.3 trillion market cap).

“This moment is bigger than any one company, or any one country. It will take all of us, working together, to ensure this technology goes well for us and the many generations to come,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in a statement posted on X on Thursday.

Anthropic priced the offering Wednesday night at $83 a share, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, giving the company a $1.5 trillion valuation. Demand was strong enough that it raised the deal to 980 million shares from 825 million.

There had been endless speculation about whether Anthropic would top SpaceX as the largest IPO of all time. At a $1.5 trillion IPO valuation, Anthropic would be the second most valuable IPO of all time, behind SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO in June. Measured by capital raised however, Anthropic’s $79 billion ($81.4 billion, if stock sold by insiders is included) topped the $75 billion raised by SpaceX.

Seven strategic partners, including Google and Nvidia, have also agreed to buy $26 billion of nonvoting Anthropic stock at the IPO price. And the deal’s underwriters also have a “greenshoe” option to purchase an additional 147 million shares of Anthropic stock. If exercised, that would bring the total proceeds of Anthropic’s IPO to $118 billion.

The offering will provide Anthropic with a vital infusion of capital as it seeks to stay ahead in the AI race and to invest in the computing infrastructure to train its models. It will also make instant billionaires out of numerous Anthropic employees and early investors, particularly the seven cofounders who created Anthropic. At least 400 early hires will be worth $100 million or more, according to CNBC.

“Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said in his statement Thursday. “We will not bend to either business or political pressure,” Amodei said, invoking the company’s stated commitment to develop AI technology with safeguards.

Anticipation for the IPOs of Anthropic and its archrival, OpenAI, has been building ever since OpenAI ignited the generative AI boom in late 2022 with the launch of ChatGPT. With OpenAI holding off on its IPO until at least 2027, Anthropic becomes the first pure-play maker of frontier AI models to go public (SpaceX also makes rockets, and Google and Meta both have massive businesses in search and social media).

But the Anthropic IPO also comes at a tenuous time for the AI industry. It’s been barely a week since the sector lost one of its most powerful figures. Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last Thursday, following reports that he had engaged in two extramarital affairs: one with a customer suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese intelligence asset, and one with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. His exit added fresh pressure to a listing that was already seen as a stress test of investors’ appetite for AI.

Analysts and investors told Fortune they didn’t expect the Nvidia shock to derail the offering or touch Anthropic’s core business. The bigger risk, they said, may come later. Seaport Research Partners analyst Jay Goldberg warned that turmoil at Nvidia could bring Anthropic “much tougher questions” once it starts reporting quarterly results as a public company. Georgetown associate professor Jason Schloetzer predicted closer scrutiny of Anthropic’s ties to Nvidia and to customers associated with the chipmaker.

Anthropic’s revenue has soared thanks to strong demand from business customers, a market in which Anthropic has been especially successful. In the nine months ending Sept. 30, Anthropic generated $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. The company posted a $104 billion net loss in its most recent nine-month period, though the bulk of the red ink is because of the way it accounted for its convertible notes.

But the high share price straight out of the gates will put immense pressure on Anthropic as it seeks to justify its valuation to investors and to prove that AI tools can deliver the massive payoff Wall Street expects.

Anthropic CEO Amodei, once the VP of research at OpenAI, left to cofound Anthropic at the end of 2020, along with sister Daniela and several other OpenAI employees, when they became disillusioned with OpenAI’s approach to AI safety. Still, the company’s IPO prospectus is replete with warnings of the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence including “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

The IPO also comes amid growing public backlash to AI data centers, underscored by the results of the U.S. midterm elections. High-profile incidents of rogue AI agents, from OpenAI as well as Anthropic, have added to the unease over the technology.

Anthropic has sought to allay some of these concerns by touting its structure as a public benefit corporation, which requires the company to balance shareholder interests with its corporate mission of “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.” The structure also ensures that Amodei and the other six cofounders maintain majority voting control via multiple classes of shares with different voting rights.

The stakes of Thursday’s IPO reach well beyond one company. Anthropic has more than 400 backers, and nearly every major venture firm owns a piece of it, so the IPO is effectively a liquidity event for the AI boom itself. A strong debut and a stable stretch of trading afterward would suggest the boom has more runway. A stumble would be read as a sign the bubble is near its peak. At least one investor argued that Huang’s departure could even help Anthropic: CEO Dario Amodei had clashed with Huang over chip exports to China and over AI regulation.

Several Wall Street research firms, including Wolfe Research, Citizens, and Melius Research initiated coverage of Anthropic with buy ratings.

Beatrice Nolan is a tech reporter on Fortune’s AI team, covering artificial intelligence and emerging technologies and their impact on work, industry, and culture. #5416. More Than 20,000 Small Businesses Use His Technology. Here’s His Data-Driven Advice—And AI Shortcuts—for Capitalizing On a $1 Trillion Holiday Season.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Andrew Stern, co-founder and CEO of Quilt Software, breaks down the success strategies.

The holiday shopping season is in full swing — and it started early this year.

New data from specialized point-of-sale software company Quilt Software, which serves more than 20,000 independent retailers, from jewelers and pet stores to liquor stores and grocers, showed a 7.6% same-store sales growth spike in October year over year.

That’s in stark contrast to the Q1 through Q3 2.7% to 3.2% bump, which might largely be attributed to inflation, Quilt Software co-founder and CEO Andrew Stern tells Entrepreneur.

What’s more, customers aren’t just getting a head start; they’re also making more frequent shopping trips. Year-over-year transactions per store grew 6% in Q3 and 7.9% in October, per Quilt’s data.

This year, Small Business Saturday, which saw an estimated $18 billion in spending at independent retailers in 2025, falls on November 28, just 27 days before Christmas.

With customers opting for earlier and more frequent purchasing, independent retailers that want to make the most of the limited window need to stay on top of which items are selling in real time to remain ahead of trends and maintain inventory, Stern notes.

The CEO also cautions independent shops against attempting to compete with big-box retailers like Amazon or Walmart on price or convenience, calling it a “race to the bottom.”

Instead, Stern suggests a two-pronged approach for independent retailers: Lean into what makes them special, and use AI in a way that works for them (it won’t look like it does for mega-retailers).

“ For our small independent merchants, they opened their store for a reason,” Stern says. “They thought they were bringing something really unique that no one else had. So lean into that, because you’re probably right.”

One in five holiday shoppers plan to purchase gifts and other holiday items at small or local businesses this year, according to the National Retail Federation’s (NRF) October Holiday Consumer survey.

Shoppers planning to buy from small businesses cited reasons including supporting the community (71%), seeking unique gifts and décor (56%), championing artists through handmade purchases (37%) and finding high-quality products (33%), per the report.

It’s clear that holiday shoppers want what independent retailers have to offer — but it’s crucial that those stores put themselves on people’s radar.

“ Make sure that [customers] can see you, that you’re visible when people do their Google searches, or increasingly their ChatGPT searches,” Stern says. “Make sure that you come up because they want to find you.”

Nowadays, independent retailers must have an answer engine optimization (AEO) strategy to stay relevant and show up in search results. Earlier this month, Entrepreneur spoke with Courtney Sandora, founder of digital marketing agency Go Social, to learn more about how brands can compete in the AEO landscape.

Sandora notes that customers use LLM-powered search engines to ask specific questions, so savvy businesses should hone in on the queries they can reliably and successfully own, “seeding” stories and copy that bolster their authority.

“That storytelling extends across everything from PR to creators, even how you appear on a retailer website,” Sandora says. “Typically, on retailer websites, there’s a short description. Is the message you want to tell in that retailer website description? Consistency matters.”

It’s critical that small businesses use rapidly advancing AI technologies to their advantage.

However, that won’t look exactly like it does for major retailers, which might harness AI to manage six-month supply chains or optimize warehouse logistics, Stern says.

Instead, independent retailers should focus on taking small steps with significant impact, like using agentic solutions to outsource specific tasks they might not have time to execute to their fullest potential.

For example, the right AI tool can give shop owners the marketing support they’ve never had, unfolding in the background as they help customers at the counter. Quilt offers its retailers an AI marketing assistant that can create campaigns for customers with their own inventory.

“ This generative AI is able to create copy that’s in their voice,” Stern says, “that’s tailored to different cohorts of customers and can say, ‘Hey, come in, I think we have some products that you might be interested in. Here they are.’”

Quilt also offers an AI assistant that can help small retailers navigate unwieldy piles of inventory.

Stern points to thrift stores, which tend to rely on volunteer staff to sift through large amounts of donations quickly, as an example. Shops can snap a picture of a leather couch and receive a price estimate immediately.

The AI tool can also help them identify rare and valuable items that might otherwise go unnoticed. “ We’ve had some crazy cases like, ‘Oh, that looks like a Tiffany lamp. Look at the bottom of it and see if there’s a signature that says Tiffany. If so, do not charge $5 for that lamp,’” Stern says.

The NRF expects retail sales in November and December to grow 4.2% over 2025, for a total spending surpassing $1 trillion. That’s a massive opportunity for independent retailers that opt out of competition with big-box retailers and leverage the data to win their share.

#5415. Seattle tech vet and Sounders FC minority owner Chee Chew joins front office to lead AI push

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am

Chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a new job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI.

Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club announced Tuesday.

“His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer said in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.”

Chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation company toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment.

He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the company’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live.

Chew said his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams.

“In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.”

Chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he said. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids.

The couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry. Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others.

A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew said.

The job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he said.

Talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew said.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years. It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”

Chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help?

On the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with Anthropic’s Claude. “By the time I landed, I sent it to them and said, ‘OK, give this a try,’” he said. The club used it in an experiment to scale up performance marketing before a match.

It’s the kind of hands-on building Chew says he’s been doing a lot of lately.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years,” he said. “It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”

He recently ran an AI analysis of one player’s game, based on stats such as touches, expected goals and distance run. It pointed out strengths and areas to improve. The player was “very hungry for it,” Chew said, and asked if they could do it every game.

The club’s performance analytics group, led by data analyst Tyler Cox, was already ahead of much of the organization, and Chew said he’s helping speed up that work with AI.

The bigger challenge is getting people to change how they work, Chew said. At Zapier, he saw many companies struggle to get results from AI, with some spending “massive token budgets” without a big win. He said the answer is blending AI with traditional automation and fitting it into how people already work.

“It has to be approachable for folks,” he said. “You can’t go in and just throw everything up and start from scratch.”

The Sounders host Real Salt Lake in the wild-card round of the MLS Cup Playoffs on Thursday at Lumen Field. Asked whether AI could help figure out a win, Chew passed.

“I don’t want to get involved and interfere with our coaching staff,” he said.

#5414. ‘The whole internet screams at once’: Downdetector logged 6.4 million U.S. outage reports in a week as Microsoft, the FAA, Chase, and Apple went down

Microsoft’s email, the FAA, Chase, and Apple all went down within a week. Downdetector, the site people check when an app or a website stops working, logged 6.4 million U.S. reports in the seven days ending on Tuesday, four times a typical week’s number, and 14 million worldwide, three times its usual level. The company that runs it thinks the timing is mostly coincidence.

That puts the outage tracker at odds with the explanation taking hold in Washington, where Sen. Mark Warner has blamed organizations racing to patch software flaws that AI tools now find faster than companies can fix them. Downdetector’s data shows big outages getting rarer, and it can’t see what caused any of them. For companies watching their own update queues, the question is whether this week is a blip or the start of something.

Microsoft’s Outlook and Teams went down last week on Nov. 12 and 13, taking out email in more than 70 countries for almost 24 hours. With nearly 3.9 million U.S. reports and 7.8 million worldwide, it was Downdetector’s largest outage since Amazon Web Services went down in October 2025. Then on Friday, the FAA grounded every flight in the country in response to what it called unstable legacy equipment. Its initial investigation points to two sites, including a radio site in El Dorado, Ark., where its network contractor, L3Harris, had been installing a new router.

And on Monday, a software bug at Chase meant Chase and Wells Fargo customers couldn’t get to their money. Chase drew about 90,000 U.S. reports, roughly 165 times normal and more than twice any other U.S. bank outage this year. And on Tuesday, Apple Pay, iCloud, the App Store, and Apple Support drew about 81,000 reports as a result of what Apple said was a faulty internal update. Downdetector flagged 67 U.S. services that day, as opposed to the 16 it would get on a typical day, the broadest results of any day so far this year.

“You always wait for a bus, and then they come all at once,” Mark Giles, director of Ookla Research (Downdetector’s parent company), told Fortune. “I think this looks like a bit of a coincidence. There’s nothing really linking the outages.”

Downdetector, which collects user complaints about apps and websites, is the closest thing to a public scoreboard for these failures. Companies disclose their own outages, if at all, one at a time, and no U.S. agency publishes a running count. That’s part of what drives visitors to the site.

“We’re more connected than ever,” Giles said. “There’s these foundational points of the internet, which when something happens there, then the whole internet screams at once.”

And despite the four outages in a week, they’re becoming a rarer occurrence. Once the pandemic years are set aside, outages in Downdetector’s U.S. and U.K. data have fallen since about 2022. He said on average, Downdetector sees one large outage—which it defines as more than 50,000 U.S. reports for one company in a day—a little more than once a week. In the past year, only Christmas week and one week in June had more than this week’s four. Over the past 30 days the count is typical, because October was quiet, and Downdetector calls this week a cluster so far.

“This is a big blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he said. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite quickly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.”

Giles described a cycle he has seen in banking over the past three to four years. A company rolls out something new and spends less on making its systems resilient, and outages creep up. Then customers complain, the company invests, and outages fall. “I’m not saying that’s the case for Chase here,” he said. “A lot of these are just one-offs, maybe software problems or updates.”

The site can also overstate an outage, because it counts complaints rather than confirmed failures. Monday’s bank problems were a Chase outage, Giles said, but customers at other banks whose payments to Chase users failed reported their own banks as down. “We tend to overrepresent in some cases the actual outage,” he said. Outage news also brings more people to the site, which pushes up reports for other services.

Updates are now at the center of the explanation in Washington. Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told the Financial Times there was no sign of a cyberattack and that the outages most likely came from organizations racing to patch software. Part of it is new technology: AI tools are now finding flaws faster than companies can safely fix them, and Warner said the pressure to fix them right away is straining systems that were never designed for that speed.

On Wednesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the New York Times’ DealBook Summit that the company had already pushed at least three critical patches that day, the FT reported. Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser, whose bank reported no outages, said the volume of patches moving through the world at once is “five-, 10-fold what we’ve ever seen before.” Still, neither Microsoft nor JPMorgan Chase tied their respective outages to patching AI-found flaws.

It proves trickier for companies to stay up to speed with this new tech when there are also nefarious actors using AI. Companies are rushing because attackers have the same tools: Giles said the patch rush “has to be an increasing concern for security and IT teams,” and it “speaks to a concern that hackers with swarms of AI agents are better able to find and exploit these.”

However, none of that shows up on Downdetector’s charts. “[It’s] not something that Downdetector can pick up on, though, as a root cause,” Giles said.

Currently, Downdetector flags a service only when its reports stand out from its own normal level. It plans to build AI tools over the next year to tie related spikes together and show which company actually failed.

#5413. M&A Isn’t Just for Big Companies. Here’s How Startups Can Do It With No Cash.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Most entrepreneurs don’t realize there is another way to grow their business: through mergers and acquistions.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Most startups are so focused on building stand-alone businesses through traditional sales and marketing that they overlook other ways to grow, such as mergers and acquisitions (M&A).  They simply have not been trained on the topic and don’t know that, for some businesses, it can be a faster, more effective way to scale.

This article will provide a high-level tutorial on what M&A is, why you should consider it, and how to negotiate deals that can get to the finish line, even if you are not large enough to be bankable.

A merger is a combination of the shareholders of two businesses into one. A merger typically involves combining the management teams and operations into one.  An acquisition is exactly what it sounds like: your business is acquiring a company (or being acquired by one), with the acquiring team retaining 100% control over all key decisions in the new company. The acquired company’s operations will be integrated into the new company, however the acquiring company sees fit, as the buying company will control all decisions post-transaction. So, you will need to decide which scenario will work best for your needs.

M&A has many advantages, the key ones being speed, economies of scale and removing competition. Since the acquired business is already up and running and, hopefully, producing cash flow, it offers a much faster path to growth. For example, if a restaurant chain was trying to grow from 1 to 2 locations, it would take them over a year to find a site and build it out. But through M&A, that second location is already built and is immediately generating revenues today.

Furthermore, when you combine two businesses, you can eliminate duplicative costs and achieve economies of scale. For example, you don’t need two executive teams, two insurance policies, two marketing agencies, two accounting firms, etc. By removing these duplicative costs, the combined business will end up with a more profitable bottom-line margin, where hopefully 1+1=3.

As for the competitive advantages, by buying a competitor in the market, that will increase your market share and have you competing against one less competitor (which may help your pricing).  As an example, in my hometown of Cary, NC, one entrepreneur acquired and rolled up around 20 competing Mexican restaurants, with the goal of ensuring that no matter which Mexican restaurant you ate at, he was getting the sale, with nearly 100% market share.

That all said, things can go wrong with M&A.  Be sure to read my prior article on the potential pitfalls with M&A, so you don’t get into any trouble here, and you go into this M&A direction “eyes wide open” to prepare for potential hurdles that may arise in the future.

Depending on the size of the transaction, M&A can be funded either from the buyer’s cash account, or by raising additional capital from investors, or with no cash at all via an exchange of equity between the two businesses. Since most start-ups don’t generate much profit, it is unlikely they will be bankable. So, this last path of exchanging equity makes it possible for companies of any size to pursue M&A without any financing required at all.

The key thing about M&A is that it does not necessarily need to be dependent on economic or financial market conditions. Even if third-party investors have paused new investments during a down market, nothing prevents two businesses from merging in a cashless transaction at any time. So, if you can’t raise capital for your stand-alone restaurant chain growth, you can still be growing using M&A as the driver of that growth.

For established businesses generating revenue and profits, it is pretty easy to value those companies using historical revenue or profit multiples from past transactions in your industry. For example, if most small restaurants are sold at 3x EBITDA, it is reasonable to assume your small restaurant can be valued at 3x EBITDA. A good business broker can advise you on what the normal multipliers will be for the size of your company’s revenues, profits, and growth rate.

If you don’t have revenues or profits to value, then you need to use another metric.  Maybe that is cash invested in the business, or asset value, or the assets themselves.  For example, if one real estate owner has 4 locations and another real estate owner has 2 locations, then perhaps those two businesses could be combined into one business where the 4-location business owned 67% and the 2-location business owned 33% of the new company.

Let’s say two self-storage businesses are exploring a merger. One does $6MM in revenue, $1MM in profit, and has 300,000 square feet of buildings (all mature, open for many years). The other has $2MM in revenue, $0 in profit today (but will end up at $1MM after they fully rent out their space) and also has 300,000 square feet of buildings (but they are brand new still ramping up clients and revenues).

How do you value this? On revenues, it would be 80/20. On profits, it would be 100/0, and on square footage it would be 50/50. If I were the buyer, I would start the ownership at 75/25, and if the smaller business successfully increases its client base per its plan, it can earn its way up to 50/50 through an earn-out. That seems to be the fairest for all parties; that should get both parties to the finish line.

I am a former investment banker on Wall Street, and M&A is incorporated into my DNA. It is something I am comfortable with, as I have bought and sold many companies over my entrepreneurial career. But if you are a first-timer here, I know it can be “scary.”  But it doesn’t need to be. Surround yourself with smart M&A advisors who have “been there and done that,” both in terms of negotiating M&A and integrating companies post M&A, and everything should turn out just fine.

And hopefully your shareholders will thank you for materially accelerating your growth and helping them to expand their valuation multipliers as a bigger company. Good luck!

Most startups are so focused on building stand-alone businesses through traditional sales and marketing that they overlook other ways to grow, such as mergers and acquisitions (M&A).  They simply have not been trained on the topic and don’t know that, for some businesses, it can be a faster, more effective way to scale.

This article will provide a high-level tutorial on what M&A is, why you should consider it, and how to negotiate deals that can get to the finish line, even if you are not large enough to be bankable.

A merger is a combination of the shareholders of two businesses into one. A merger typically involves combining the management teams and operations into one.  An acquisition is exactly what it sounds like: your business is acquiring a company (or being acquired by one), with the acquiring team retaining 100% control over all key decisions in the new company. The acquired company’s operations will be integrated into the new company, however the acquiring company sees fit, as the buying company will control all decisions post-transaction. So, you will need to decide which scenario will work best for your needs.

#5412. Seattle police unleash dog-like robot whose best trick is bomb dispoal

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:43 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:43 am

Seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech. Now they’ve got a piece of tech that looks like a dog.

It’s a big upgrade for the squad, which has handled more than 600 calls so far this year. SPD’s main bomb robot is nearly 20 years old, weighs more than 100 pounds and rolls on tracks, and it can only be hauled around in the squad’s mobile workshop. Spot weighs under 100 pounds, climbs stairs and rides in a pickup truck that bomb techs drive daily.

The robot will only be used for explosive threats in the city and at the port, and it won’t carry a weapon. SPD said a weapon would go against Boston Dynamics’ rules for its robots. Spot’s 360-degree camera sends an encrypted live feed to the operator but doesn’t record or use facial recognition.

The only thing the robot does on its own is open a door, after an operator lines it up. As one bomb technician put it in SPD’s post, Spot will “be as dumb in 10 years as it is today.”

It’s not the first time SPD has turned to a four-legged partner for tech-related work.

Nala, an electronic storage detection K9 — profiled by GeekWire in 2024 — is trained to smell a chemical compound used in making electronics. The Labrador retriever helps SPD’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force find hidden phones, hard drives and micro SD cards during warrant searches. Her handler, Det. Daljit Gill, told GeekWire at the time that Nala turns up a device human searchers missed about 30% of the time.

Boston Dynamics, maker of backflipping Atlas humanoids and other viral-video robots, first unveiled the robodog in 2015. A smaller, all-electric version followed a year later.

The machines have long stirred dystopian unease. A 2017 “Black Mirror” episode featured killer robot dogs inspired by the company’s designs. Still, Spot has turned up in friendlier settings: then-Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos walked one at the company’s MARS conference in 2018 — a scene described by GeekWire’s Alan Boyle as featuring the “anxiety-inducing” robot.

Police departments have embraced the robots, too. More than 60 bomb squads and SWAT teams in the U.S. and Canada use Spot, Bloomberg reported last year, including a regional bomb unit in Portland. New York police returned one in 2021 after public backlash, then brought the robots back two years later.

Back in Seattle, SPD’s bomb technicians see more potential uses down the road, according to the department’s post, including communicating and observing from a distance as part of de-escalation. For now, Spot’s job is limited to explosives.

And the robot won’t be getting a new name, SPD said, “because it is not a toy, or a dog, even though it kind of looks like both.”

#5411. Anthropic’s IPO nets Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley $113 million apiece in fees, eclipsing their SpaceX paydays

Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO on Thursday delivered one of Wall Street’s largest underwriting paydays in history, with the banks behind the listing raking in at least $550 million in fees, eclipsing the $500 million that was earned from Elon Musk–led SpaceX’s debut in June.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, the lead underwriters on the deal, each garnered fees of $113 million, according to Anthropic’s prospectus and confirmed by a source familiar with the matter. That’s because they both took on underwriting commitments of 20.5% of the $81.3 billion IPO. It’s also more than the roughly $100 million Goldman and Morgan Stanley each raked in from fees on the SpaceX deal over the summer.

JPMorgan and Citigroup each agreed to underwrite 10% of the Claude maker’s offering, putting their estimated fees at roughly $55 million apiece if allocated in proportion to their commitments. Bank of America, which committed to underwriting 3%, would receive an estimated $16.5 million in fees.

The last IPO to generate more than Anthropic’s in underwriting commissions was Visa’s 2008 debut, which delivered a $550.2 million fee pool. Anthropic could surpass that figure if underwriters exercise the offering’s over-allotment option, which allows banks to sell up to 15% more shares than initially planned.

Anthropic shares, trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, surged 17% in their Thursday debut, giving the company a fully diluted market capitalization of $1.27 trillion at the close. The $81.3 billion offering was the largest IPO in history by deal size.

Anthropic’s listing generated roughly 30 to 40 times the commissions of a typical IPO owing to its massive size, according to Matt Kennedy, senior IPO market strategist at Renaissance Capital. “By deal count, 2026 wasn’t the blowout year many were hoping for,” Kennedy said in a statement to Fortune. “So, mega IPOs like Anthropic have done a lot of the heavy lifting to make this a standout year for investment banks.”

Morgan Chittum is a reporter at Fortune covering finance.

#5410. I’ve Been a CFO, a CPA, a Franchisee and a CEO — Here Are the Credentials That Get You Hired Now

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

I’ve worked in a variety of roles, but credentials follow you from job to job. Check out the credentials that get you hired.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’ve had a lot of impressive titles. But titles describe what you’ve already done. In today’s AI-driven market, decision-makers want proof of how you think, who will vouch for you and what you’ll do next.

Early in my career, I believed my credentials did the talking. I became a CPA with a global Big 6 firm and then worked my way into CFO and CEO roles. Later, I became a franchise business owner and learned more about grit, determination and humility than I had in the previous 20 years combined.

Each of those titles opened a door at one point. None of them, on their own, would get me hired today.

I see this play out every week. As a franchise consultant, I spend most of my time with directors, vice presidents and CXOs, many of them facing a restructuring. Their resumes are stacked. Yet the ones who land on their feet fastest, whether that means a new role, a board seat or a franchise award, rarely win on titles. They win on a different set of credentials, and some of those can be built in months, not decades.

A title says you held a job. A point of view shows how you thought while you held it. When I was a CFO at a real estate developer, my work was buried in spreadsheets and board meetings. Nobody outside the building knew how I approached the cash crunch during the Great Recession or difficult acquisitions.

When I started my national consulting firm, I had no choice but to put my thinking in public. I began posting regularly on LinkedIn about franchise ownership, career transitions and the lessons learned as a franchisee. That consistency, more than any credential on my profile, is why strangers started calling. More than 20,000 people now follow me, and many executives tell me they read my posts long before reaching out to me.

Pick two or three topics where your experience gives you a unique viewpoint and write about them every week. You aren’t building an audience for its own sake. You’re creating a searchable record of your expertise.

Earlier in my career, my network was mostly people I’d worked with directly. That works until you’re in transition or need help outside your industry, which is exactly when most people need it. I learned this through three reorganizations. Three of the four companies I worked for over 26 years no longer exist. So I started nurturing my network long before I needed it.

Franchisors taught me this lesson from the other side of the table. When candidates apply to buy a franchise, the franchisor evaluates them just as carefully as the candidate evaluates the brand. The candidates who move through smoothly are the ones other people will vouch for — former colleagues, bankers and existing owners in the system.

This is where LinkedIn Premium has earned a spot in my toolkit. I use Sales Navigator to find and follow the executives I serve and to identify mutual connections who could make a warm introduction. I don’t use it to blast messages. I use it to find a valued connection who can vouch for me, and then I ask that person directly.

Think of 25 people who will take your call tomorrow. If fewer than half of them work outside your current company, start widening the circle now, while you don’t need favors. And never send a message that doesn’t offer the other person something of value.

This credential surprises executives the most. As a CEO, I had people build the model, chase the receivables and fix the website. As a fitness franchise owner, I was the OEO — the Only Executive Officer — and I tell my candidates to expect the same.

Hiring managers and franchisors are asking a version of the same question: Will this person roll up their sleeves and do the work, not just direct it? You answer that with evidence. Maybe you’ve run a side project, advised a small business or built your own department or systems.

Today I run a national practice largely on my own. The tools I pay for earn their keep only because they let one person do the work a small team used to do.

Identify one hands-on accomplishment from the past two years that didn’t depend on a team and make it visible.

The fastest way to look obsolete is to describe how things were done a decade ago. The old adage “if it isn’t broken, don’t fix it” doesn’t apply today. The executives I see winning today are adaptable. One of my candidates just bought a second franchise in a different industry because she has an insatiable appetite for learning.

After more than 30 years in business, I’m still learning. I’m working on a second edition of my book because some of my original advice needs updating. Admitting that isn’t a weakness. It tells people I’m paying attention.

Be ready to explain, in two sentences, something you’ve learned in the past six months and how you’ve applied it. I’m not dismissing traditional credentials. My CPA background is the reason candidates trust me to walk them through financing options. My years as a CFO and CEO gave me pattern recognition no course could teach.

But titles are only a starting point. They tell people what you’ve done. The four points above tell them what you’ll do next.

Start this week. Write one post that shares a real lesson from your career. Reach out to three people outside your company. Add something to your profile that you built, not just something you managed. Those small moves compound faster than you’d expect.

If you want a head start, LinkedIn’s Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to find the ones that fit the way you work.

I’ve had a lot of impressive titles. But titles describe what you’ve already done. In today’s AI-driven market, decision-makers want proof of how you think, who will vouch for you and what you’ll do next.

Early in my career, I believed my credentials did the talking. I became a CPA with a global Big 6 firm and then worked my way into CFO and CEO roles. Later, I became a franchise business owner and learned more about grit, determination and humility than I had in the previous 20 years combined.

Each of those titles opened a door at one point. None of them, on their own, would get me hired today.

#5409. Microsoft jabs at OpenAI and Anthropic, touting cheaper, customizable AI models of its own

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:57 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:33 pm

Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the company’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor.

“Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” said Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the company’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.

Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he said.

The full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou said.

Microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude.

For “advanced” users of each company’s agent tools, it showed $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat.

The numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude.

Partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The company is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects.

The companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks.

The product has less than a tenth as many weekly users as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report said.

New MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella announced that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry.

The lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft says it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose.

Microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it says matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other new models cover image editing, live speech and transcription.

The other new business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Company consulting arm. AT&T used an earlier version of the program, Custom Models, to build a MAI model for 5G network analytics.

It’s the latest step in Microsoft’s push for what Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called “long term self-sufficiency,” which started with seven homegrown models at Build in June.

Keeping costs in check: The cost theme ran through the keynote. In a demo, Althoff showed Copilot building a keynote outline, a slide deck and a customer tracker for a retail conference, plus an agent he named Amelia to keep the work going.

The cost of his two-hour Sunday session: about 10,000 credits, or roughly $100. Althoff presented that as a bargain compared with the staff time it would have taken: “my team hits the ground running for NRF without me bothering them,” he said.

Microsoft is also selling tools to keep that bill in check. A new Agent 365 Business Analytics feature shows business leaders what’s driving their AI spending and what they’re getting for it, and a companion Cost Management tool lets IT set spending policies and get alerts. Microsoft cited a McKinsey survey in which 93% of respondents reported exceeding their AI budgets.

In another notable announcement, Microsoft and Salesforce unveiled “Copilotforce,” bringing Salesforce customer data and actions into Copilot, Teams and Fabric. The Copilot plugin is available in preview.

Earlier, Nadella opened the keynote by addressing last week’s global Outlook outage.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5408. Sound Ventures turned $435 million into a $7 billion Anthropic stake. Ashton Kutcher left months before the IPO

When Anthropic, the company behind the AI assistant Claude and a suite of large language models and coding tools, went public this morning, the numbers were eye-popping. The San Francisco AI firm raised about $81.3 billion, the most money ever raised in an initial public offering, and began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

Anthropic priced its shares at $83, above its expected range of $70 to $78. They opened at $111.50 and had cooled to around $98 by mid-afternoon, per Yahoo Finance.

That’s a windfall for Anthropic’s earliest backers, and one of them has a Hollywood pedigree. Sound Ventures, the venture capital firm cofounded in 2015 by talent manager Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, owns roughly 0.5% of Anthropic, a stake worth about $7 billion, according to Bloomberg.

For context, the previous record belonged to SpaceX’s June launch, which raised $75 billion. Third, distantly, is South Korean memory-chip maker SK Hynix, which raised $26.5 billion in a U.S. listing in July, per Renaissance Capital.

At its IPO price, Anthropic was valued at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, nearly on par with Meta Platforms and Tesla, worth about $1.58 trillion and $1.52 trillion, respectively, per recent data from The Motley Fool. (SpaceX still holds the record for the richest IPO valuation, at $1.77 trillion, which is why Anthropic’s lower-than-expected pricing drew scrutiny last week.)

That valuation exceeds the GDP of many industrialized nations, including Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and Switzerland, per Worldometer. Anthropic was founded in 2021.

Sound Ventures first invested in 2023, putting $35 million into Anthropic’s Series C round, TechCrunch reported. It kept writing checks in later rounds and has invested about $435 million in total, per Bloomberg. That same spring, the firm launched a $240 million fund dedicated to AI, with stakes in both Anthropic and OpenAI.

Bloomberg’s $7 billion figure was based on Anthropic’s $1.4 trillion target valuation, so at Thursday’s trading prices the stake is worth more.

How much of that belongs to Kutcher hasn’t been disclosed; most of the stake belongs to the fund’s investors. And the former That ’70s Show star is no longer running the firm. He stepped away from Sound Ventures this year to start a new venture firm with Morgan Beller focused on AI infrastructure, energy, and deep tech, the Wall Street Journal reported in July. He remains an advisor to Sound.

The biggest individual winners are Anthropic’s seven cofounders, including CEO Dario Amodei and president Daniela Amodei. Together they hold about 1.69 billion shares, or roughly 10% of the company, according to its S-1, as Fortune reported last month.

At the $83 IPO price, each cofounder’s stake was worth roughly $19 billion to $20 billion. At Thursday afternoon’s price of around $98, each is worth roughly $23 billion to $24 billion. The cofounders have pledged to give away most of their wealth.

Still, investors big and small have reason to stay circumspect, cautions Jay Ritter, an emeritus professor at the University of Florida’s Warrington College of Business who studies IPOs.

“SpaceX and Anthropic are in a league of their own, with valuations at the time of the IPO approximately 10 times bigger than any prior U.S. company going public,” Ritter said.

He offered a historical yardstick. “United Parcel Service (UPS), the prior record holder, went public in 1999 at a valuation, in 2026 dollars, of $162 billion at the end of the first day. It jumped by 36.25% on its first day of trading, but then declined by 10% in the next six months,” Ritter told Fortune. “UPS was 92 years old at the time of its IPO, with annual revenue of $26.3 billion. On an inflation-adjusted basis, Anthropic’s $35.2 billion trailing 12-month revenue is almost that high less than six years after its founding.”

That doesn’t promise a smooth ride. “As with SpaceX, for which the stock price varied by over $27 on its first day of trading and by over $120 since going public in June, with a low of $104.83 and high of $225.64, Anthropic’s stock will be volatile,” Ritter said.

#5407. If Your Business Can’t Run Without You, You Have a Bigger Problem Than You Think

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Being indispensable might feel like success, but it can quietly limit your company’s growth.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

There’s a particular kind of exhaustion that comes with running a business. You can hire talented people, build a capable team and invest in better systems, yet somehow still find yourself answering questions that shouldn’t require your involvement.

A client needs an update. Someone needs approval. A project hits a roadblock. An employee wants reassurance before making a decision. Individually, none of these requests seems unreasonable. But when they all come to you, every single day, you eventually become the reason things aren’t moving faster.

I’ve spent much of my career managing complex projects and leading teams. I’ve also experienced the challenges that come with building a business.

One lesson I’ve learned is that being needed and being effective are not always the same thing. And for entrepreneurs, recognizing that difference can change how a company grows.

In the beginning, founders have to do almost everything.

You win the business, manage customers, handle finances and solve problems because there isn’t anyone else. You know where everything stands. You remember the commitments you’ve made. You understand why certain decisions were taken.

That knowledge becomes an advantage. But as your company grows, it can also become a problem.

Employees get accustomed to asking you because you know the answer. Customers prefer speaking directly with you because you’ve always been available. And gradually, even decisions that should be made elsewhere find their way back to your desk.

The strange part is that this can feel rewarding. Being the person everyone needs reinforces the belief that you’re essential to the company’s success.

But ask yourself something uncomfortable: If the business requires your involvement in nearly every decision, have you actually built an organization, or have you simply created a more demanding job?

I’ve seen business owners respond to overwhelming workloads by hiring additional employees. Sometimes that’s exactly what the business needs. But adding people doesn’t automatically reduce the founder’s workload.

If nobody has the authority to make decisions, additional employees may simply create additional questions. I previously explored this problem in an Entrepreneur article about examining workflows before hiring.

The underlying issue is often less about headcount and more about how work moves through an organization.

Consider a project manager who is responsible for delivering a client project but needs the founder’s approval for every minor adjustment. Technically, the project has been delegated. In reality, the founder is still managing it.

The project manager has responsibility without sufficient authority, and that creates frustration on both sides. Delegation only works when people know which decisions they can make independently, what boundaries apply and when something genuinely needs to be escalated.

This is the part of leadership that requires some self-reflection. It’s easy to complain that employees keep asking questions. It’s harder to recognize that our own behavior may have encouraged it.

If a manager makes a reasonable decision and we immediately reverse it, we’re teaching that person to seek approval next time. If we insist on reviewing every email, presentation and customer response, we’re communicating that we don’t trust others to exercise judgment. And if we consistently step in to solve problems before employees have a chance to work through them, we’re reinforcing the very dependency we want to eliminate.

I’ve learned that people need room to make decisions, including decisions that may not be exactly the ones I would have made. That doesn’t mean lowering standards. It means being clear about the result you expect while allowing capable employees to determine how to achieve it.

A team doesn’t become independent because the founder announces that everyone should take more ownership. Independence develops when people are genuinely given the opportunity to exercise it.

One aspect of running a business that doesn’t receive enough attention is the mental burden of keeping everything moving.

You may delegate the preparation of a report, but still be the person remembering when it’s due. You may assign someone to manage a client, but still feel responsible for anticipating every issue that could arise. You may have a team handling operations while remaining the person mentally tracking every unresolved problem.

The work has been distributed, but the responsibility hasn’t. This distinction reminds me of the concept of the mental load, often discussed in the context of family responsibilities and working mothers.

The same principle applies to leadership. There’s a difference between completing a task and being responsible for remembering, organizing and following through on everything associated with it.

If a founder continues carrying all of that responsibility, delegation may provide temporary relief without changing the underlying problem. True ownership means someone else is accountable for both the task and the outcome.

I would encourage entrepreneurs to run a simple experiment.

Choose five business days when you deliberately step away from routine operational decisions. You don’t need to disappear completely. Remain available for genuine emergencies and decisions involving significant financial, legal or reputational risk. But resist the temptation to intervene in every ordinary problem.

Before the experiment begins, clarify who owns each function and what decisions they can make. Then pay attention to what happens.

Do projects continue moving? Can customers get answers? Are managers comfortable making decisions? Where does work stall? More importantly, why?

Perhaps employees lack access to information. Maybe approval limits are unclear. Or perhaps certain processes exist only in your head. Those are the issues worth fixing.

When the five days are over, review the decisions your team handled successfully alongside the problems they encountered.

Don’t use the exercise to identify who failed. Use it to understand where the business remains unnecessarily dependent on you.

Entrepreneurs often associate growth with more customers, higher revenue and larger teams. Those are important measures.

But I would add another: How much can your business accomplish without requiring the founder to supervise every detail?

This doesn’t mean becoming disconnected from your company. A founder should remain closely involved in strategy, major relationships and decisions that shape the future of the business. But there’s a difference between leading an organization and personally keeping every part of it functioning.

As you plan the next stage of growth, look beyond what your business is accomplishing and examine how it’s accomplishing it.

Are you developing leaders who can make sound decisions? Have you created processes that survive someone’s absence? Can your team solve problems without waiting for you? If not, you may have a business that’s growing in size without growing in capability.

Here’s the challenge I’d leave every entrepreneur with: Take five working days away from routine decisions and see what breaks.

Whatever stops working deserves your attention when you return. Because the goal of building a business shouldn’t be to make yourself indispensable forever. It should be to build something strong enough that you don’t have to be.

There’s a particular kind of exhaustion that comes with running a business. You can hire talented people, build a capable team and invest in better systems, yet somehow still find yourself answering questions that shouldn’t require your involvement.

A client needs an update. Someone needs approval. A project hits a roadblock. An employee wants reassurance before making a decision. Individually, none of these requests seems unreasonable. But when they all come to you, every single day, you eventually become the reason things aren’t moving faster.

I’ve spent much of my career managing complex projects and leading teams. I’ve also experienced the challenges that come with building a business.

#5406. Seattle startup Aarden raises $8M to help landowners navigate the AI and energy building boom

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 1:36 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 2:36 pm

Seattle startup Aarden AI on Tuesday announced $8 million in new funding to grow its team and accelerate its work helping landowners evaluate potential uses for their properties and navigate deals with developers building data centers, clean energy projects, housing and other developments.

Founded last year, the company says its clients collectively own or manage approximately 14 million acres worldwide — nearly the land area of West Virginia. Aarden’s team said it has evaluated more than $500 million worth of land deals.

“But land markets remain opaque and manual with far too much friction. Finding the right site, and building trust with the right partners quickly, is more important than ever for our economy and our environment,” founder and CEO Danan Margason said in a statement.

The company combines data on hundreds of land attributes with historical market data and proprietary models to assess development suitability, valuation trends, ownership and community sentiment. Its tools and services also help developers identify sites and connect with landowners.

Aarden generates revenue through subscriptions to its technology, which includes AI-native data, models and investment tools, and through fees for services tied to specific deals or analyses.

The new round brings Aarden’s total funding to $12 million. Overture Ventures led the round, with participation from Madrona and Propeller Ventures. The startup previously raised $4 million in a round led by Planeteer in June 2025. The company has 13 employees and plans to nearly double in size over the next 12 months.

Margason said he launched the business on the premise that while there have long been tools to support developers, landowners have been largely on their own to evaluate and optimize deals so they’re not taken advantage of or end up partnering with untrustworthy organizations.

One customer, timberland investment manager Resource Management Service, uses Aarden to evaluate whether tracts are best suited for continued timber production, conservation, solar development or other uses.

“Diligence that used to take months now produces investment-grade answers we can act on, and that is shaping how we manage value across our portfolio,” said Alex Hinson, president and CEO of Resource Management Service.

Other companies offering property research and analysis tools include Acres, which provides land data, valuations and due diligence tools, and Land id, which offers property insights and mapping tools.

Ben Eidelson, a partner at Stepchange Ventures, which participated in the startup’s first funding round, said the company is already having an impact.

“We now have the capability to make smarter decisions about land, optimizing for the outcomes that matter from conservation to the local economy,” Eidelson said on LinkedIn.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5405. China’s Greater Bay Area was built to rival Silicon Valley. Nearly a decade on, is it finally living up to the hype?

Watch the sunset from Macau, China’s gambling capital, and you’ll see the sun drop behind a cluster of gleaming skyscrapers on an island across a narrow strait.

As recently as 2009, Hengqin—an island in the mainland Chinese city of Zhuhai, just across from Macau—was home to oyster farmers and fishermen. Today the island, three times Macau’s size, is home to an “In-Depth Cooperation Zone,” a development initiative run by Guangdong province and the Macau Special Administrative Region to help the latter diversify its economy away from gambling by tapping mainland talent and manufacturing capacity.

But Hengqin’s multilane highways, striking architecture, and manicured parks haven’t yet brought people with them. In 2009, authorities hoped Hengqin would have 280,000 residents by 2020; by the end of 2025, it had just 50,000.

Hengqin is one test of a much larger integration project: the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macau Greater Bay Area (GBA), which comprises nine cities around the Pearl River Delta in Guangdong province, including Shenzhen, Zhuhai, and Guangzhou, plus the Hong Kong and Macau special administrative regions. Can the GBA turn connectivity and deeper integration into growth?

The GBA spans three legal systems, currencies, and customs territories. With 88 million people, the region has a larger population than Germany or Turkey; with a GDP of $2.1 trillion, its economy approaches Canada’s in size. Connecting the region’s capital, startups, and manufacturing could create a world-class innovation ecosystem.

At least, that’s how the argument goes. Beijing has chased the idea of the GBA for around a decade, but the benefits of integration have only recently begun to emerge. The GBA is real, but it remains a Hong Kong–Shenzhen story for now, pairing the former’s financial heft with the latter’s hardware and software prowess. The next question is whether the other cities will get to join in.

The Pearl River Delta has been one of China’s core economic engines for over four decades, since the country designated Shenzhen, a border market town near the then–British colony of Hong Kong, as a business-friendly “special economic zone.”

That decision helped grow this part of southern China into an economic powerhouse: Hong Kong’s financial sector surged as China opened up; Shenzhen attracted founders from across the country; and surrounding cities like Dongguan and Foshan provided manufacturing scale to make the region the “world’s factory.”

“There are very few Chinese cities where the idea of ‘build it and they will come’ has not worked out.”

The GBA, formalized in 2017, wants to double down on those ingredients. “The original idea was to compete with the [U.S.] Bay Area. That’s exactly why the name is the Greater Bay Area,” says Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for Asia-Pacific at Natixis.

“The development of the GBA does not seek to make cities in the GBA identical, or flatten their distinctive edges, but rather aims for interoperability and complementarity across different cities and systems,” says Pamela Lam, Hong Kong’s commissioner for the development of the Greater Bay Area. The goal is to build “a complete innovation and industrial ecosystem” to enable a “high-value-adding supply chain that links the entire pipeline from lab to factory.”

Connective infrastructure is a key policy focus. Hundreds of kilometers of railway lines and projects such as the Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macau Bridge, the world’s longest bridge-and-tunnel sea crossing costing an estimated $20 billion, have been built between cities. The goal is to create a “one-hour living circle”—bringing travel time between major GBA cities to within an hour—to foster collaboration.

“The Greater Bay Area and the U.S. Bay Area are running different operating systems,” says Mehran Gul, author of The New Geography of Innovation. “The U.S. Bay Area is more organic … It almost happened by accident.” In the GBA, he says, “the division of labor has been central to making it happen.”

This greater connectivity of capital, R&D, talent, and manufacturing may already be boosting innovation. The Global Innovation Index, published by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), ranked Shenzhen–Hong Kong–Guangzhou as the world’s leading innovation cluster in both 2025 and 2026. The GBA’s nine mainland cities filed more than a third of China’s international patent applications in 2025, according to state media; the region also accounts for a fifth of the country’s unicorn startups.

“Ten years ago, you could still make the argument that the Chinese tech industry is a mirror image of the U.S. that lags by about five or six years,” Gul says. “But China’s tech industry is now driven a lot more by fundamental innovation. The fact that Chinese companies have made that transition means that those linkages have been made. The GBA was a big part of that.”

Economic data is painting a less positive picture. Guangdong has grown more slowly than the national average every year from 2021 to 2025. “Growth-wise, before COVID, the GBA was excelling compared to the rest of China. Not anymore,” Garcia-Herrero says, adding that China’s property market slump and youth unemployment weigh particularly heavily on Guangdong, the latter exacerbated by increased AI-powered industrial automation.

Growth within the region is lopsided, too. “A failing of the GBA is that the increase in productivity and value creation is not being spread out that widely,” says Jerry Patchell, associate professor emeritus at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and author of a book on the region. “Shenzhen and Hong Kong are pulling away from the pack. Guangzhou’s not too far behind, but a lot of the other cities are not progressing at the same rate. The absolute differences in per capita income between them are significant.” (Hong Kong’s per capita GDP is more than five times Zhaoqing’s, the poorest city in the GBA; Shenzhen’s is three times.)

Nor is Hong Kong’s financial heft favoring its neighbors. “Specific measures to treat the Greater Bay Area preferentially aren’t really there. I think the key point would be for Hong Kong to financially feed Guangdong. But the reality is that Hong Kong is feeding the whole mainland,” Garcia-Herrero adds.

Still, there are early signs that growth may be recovering. In the first three quarters of 2026, Guangdong’s economy grew 4.6%—matching the national growth rate for the first time since the third quarter of 2021, according to its provincial statistics bureau.

The growth in demand for AI infrastructure, as well as robotics, autonomous vehicles, and other applications of physical AI, is “bringing important new growth impetus” to the GBA, says Stephanie Gao, a professor of practice at City University of Hong Kong, with the region gaining an edge from its “tight integration of hardware design, component supply, and software algorithm iteration.”

Gul credits that edge to the speed with which companies iterate on the products they make, “measured in days rather than months.”

Elwin Ho, a Macau native and cofounder and CEO of Pachira, a speech-recognition AI company headquartered in Hengqin, sees the same pattern. “I just visited the [U.S.] Bay Area a couple of weeks ago. I saw a lot of companies that [build] their software and algorithms in the Bay Area, but for the hardware they go to Shenzhen.”

He is bullish on Hengqin, too: “It just needs a little bit more time; the area will have a very good future.”

Gul, too, thinks the region’s underutilized spaces will get their residents and businesses in the years to come: “There are very few Chinese cities where the idea of ‘Build it and they will come’ has not worked out.”

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027: Asia issue of Fortune.
